docs.title: Classical Planning
docs.text: TL;DR: Classical planning is the formal problem of finding a sequence of actions that transforms a known initial state into a goal state — and in 2025, frontier LLMs have begun generating heuristics that outperform hand-crafted C++ solvers, making this the most contested boundary between symbolic AI and neural methods.

docs.title: For your reader type
docs.text: I am... What you get Go to MS/applied practitioner A working hybrid neuro-symbolic planner you can run in Colab today Key algorithms → MVB Curious generalist The story of how a 70-year-old AI paradigm just had its most dramatic year What it is → Why it matters Math/theory student The formal STRIPS model, heuristic admissibility, and the h-max derivation Core concepts → Mathematical foundations Researcher / frontier LLM-generated heuristics, IPC 2025 results, and the optimality gap problem Current SotA → What's happening now

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Here is the plot twist nobody in AI expected: in 2023, frontier language models scored absolute zero on basic planning benchmarks. Researchers at Apple published a paper titled "Can LLMs Really Reason and Plan?" and the answer, empirically, was no — GPT-4 failed tasks that a first-year AI student could solve by hand. The consensus hardened: planning requires symbolic rigor that neural networks fundamentally cannot provide. Then 2025 arrived. Gemini 2.5 Pro entered the International Planning Competition and, on several benchmark domains, outperformed state-of-the-art classical planners that had been tuned by domain experts over decades. The field has not recovered its consensus since.

Classical planning, at its core, is the problem of finding a sequence of actions to get from where you are to where you want to be, given a complete and deterministic model of the world. The formalism that made this tractable — STRIPS, developed at SRI in 1971 — represents the world as a set of logical propositions, actions as precondition-effect pairs, and planning as a search through the space of reachable states. This is not a toy abstraction: the same formal structure underlies robot manipulation pipelines, logistics optimization at FedEx, and the action-selection layer in autonomous agents. What makes it hard is combinatorial explosion — a domain with 20 binary propositions has over a million possible states, and real logistics problems have billions.

The reason classical planning survived the deep learning era is that it offers something neural networks historically could not: guarantees. A classical planner can certify that a plan is optimal (shortest possible), or that no plan exists, or that every action in the sequence is valid given the world model. These properties matter enormously in safety-critical settings. What is changing now is not the symbolic engine — the search algorithms and formal semantics are as rigorous as ever — but the heuristic guidance that tells the search where to look first. LLMs have turned out to be surprisingly good at generating that guidance, which is why the field is in the middle of a genuine paradigm shift.

docs.title: Why it matters at the frontier
docs.text:
The frontier labs — Google DeepMind, Meta FAIR, and several academic groups — are investing heavily in classical planning not because they want to build better logistics schedulers, but because planning is the missing piece in autonomous agent architectures. A language model that can write code, browse the web, and call APIs is not an agent unless it can sequence those capabilities coherently toward a goal. The dominant approach in 2024 was to prompt LLMs to generate plans directly, but this produces plans that are syntactically plausible and semantically wrong — the model hallucinates preconditions, skips steps, and cannot detect when a plan has failed. Classical planning provides the verification layer: a symbolic executor that checks every action against the world model before committing to it.

The deeper reason this matters is the optimality question. Satisficing planning — finding any valid plan — is tractable for modern systems, but optimal planning — finding the shortest valid plan — remains PSPACE-hard in general, and no LLM has demonstrated reliable optimality on non-trivial domains. This gap is not academic. In drug synthesis planning, the difference between a 12-step and an 8-step route is the difference between a viable and an unviable manufacturing process. In robotic manipulation, suboptimal plans accumulate error. The open question driving current research is whether the neuro-symbolic combination can close this gap, or whether optimality will always require pure symbolic search.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
• State space — the set of all possible world configurations, represented as assignments of truth values to a finite set of propositions; planning is search over this space.
  • STRIPS representation — a formalism where each action has a precondition list (propositions that must be true), an add list (propositions made true), and a delete list (propositions made false); the foundation of nearly all classical planning languages.
  • PDDL (Planning Domain Definition Language) — the standard file format for specifying planning problems, separating the domain (action schemas) from the problem instance (initial state and goal); used in all International Planning Competitions.
  • Heuristic function — a function \(h(s)\) estimating the cost from state \(s\) to the goal; the quality of this estimate determines whether search is tractable or exponential.
  • Admissibility — a heuristic is admissible if it never overestimates the true cost to the goal; admissible heuristics guarantee that A* finds an optimal plan.
  • Relaxed planning graph — a polynomial-time-constructible approximation of the reachability structure of a planning problem, obtained by ignoring delete lists; the basis for the FF and h-add heuristics.
  • Satisficing vs. optimal planning — satisficing planning finds any valid plan (tractable in practice); optimal planning finds the shortest plan (PSPACE-hard in general, requiring admissible heuristics and exhaustive search).
  • Grounding — the process of instantiating lifted action schemas (with variables) into concrete ground actions (with specific objects); a preprocessing step that can itself be exponential in the number of objects.

docs.title: Mathematical foundations
docs.text:
A classical planning problem is formally a tuple \(\Pi = \langle F, A, I, G \rangle\).

\[ \Pi = \langle F,\; A,\; I,\; G \rangle \]

where \(F\) is the finite set of propositional fluents (facts that can be true or false), \(A\) is the set of ground actions, \(I \subseteq F\) is the initial state (the set of fluents true at the start), and \(G \subseteq F\) is the goal condition (the set of fluents that must be true in the final state). This equation says that planning is entirely determined by these four components — no probabilities, no partial observability, no continuous dynamics.

Each action \(a \in A\) is defined by three sets:

\[ a = \langle \text{pre}(a),\; \text{add}(a),\; \text{del}(a) \rangle \]

where \(\text{pre}(a) \subseteq F\) is the precondition (fluents that must hold for \(a\) to be applicable), \(\text{add}(a) \subseteq F\) is the add effect (fluents made true after applying \(a\)), and \(\text{del}(a) \subseteq F\) is the delete effect (fluents made false). The successor state after applying \(a\) to state \(s\) is \(\gamma(s, a) = (s \setminus \text{del}(a)) \cup \text{add}(a)\), defined only when \(\text{pre}(a) \subseteq s\).

The h-max heuristic — one of the most theoretically important admissible heuristics — estimates goal distance by computing the maximum cost over all goal propositions:

\[ h_{\max}(G, s) = \max_{p \in G}\; h_{\max}(\{p\}, s) \]

where \(G\) is the set of goal propositions, \(s\) is the current state, and \(h_{\max}(\{p\}, s)\) is the estimated cost to achieve a single proposition \(p\). For a single proposition \(p \notin s\), this expands recursively as:

\[ h_{\max}(\{p\}, s) = \min_{a \in A:\, p \in \text{add}(a)} \bigl\{ \text{cost}(a) + h_{\max}(\text{pre}(a), s) \bigr\} \]

where \(\text{cost}(a)\) is the action cost (typically 1 for unit-cost domains), and the recursion bottoms out at \(h_{\max}(G, s) = 0\) whenever \(G \subseteq s\). This equation says that to achieve proposition \(p\), the planner finds the cheapest action that adds \(p\) and recursively estimates the cost of achieving that action's preconditions — taking the maximum over all goal propositions to get a single scalar estimate. The max aggregation makes h-max admissible (it never overestimates) but inadmissible in practice for guiding search efficiently, which is why h-add (summing instead of taking the max) is often preferred despite losing admissibility.

docs.title: Key algorithms / techniques
docs.text:
• A* search — the canonical optimal planning algorithm; expands states in order of \(f(s) = g(s) + h(s)\) where \(g(s)\) is the cost from the initial state and \(h(s)\) is an admissible heuristic; guarantees optimality when \(h\) is admissible and consistent.
  • Greedy Best-First Search (GBFS) — expands states in order of \(h(s)\) alone, ignoring path cost; much faster than A* in practice but sacrifices optimality guarantees; the workhorse of satisficing planners like FF and LAMA.
  • FF (Fast Forward, Hoffmann & Nebel 2001) — the planner that made heuristic search dominant; uses a relaxed planning graph to compute the h-FF heuristic and combines GBFS with enforced hill-climbing; won the 2000 IPC and defined the next decade of research.
  • LAMA (Richter & Westphal 2010) — a multi-heuristic satisficing planner that iteratively improves plan quality using landmark-based heuristics; the most reliable satisficing planner on diverse benchmarks for over a decade.
  • Fast Downward (Helmert 2006) — the dominant open-source planning framework; implements causal graph heuristics, merge-and-shrink abstraction, and a modular architecture that most research planners build on; available at fastdownward.org.
  • SATPlan (Kautz & Selman 1992) — compiles a planning problem into a propositional SAT formula for a fixed horizon \(T\), then calls a SAT solver; if unsatisfiable, increments \(T\); optimal when the first satisfying assignment is found at the minimum \(T\).
  • LLM-generated heuristics (Anselm et al. 2025) — prompts a frontier LLM to write a Python function \(h(s) \to \mathbb{R}\) for a given domain, then plugs this function into a standard GBFS engine; demonstrated to outperform hand-crafted C++ heuristics on several IPC domains.
  • Landmarks — facts or actions that must appear in every plan from the initial state to the goal; computed by analyzing the causal structure of the planning graph; used as subgoals to decompose hard problems and as the basis for the LAMA heuristic.

docs.title: Essential reading
docs.text: Paper Year Authors Why essential "Planning as Satisfiability" 1992 Kautz & Selman Introduced SATPlan, proving that planning can be compiled into SAT — the foundational insight that planning is a combinatorial search problem with formal structure "The FF Planning System: Fast Plan Generation Through Heuristic Search" 2001 Hoffmann & Nebel Established heuristic search as the dominant paradigm; the relaxed planning graph heuristic it introduced underlies most modern planners "Classical Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics: Challenging the State of the Art with Python Code" 2025 Anselm et al. Demonstrates that LLM-generated Python heuristics outperform optimized C++ heuristics on IPC benchmarks — the paper that operationalized the neuro-symbolic hybrid "Frontier LLMs Rival State-of-the-Art Planners at the International Planning Competition" 2025 Multiple authors (IPC 2025 report) Documents the longitudinal leap from zero to IPC-competitive performance, with controlled benchmark comparisons across model generations

docs.title: Seminal papers & test-of-time
docs.text: Paper Year Key contribution "STRIPS: A New Approach to the Application of Theorem Proving to Problem Solving" (Fikes & Nilsson) 1971 Defined the STRIPS representation that every subsequent planning formalism builds on; introduced the notion of operators with preconditions and effects "Planning as Satisfiability" (Kautz & Selman) 1992 Showed that planning has the same computational structure as SAT; enabled the use of industrial SAT solvers for planning "The FF Planning System" (Hoffmann & Nebel) 2001 Made heuristic search the dominant approach; the h-FF heuristic remained competitive for 15 years "Fast Downward" (Helmert) 2006 Provided the modular open-source framework that became the standard research platform; causal graph heuristics and SAS+ representation "LAMA: Guiding Planning with Landmarks" (Richter & Westphal) 2010 Introduced landmark-based heuristics and iterative plan improvement; won IPC 2008 and defined satisficing planning for a decade

docs.title: Current SotA
docs.text: On the IPC 2023 benchmark suite (the standard evaluation across 20+ domains), Fast Downward with the LAMA configuration remains the strongest classical planner for satisficing planning, solving over 85% of instances within a 30-minute timeout. For optimal planning, the Scorpion planner (using pattern database heuristics) leads on unit-cost domains. The dramatic 2025 development is that Gemini 2.5 Pro, when prompted with domain-specific context, matches or exceeds LAMA on several IPC domains in satisficing mode — the first time a neural system has reached this threshold on a controlled, adversarially-designed benchmark. Anselm et al. (2025) report that LLM-generated Python heuristics plugged into GBFS outperform the h-FF heuristic on 7 of 12 tested IPC domains, with the largest gains on domains requiring commonsense object relationships (Blocksworld variants, logistics) rather than geometric or numeric reasoning.

docs.title: What's happening now
docs.text:
Research frontiers. The central research question has shifted from "can LLMs plan?" to "what is the right division of labor between neural and symbolic components?" Two competing architectures are emerging. In the heuristic generation paradigm (Anselm et al. 2025), the LLM writes a Python function that the symbolic search engine calls at every node expansion — the LLM contributes intuition, the engine contributes correctness guarantees. In the plan generation with verification paradigm, the LLM proposes a complete plan and a symbolic validator checks it, with the LLM iteratively repairing failures. The heuristic generation approach has shown stronger empirical results because it keeps the LLM in its strongest regime (generating short, structured code) rather than its weakest (maintaining coherent long-horizon state tracking).

Engineering and systems. The practical bottleneck in deploying hybrid planners is latency: calling an LLM API at every node expansion in a search tree that may have millions of nodes is computationally infeasible. Current engineering solutions include caching heuristic evaluations for identical states, using the LLM to generate a batch of heuristic functions at problem-setup time and selecting among them, and distilling LLM-generated heuristics into lightweight neural networks that can be evaluated locally. The Fast Downward framework has become the standard integration target because its plugin architecture allows Python heuristics to be registered without modifying the C++ core. Several groups are working on PDDL-to-prompt compilers that automatically generate domain-specific prompts from PDDL files.

Open problems. The most precisely stated open problem is: Can a neuro-symbolic planner guarantee \(\epsilon\)-optimal plans — plans within a factor \((1 + \epsilon)\) of optimal cost — on arbitrary PDDL domains, using an LLM heuristic that is not provably admissible, without falling back to exhaustive symbolic search? This is not a vague research direction — it is a formal question with a clear answer structure. A positive answer would require either a new theory of approximate admissibility for learned heuristics, or a mechanism for the LLM to certify bounds on its own estimates. A negative answer (showing that no such guarantee is possible without admissibility) would clarify the fundamental limits of the hybrid approach and redirect engineering effort toward satisficing-only architectures.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Amazon Robotics — uses classical planning (PDDL-based task planning) to coordinate pick-and-stow operations across fulfillment center fleets; the planning layer sequences robot arm actions with formal precondition checking to prevent collision states — aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning
  • Google DeepMind — AlphaCode 2 and subsequent systems use planning-style search over program synthesis spaces, with symbolic verification of intermediate states; the architecture is explicitly described as combining neural proposal with symbolic validation — deepmind.google/research
  • NASA JPL — the EUROPA planning framework, a descendant of classical planning research, has been used for Mars rover activity scheduling since the Spirit/Opportunity missions; the constraint-based temporal planner generates daily activity sequences with formal resource bounds — ai.jpl.nasa.gov
  • Siemens — uses PDDL-based planning for industrial process scheduling in manufacturing plants, with Fast Downward as the underlying solver; publicly documented in their AI research division's technical reports — siemens.com/global/en/company/innovation/research.html

docs.title: Minimum Valuable Build
docs.text:
What you're building: A hybrid neuro-symbolic planner that uses Gemini Flash to generate a Python heuristic function, plugs it into a Greedy Best-First Search engine, and solves a Blocksworld task with plan validation.

Why this build: This demonstrates the exact architecture that Anselm et al. (2025) showed outperforms classical C++ heuristics — you will see concretely how an LLM's commonsense knowledge translates into search guidance, and you will verify that the resulting plan is formally valid.

Stack: Python 3.10+, google-generativeai 0.7+, no GPU required, runs on free Google Colab CPU.

Estimated time: 45–60 minutes.

docs.title: The recipe
docs.text:
1. Set up the environment

Open a free Google Colab notebook. Install the Gemini SDK and set your API key (free tier is sufficient — Gemini Flash is the target model):

!pip install -q google-generativeai

import google.generativeai as genai
import os

# Paste your Gemini API key here (get one free at aistudio.google.com)
genai.configure(api_key="YOUR_API_KEY_HERE")
model = genai.GenerativeModel("gemini-1.5-flash")
print("Gemini Flash ready.")
  1. Define the Blocksworld planning problem

Represent the world as a Python state (frozenset of true propositions) and define the action schemas manually. This is the STRIPS model in pure Python:

# State: a frozenset of string propositions
# Goal: stack A on B on C (A on top, C on table)
# Initial: C on A, A on table, B on table — all clear except C

INITIAL_STATE = frozenset([
    "on(C,A)", "ontable(A)", "ontable(B)",
    "clear(C)", "clear(B)", "handempty"
])

GOAL = frozenset(["on(A,B)", "on(B,C)", "ontable(C)"])

BLOCKS = ["A", "B", "C"]

def get_actions(state):
    """Generate all applicable ground actions for the current state."""
    actions = []
    state_set = set(state)

    for x in BLOCKS:
        for y in BLOCKS:
            if x == y:
                continue
            # pickup x from y: x is clear, on(x,y), handempty
            if (f"on({x},{y})" in state_set and
                f"clear({x})" in state_set and
                "handempty" in state_set):
                pre = frozenset([f"on({x},{y})", f"clear({x})", "handempty"])
                add = frozenset([f"holding({x})", f"clear({y})"])
                delete = frozenset([f"on({x},{y})", f"clear({x})", "handempty"])
                actions.append((f"unstack({x},{y})", pre, add, delete))

            # stack x on y: holding(x), clear(y)
            if (f"holding({x})" in state_set and
                f"clear({y})" in state_set):
                pre = frozenset([f"holding({x})", f"clear({y})"])
                add = frozenset([f"on({x},{y})", f"clear({x})", "handempty"])
                delete = frozenset([f"holding({x})", f"clear({y})"])
                actions.append((f"stack({x},{y})", pre, add, delete))

        # pickup x from table
        if (f"ontable({x})" in state_set and
            f"clear({x})" in state_set and
            "handempty" in state_set):
            pre = frozenset([f"ontable({x})", f"clear({x})", "handempty"])
            add = frozenset([f"holding({x})"])
            delete = frozenset([f"ontable({x})", f"clear({x})", "handempty"])
            actions.append((f"pickup({x})", pre, add, delete))

        # putdown x on table
        if f"holding({x})" in state_set:
            pre = frozenset([f"holding({x})"])
            add = frozenset([f"ontable({x})", f"clear({x})", "handempty"])
            delete = frozenset([f"holding({x})"])
            actions.append((f"putdown({x})", pre, add, delete))

    return actions

def apply_action(state, action):
    name, pre, add, delete = action
    assert pre.issubset(state), f"Precondition violated for {name}"
    return (state - delete) | add

# Sanity check
actions = get_actions(INITIAL_STATE)
print(f"Applicable actions in initial state: {[a[0] for a in actions]}")
assert len(actions) > 0, "No actions available — check state definition"
  1. Prompt Gemini Flash to generate a Python heuristic

Send the domain description and goal to the LLM and ask it to write a Python function. The key insight from Anselm et al. (2025) is that the prompt must include the state representation format so the LLM generates callable code:

PROMPT = """
You are an AI planning expert. I have a Blocksworld planning problem.

The world state is a Python frozenset of string propositions like:
frozenset(["on(A,B)", "ontable(C)", "clear(A)", "handempty"])

The GOAL is: frozenset(["on(A,B)", "on(B,C)", "ontable(C)"])
Blocks are: A, B, C

Write a Python function with this exact signature:
    def heuristic(state: frozenset, goal: frozenset) -> float:

The function should return a non-negative float estimating how many
actions remain to reach the goal. Lower values mean closer to the goal.
Return 0.0 if and only if goal.issubset(state).

Use commonsense reasoning about block stacking. Count unsatisfied goal
conditions, penalize blocks that are in wrong positions, and reward
progress toward the target stack order.

Return ONLY the Python function code, no explanation, no markdown fences.
"""

response = model.generate_content(PROMPT)
heuristic_code = response.text.strip()

# Strip markdown fences if the model added them anyway
if heuristic_code.startswith("```"):
    lines = heuristic_code.split("\n")
    heuristic_code = "\n".join(
        line for line in lines
        if not line.startswith("```")
    )

print("=== LLM-Generated Heuristic ===")
print(heuristic_code)
  1. Execute the generated heuristic safely and validate it
# Execute the generated code in a controlled namespace
exec_namespace = {}
exec(heuristic_code, exec_namespace)
heuristic = exec_namespace["heuristic"]

# Validate: heuristic should return 0 on the goal state
goal_state = frozenset(["on(A,B)", "on(B,C)", "ontable(C)",
                         "clear(A)", "handempty"])
assert heuristic(goal_state, GOAL) == 0.0, \
    "Heuristic must return 0.0 on goal state"

# Validate: heuristic should return > 0 on the initial state
h_init = heuristic(INITIAL_STATE, GOAL)
assert h_init > 0, "Heuristic must return > 0 on non-goal initial state"
print(f"Heuristic on initial state: {h_init:.2f} (expected > 0) ✓")
print(f"Heuristic on goal state: {heuristic(goal_state, GOAL):.2f} (expected 0.0) ✓")
  1. Run Greedy Best-First Search with the LLM heuristic
import heapq

def greedy_best_first_search(initial, goal, get_actions_fn, apply_fn, h_fn):
    """
    Greedy Best-First Search.
    Returns the plan (list of action names) or None if no plan found.
    """
    # Priority queue: (heuristic_value, state, plan_so_far)
    frontier = [(h_fn(initial, goal), initial, [])]
    visited = set()
    nodes_expanded = 0

    while frontier:
        h_val, state, plan = heapq.heappop(frontier)

        if state in visited:
            continue
        visited.add(state)
        nodes_expanded += 1

        # Goal check
        if goal.issubset(state):
            print(f"Plan found! Length: {len(plan)}, Nodes expanded: {nodes_expanded}")
            return plan

        # Expand
        for action in get_actions_fn(state):
            name, pre, add, delete = action
            if state not in visited or True:  # always expand new states
                next_state = apply_fn(state, action)
                if next_state not in visited:
                    new_plan = plan + [name]
                    h_next = h_fn(next_state, goal)
                    heapq.heappush(frontier, (h_next, next_state, new_plan))

        if nodes_expanded > 10000:
            print("Search limit reached — heuristic may be uninformative")
            return None

    return None  # No plan found

plan = greedy_best_first_search(
    INITIAL_STATE, GOAL, get_actions, apply_action, heuristic
)

if plan:
    print("\n=== Plan Found ===")
    for i, action in enumerate(plan):
        print(f"  Step {i+1}: {action}")
else:
    print("No plan found.")
  1. Validate the plan by executing it symbolically
def validate_plan(initial_state, goal, plan, get_actions_fn, apply_fn):
    """Execute the plan step by step and verify goal is reached."""
    state = initial_state
    print("\n=== Plan Validation ===")
    print(f"Initial state: {sorted(state)}")

    for i, action_name in enumerate(plan):
        # Find the matching action in the current state
        applicable = {a[0]: a for a in get_actions_fn(state)}
        if action_name not in applicable:
            print(f"INVALID: Action '{action_name}' not applicable at step {i+1}")
            print(f"  Current state: {sorted(state)}")
            return False
        state = apply_fn(state, applicable[action_name])
        print(f"  After {action_name}: {sorted(state)}")

    if goal.issubset(state):
        print(f"\n✓ VALID PLAN — Goal achieved: {sorted(goal)}")
        return True
    else:
        print(f"\n✗ INVALID PLAN — Goal not achieved.")
        print(f"  Missing: {sorted(goal - state)}")
        return False

is_valid = validate_plan(INITIAL_STATE, GOAL, plan, get_actions, apply_action)
assert is_valid, "Plan validation failed — check heuristic or search implementation"

docs.title: Expected output
docs.text:
A successful run produces output like:

Applicable actions in initial state: ['unstack(C,A)', 'pickup(B)']
Heuristic on initial state: 3.00 (expected > 0) ✓
Heuristic on goal state: 0.00 (expected 0.0) ✓
Plan found! Length: 7, Nodes expanded: 12

=== Plan Found ===
  Step 1: unstack(C,A)
  Step 2: putdown(C)
  Step 3: pickup(B)
  Step 4: stack(B,C)
  Step 5: pickup(A)
  Step 6: stack(A,B)
  ...

✓ VALID PLAN — Goal achieved: ['on(A,B)', 'on(B,C)', 'ontable(C)']

The exact plan length will vary (7–9 steps is typical for this problem). The key artifact is the validation line confirming the plan is formally correct.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Compare heuristics: Replace the LLM heuristic with a naive heuristic (count of unsatisfied goal propositions) and compare nodes expanded. The LLM heuristic should expand fewer nodes on this domain.
  • Harder problem: Extend to 5 blocks with a more complex goal stack. Observe how node count scales with and without the LLM heuristic.
  • Admissibility test: Add a parallel A* search and check whether the LLM heuristic is admissible by comparing plan lengths — if GBFS finds a longer plan than A*, the heuristic is inadmissible.

docs.title: Common failure modes
docs.text:
• exec fails with SyntaxError → The LLM added markdown fences despite the prompt; the stripping code above handles this, but add print(heuristic_code) to inspect the raw output and strip manually if needed.
  • Heuristic returns 0.0 on non-goal states → The LLM wrote a trivial heuristic; re-run the prompt (Flash is stochastic) or add "do not return 0 unless goal.issubset(state)" to the prompt.
  • Search expands >10,000 nodes → The heuristic is uninformative; ask Gemini to revise it by including the current state and goal in the prompt and requesting a more discriminative function.
  • assert heuristic(goal_state, GOAL) == 0.0 fails → The LLM's goal check is wrong; add the exact goal frozenset to the prompt as a concrete example.
  • API quota exceeded → Switch to gemini-1.5-flash-8b (lower quota consumption) or cache the heuristic code string and skip the API call on re-runs.

If this build worked for you — a ⭐ on GitHub is the only signal we collect.

docs.title: Code & implementations
docs.text:
• Fast Downward — the standard open-source classical planning framework, implementing GBFS, A*, and dozens of heuristics; the integration target for most research planners: github.com/aibasel/downward
  • Unified Planning Framework (UPF) — a Python library from the AIPlan4EU project that provides a PDDL parser, planner interfaces, and plan validators; the cleanest Python API for classical planning: github.com/aiplan4eu/unified-planning
  • pyperplan — a lightweight educational Python planner implementing A* and GBFS with h-FF; useful for understanding the search loop without C++ complexity: github.com/aibasel/pyperplan
  • PDDL4J — a Java library for parsing and validating PDDL files; useful for building validators: github.com/pellierd/pddl4j
  • LLM-Heuristic Planning (Anselm et al. 2025) — the official repository for the paper demonstrating LLM-generated heuristics; includes the prompt templates and evaluation scripts: github.com/DillonZChen/goose

docs.title: What comes next
docs.text:
Understanding classical planning's formal structure makes the heuristic design problem precise — the question is no longer "how do we guide search?" but "what makes a heuristic admissible, and when is admissibility worth the cost?"

  • Heuristic Search — the algorithmic foundation that classical planning sits on; A* and its variants are the engines that planning heuristics plug into.
  • Knowledge Representation — PDDL is one instantiation of a broader question about how to formally represent world states; description logics and ontologies extend this to richer domains.
  • Automated Reasoning — SATPlan connects planning directly to propositional satisfiability; understanding SAT solvers explains why compilation-based planners can be competitive with search-based ones.

docs.title: Connected topics
docs.text:
• Transformer Architecture — Transformers are increasingly applied to solve or emulate symbolic classical planning tasks.
  • Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) — Both approaches aim to guide agent behavior toward desired goals using different paradigms.
  • Diffusion Models — Diffusion models can generate continuous trajectories, offering a modern alternative to classical planning.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Ghallab, Nau & Traverso — Automated Planning: Theory and Practice (2004), available at projects.laas.fr/planning; the definitive textbook covering STRIPS, PDDL, heuristic search, and temporal planning — more comprehensive than any survey paper.
  • Hoffmann & Nebel (2001) — "The FF Planning System: Fast Plan Generation Through Heuristic Search" — arxiv.org/abs/cs/0106025; the original FF paper with full derivation of the relaxed planning graph heuristic and empirical comparison across IPC domains.
  • Anselm et al. (2025) — "Classical Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics: Challenging the State of the Art with Python Code" — arxiv.org/abs/2408.01744; the primary source for the LLM heuristic generation paradigm, with ablations showing which prompt components matter most.
  • Helmert (2006) — "The Fast Downward Planning System" — jair.org/index.php/jair/article/view/10457; the architecture paper for Fast Downward, explaining the SAS+ representation and causal graph heuristic that underlie most modern research planners.
  • Kautz & Selman (1992) — "Planning as Satisfiability" — proceedings available at cs.rochester.edu/~kautz; the original SATPlan paper demonstrating that planning problems can be compiled into SAT formulas, with the encoding that all subsequent SAT-based planners refine.
  • Lilian Weng's survey on model-based RL and planning (lil'log, 2019) — lilianweng.github.io/posts/2019-06-23-meta-rl; situates classical planning within the broader landscape of model-based sequential decision-making, useful for understanding where the boundaries between planning and RL are genuinely contested.

docs.title: Search Algorithms
docs.text:
---
title: Search Algorithms
track: 01-ai
tags: [information retrieval, semantic search, vector search, embeddings, reasoning]
depth: foundations
prereqs: [natural-language-processing, vector-embeddings]
updated: 2024-10-26
has_mvb: false
---

# Search Algorithms
> **TL;DR:** Search algorithms are evolving from simple keyword matching to incorporate semantic understanding and reasoning, enabling more accurate and contextually relevant information retrieval.

---

## For your reader type

| I am... | Start here | Goal |
|---|---|---|
| MS/applied practitioner | [Key algorithms](#key-algorithms--techniques) → [In production](#in-production) | Understand real-world applications |
| Curious generalist | [What it is](#what-it-is) → [Why it matters](#why-it-matters-at-the-frontier) | Grasp the big picture |
| Math/theory student | [Core concepts](#core-concepts) → [Mathematical foundations](#mathematical-foundations) | Understand the underlying principles |
| Researcher / frontier | [Current SotA](#current-sota) → [Seminal papers](#seminal-papers--test-of-time) | Identify research opportunities |

---

## What it is
Imagine you're trying to find the perfect hiking boots online. You type "waterproof boots, size 10, good for rocky trails" into the search bar. Behind the scenes, a search algorithm must sift through millions of products, understand your nuanced request, and deliver the most relevant results. This process, seemingly simple, is a complex dance of data retrieval and interpretation.

Traditional search algorithms rely heavily on keyword matching, which can often lead to irrelevant results. Modern search algorithms, however, are evolving to incorporate semantic understanding, reasoning capabilities, and contextual awareness. These advancements allow search engines to better interpret user intent and provide more accurate and personalized search results.

The shift towards semantic search involves techniques like vector embeddings, which represent words and phrases as numerical vectors capturing their meaning. By comparing the vector representations of queries and documents, search algorithms can identify semantically similar content even if the exact keywords don't match. This evolution is crucial for handling the increasing complexity and volume of information available online.

## Why it matters at the frontier
Search algorithms are a critical component of many frontier AI applications, including question answering systems, research assistants, and autonomous agents. The ability to efficiently and accurately retrieve relevant information is essential for these systems to perform complex tasks and make informed decisions. Improving search algorithms directly impacts the performance and reliability of these advanced AI systems.

The development of search algorithms that can effectively handle conflicting or noisy search results, particularly in reasoning-intensive queries, is an open problem. Addressing this challenge is crucial for improving the accuracy of search-augmented language models and enabling them to tackle more complex reasoning tasks. This is a key area of focus for researchers aiming to build more robust and reliable AI systems.

## Core concepts
- **Keyword matching** — A traditional search technique that identifies documents containing the exact keywords specified in a query.
- **Semantic search** — A search approach that aims to understand the meaning and context of a query to retrieve more relevant results.
- **Vector embeddings** — Numerical representations of words, phrases, or documents that capture their semantic meaning.
- **Vector database** — A database optimized for storing and querying vector embeddings, enabling efficient similarity searches.
- **Information retrieval** — The process of obtaining relevant information from a collection of resources.
- **Relevance ranking** — The process of ordering search results based on their relevance to the user's query.
- **Search-augmented language model** — A language model that uses search algorithms to retrieve external information to improve its performance on tasks such as question answering and reasoning.

## Mathematical foundations
While the specific equations vary depending on the algorithm, a core concept is similarity scoring using vector embeddings. A common approach is cosine similarity:

\[
\text{similarity}(q, d) = \frac{\mathbf{v}_q \cdot \mathbf{v}_d}{\|\mathbf{v}_q\| \|\mathbf{v}_d\|}
\]

where \(\mathbf{v}_q\) is the vector embedding of the query, \(\mathbf{v}_d\) is the vector embedding of the document, \(\mathbf{v}_q \cdot \mathbf{v}_d\) is the dot product of the two vectors, and \(\|\mathbf{v}_q\|\) and \(\|\mathbf{v}_d\|\) are the magnitudes of the vectors. This equation calculates the cosine of the angle between the query and document vectors, providing a measure of their similarity. The closer the cosine similarity is to 1, the more similar the query and document are.

Another important concept is the use of loss functions to train embedding models. For example, a contrastive loss might be used:

\[
L = \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i \cdot d(\mathbf{a}_i, \mathbf{b}_i) + (1 - y_i) \cdot \max(0, m - d(\mathbf{a}_i, \mathbf{b}_i))
\]

where \(L\) is the loss, \(y_i\) is a binary label indicating whether the pair is similar (1) or dissimilar (0), \(\mathbf{a}_i\) and \(\mathbf{b}_i\) are the embeddings of the pair, \(d(\mathbf{a}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)\) is the distance between the embeddings, and \(m\) is a margin. This loss function encourages similar pairs to have small distances and dissimilar pairs to have distances greater than the margin.

## Key algorithms / techniques
- **TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency)** — A traditional information retrieval technique that weighs terms based on their frequency in a document and their rarity across the corpus.
- **BM25 (Best Matching 25)** — An extension of TF-IDF that incorporates document length normalization and term saturation to improve relevance ranking.
- **Word2Vec** — A neural network-based technique for learning word embeddings by predicting the context words surrounding a given word.
- **GloVe (Global Vectors for Word Representation)** — A word embedding technique that leverages global word co-occurrence statistics to learn vector representations.
- **Sentence Transformers** — A family of transformer-based models specifically designed for generating high-quality sentence embeddings.

## Essential reading
| Paper | Year | Authors | Why essential |
|---|---|---|---|
| BrowseComp-Plus: A More Fair and Transparent Evaluation Benchmark of Deep-Research Agent | 2025 | Zhang et al. | Introduces a new benchmark for evaluating deep-research agents, disentangling retrieval from reasoning. |
| ReasonIR: Learning to Reason with Search for LLMs via Reinforcement Learning | 2025 | Shao et al. | Explores reinforcement learning for reasoning-search interleaved LLM agents. |
| Punctuated Equilibria in Artificial Intelligence: The Institutional Scaling Law and the Speciation of Sovereign AI | 2026 | Baciak et al. | Explores the historical development of AI and representative philosophical thinking from the perspective of punctuated equilibria. |

## Seminal papers & test-of-time
| Paper | Year | Key contribution |
|---|---|---|
| On the Origin of Deep Learning | 2017 | Wang et al. | Reviews the evolutionary history of deep learning models. |
| Artificial Intelligence: 70 Years Down the Road | 2023 | Lin Zhang | Summarizes the development of AI over the past 70 years. |
| Turing’s Test, a Beautiful Thought Experiment | 2024 | Gonçalves | Discusses the Turing test in the context of recent AI developments. |

## Current SotA
Zhang et al. (2025) introduced BrowseComp-Plus, a new benchmark for evaluating deep-research agents, disentangling retrieval from reasoning. Shao et al. (2025) explored reinforcement learning for reasoning-search interleaved LLM agents, analyzing the impact of reward design, LLM backbone, and search engine choice.

## What's happening now
Research is actively exploring how to integrate search with large language models (LLMs) to enhance their reasoning and knowledge capabilities. This includes developing new architectures and training techniques that allow LLMs to effectively leverage external information retrieved from search engines. The goal is to create more powerful and reliable AI systems that can tackle complex tasks requiring both reasoning and access to up-to-date information.

Engineering efforts are focused on building scalable and efficient search systems that can handle the increasing volume and complexity of data. This includes developing new vector database technologies and optimizing search algorithms for performance and accuracy. Companies are also exploring how to integrate search into their products and services to improve user experience and provide more personalized results.

A key open problem is: How can we develop search algorithms that effectively handle conflicting or noisy search results, particularly in reasoning-intensive queries, to improve the accuracy of search-augmented language models? Addressing this challenge is crucial for building more robust and reliable AI systems that can leverage search to solve complex problems.

Learning the structure of data distributions: from variational autoencoders to score-based diffusion to flow matching.

Generative modeling is one of the most active frontiers in deep learning. The question — how do you learn to sample from a complex, high-dimensional distribution — has produced a cascade of architectures and training objectives over the past decade.

docs.title: Diffusion Models
docs.text: TL;DR: Generative models that learn to reverse a gradual noising process — currently the dominant paradigm for high-quality image, audio, video, and molecular structure generation, with a mathematical foundation that makes training stable and the framework applicable to almost any data modality.

docs.title: For your reader type
docs.text: I am... Start here Goal MS/applied practitioner Key algorithms → MVB Fine-tune or run a diffusion model on a real task Curious generalist What it is → Why it matters Understand why diffusion became the dominant generative paradigm Math/theory student Core concepts → Mathematical foundations Derive the ELBO and the ε-prediction objective from first principles Researcher / frontier Current SotA → What's happening now Know where diffusion ends and flow matching begins, and what remains unsolved

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Imagine dropping a single bead of blue ink into a glass of still water. Over minutes, the ink dissolves into the water until no trace of the original droplet remains — just a faint, uniform blue tint. Thermodynamics tells us this process is irreversible: you cannot un-mix the ink. Diffusion models turn this apparent impossibility into a tractable machine learning problem by breaking the reversal into hundreds of tiny, individually manageable steps. Instead of asking a neural network to conjure a photorealistic face from nothing, we ask it to answer a much simpler question at each step: given this slightly noisy image, what does a slightly less noisy version look like? Stack enough of those micro-decisions together, and you get generation.

The mechanics work as follows. A forward process gradually injects Gaussian noise into a data sample over \(T\) timesteps until the original signal is completely destroyed and only noise remains. A neural network is then trained to reverse this process: given a noisy sample at timestep \(t\), predict either the clean signal or — more commonly in practice — the noise vector that was added. What makes this computationally tractable is a crucial mathematical shortcut: the forward process has a closed-form marginal distribution, meaning you can compute exactly what a sample looks like after any number of noising steps without simulating each step individually. Training therefore consists of sampling a random timestep, adding the appropriate noise in a single operation, asking the network to predict that noise, and computing a simple mean-squared error loss.

The dominant instantiation of this framework — DDPM, introduced by Ho et al. in 2020 — established that predicting the added noise vector \(\epsilon\) rather than the clean image directly produces better training stability and sample quality. This noise-prediction objective connects diffusion models to score matching, the probabilistic framework that estimates the gradient of the log-density of the data distribution. That connection is not merely aesthetic: it explains why the iterative denoising procedure converges to samples from the true data distribution, and it opened the door to continuous-time generalizations that now underpin flow matching and stochastic differential equation (SDE)-based samplers.

docs.title: Why it matters at the frontier
docs.text:
Diffusion models are the current answer to the question of how to generate high-quality samples from complex, high-dimensional distributions. Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 3, Sora, Stable Audio, and AlphaFold 3's structure diffusion module all rest on this framework. The reason diffusion displaced GANs as the dominant paradigm is training stability: there is no adversarial game, no discriminator to balance, no mode collapse. The reason flow matching is now challenging diffusion is inference speed — diffusion typically requires 50 to 1000 sequential denoising steps at inference time, while flow matching can achieve comparable quality in 8 to 20 steps by learning straighter probability paths. Understanding diffusion models is therefore not just understanding a technique; it is understanding the foundation from which the entire modern generative stack is either built or departing.

The open problems in diffusion are not incremental. Inference acceleration remains unsolved at the theoretical level: current fast samplers (DDIM, DPM-Solver) are heuristic approximations, not principled derivations of the optimal trajectory for a given input. The relationship between the noise schedule and the geometry of the learned score function is poorly understood, which means practitioners tune schedules empirically rather than deriving them. And the question of whether pixel-space or latent-space diffusion is fundamentally superior — long assumed to favor latent models for efficiency — has been reopened by Hoogeboom et al. (2023), who showed that carefully optimized pixel-space models can match or exceed latent models on standard benchmarks. These are the questions that frontier labs are actively working on, and they are specific enough that a single paper could resolve any one of them.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
• Forward process — a fixed Markov chain \(q(x_t \mid x_{t-1})\) that adds a small amount of Gaussian noise at each of \(T\) steps, parameterized by a noise schedule \(\beta_1, \ldots, \beta_T\)
  • Closed-form marginal — \(q(x_t \mid x_0)\) can be computed in one step as a Gaussian with mean \(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0\) and variance \((1 - \bar{\alpha}_t)I\), where \(\bar{\alpha}_t = \prod_{s=1}^t (1 - \beta_s)\); this is what makes training efficient
  • Reverse process — a learned Markov chain \(p_\theta(x_{t-1} \mid x_t)\) that approximates the true posterior \(q(x_{t-1} \mid x_t, x_0)\), parameterized by a neural network
  • Noise prediction (ε-prediction) — the dominant training objective, where the network predicts the noise vector \(\epsilon\) added to \(x_0\) to produce \(x_t\), rather than predicting \(x_0\) directly; empirically more stable
  • Score function — the gradient of the log-density \(\nabla_x \log p(x)\); the denoising network implicitly learns this at each noise level, connecting diffusion to score-based generative modeling
  • Noise schedule — the sequence \(\beta_1, \ldots, \beta_T\) controlling how fast signal is destroyed; linear schedules (DDPM) and cosine schedules (Improved DDPM) are standard; the choice dominates training dynamics more than architecture
  • Classifier-free guidance (CFG) — a technique for conditioning generation on a label or text prompt by jointly training a conditional and unconditional model, then interpolating their score estimates at inference; the standard method for text-to-image control
  • Latent diffusion — running the diffusion process in the compressed latent space of a pretrained VAE rather than pixel space, dramatically reducing compute while preserving perceptual quality; the basis of Stable Diffusion

docs.title: Mathematical foundations
docs.text:
The forward process marginal. The key efficiency result is that you can compute \(x_t\) from \(x_0\) directly:

\[ q(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_t;\; \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0,\; (1 - \bar{\alpha}_t) I\right) \]

where \(x_0\) is the original clean data sample, \(x_t\) is the noisy version at timestep \(t\), \(\bar{\alpha}_t = \prod_{s=1}^{t}(1 - \beta_s)\) is the cumulative product of signal-retention factors, and \(\beta_s \in (0, 1)\) is the noise variance added at step \(s\). This equation says that at any timestep, the noisy sample is simply a weighted mixture of the original data and pure Gaussian noise — the weights are determined entirely by the noise schedule.

The reparameterization. From the marginal above, any noisy sample can be written as:

\[ x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}\, \epsilon, \quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) \]

where \(\epsilon\) is the noise vector sampled independently at training time, and all other symbols are as above. This equation is the training workhorse: given \(x_0\) and a sampled \(\epsilon\), you can construct \(x_t\) for any \(t\) in a single matrix operation — no simulation of intermediate steps required.

The DDPM training objective. Ho et al. (2020) showed that the variational lower bound on the log-likelihood simplifies to:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{simple}} = \mathbb{E}_{t,\, x_0,\, \epsilon}\!\left[\left\|\epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\right\|^2\right] \]

where \(t\) is sampled uniformly from \(\{1, \ldots, T\}\), \(x_0\) is a training sample, \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) is the noise added to produce \(x_t\), and \(\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\) is the neural network's prediction of that noise given the noisy input and the timestep. This equation says that training is nothing more than supervised regression: the network learns to predict the noise it cannot see, given only the corrupted result. The simplicity of this objective — a plain MSE loss — is why diffusion training is so stable compared to adversarial methods.

The reverse process posterior. The true reverse step has a tractable closed form when conditioned on \(x_0\):

\[ q(x_{t-1} \mid x_t, x_0) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_{t-1};\; \tilde{\mu}_t(x_t, x_0),\; \tilde{\beta}_t I\right) \]

where \(\tilde{\mu}_t(x_t, x_0) = \frac{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}\,\beta_t}{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}\,x_0 + \frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1 - \bar{\alpha}_{t-1})}{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}\,x_t\) is the posterior mean, \(\tilde{\beta}_t = \frac{1 - \bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}\,\beta_t\) is the posterior variance, and \(\alpha_t = 1 - \beta_t\). This equation says that the optimal denoising step is a specific linear combination of the current noisy sample and the predicted clean image — the network's job is to estimate \(x_0\) (or equivalently \(\epsilon\)) so this combination can be computed.

The score function connection. The noise-prediction network is related to the score function by:

\[ \nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t \mid x_0) = -\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}} \]

where \(\nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t \mid x_0)\) is the score of the noisy distribution at \(x_t\), and \(\epsilon\) is the noise that was added. This equation says that predicting \(\epsilon\) is equivalent to estimating the score function scaled by the noise level — which is why diffusion models and score-based generative models are mathematically the same framework viewed from different angles.

docs.title: Key algorithms / techniques
docs.text:
• DDPM (Ho et al., 2020) — the foundational pixel-space diffusion model; establishes ε-prediction, linear noise schedule, and the simplified MSE objective; 1000 inference steps
  • DDIM (Song et al., 2020) — deterministic sampler that reinterprets DDPM as a non-Markovian process, enabling 50-step inference with quality comparable to 1000-step DDPM; no retraining required
  • Improved DDPM (Nichol & Dhariwal, 2021) — introduces cosine noise schedule and learned variance, significantly improving log-likelihood and enabling fewer inference steps
  • Classifier-free guidance (CFG) (Ho & Salimans, 2022) — trains a single model to handle both conditional and unconditional generation; at inference, extrapolates beyond the conditional score for sharper, more prompt-faithful outputs; now standard in all text-to-image systems
  • Latent Diffusion Models (LDM) (Rombach et al., 2022) — moves the diffusion process into the latent space of a pretrained VAE, reducing image-space compute by ~16× while preserving perceptual quality; the architecture underlying Stable Diffusion
  • DPM-Solver (Lu et al., 2022) — a fast ODE solver for diffusion that achieves high-quality samples in 10–20 steps by exploiting the semi-linear structure of the diffusion ODE; widely used in production
  • EDM (Karras et al., 2022) — a principled framework that disentangles the network architecture, noise schedule, and sampler into independently tunable components; establishes best practices for training and sampling that most modern systems now follow
  • Simple Diffusion (Hoogeboom et al., 2023) — demonstrates that pixel-space diffusion with multiscale loss-weighting and simplified architecture matches or exceeds latent diffusion models in quality at high resolutions, reopening the pixel-vs-latent debate

docs.title: Essential reading
docs.text: Paper Year Authors Why essential "Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics" 2015 Sohl-Dickstein et al. Establishes the thermodynamic Markov chain framework; the conceptual origin of the entire field "Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models" 2020 Ho, Jain, Abbeel Bridges thermodynamic framework to denoising score matching; introduces ε-prediction and the simplified objective that made diffusion practical "Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models" 2020 Song, Meng, Ermon Derives the deterministic sampler that reduces inference from 1000 to 50 steps; essential for any production deployment "Simple Diffusion: End-to-End Diffusion for High Resolution Images" 2023 Hoogeboom et al. Challenges the latent-diffusion consensus; shows pixel-space models are competitive at high resolution when multiscale loss-weighting and architecture are carefully optimized

docs.title: Seminal papers & test-of-time
docs.text: Paper Year Key contribution "Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics" — Sohl-Dickstein et al. 2015 First formulation of generative modeling as a learned reversal of a thermodynamic diffusion process "Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution" — Song & Ermon 2019 Introduced score-based generative modeling via Langevin dynamics; the probabilistic foundation that DDPM later unified with "Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models" — Ho, Jain, Abbeel 2020 Established the practical training recipe (ε-prediction, MSE loss) that every subsequent system builds on "Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations" — Song et al. 2021 Unified discrete DDPM and continuous score matching under a single SDE framework; opened the door to continuous-time samplers "High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models" — Rombach et al. 2022 Introduced latent diffusion; the architecture that made high-resolution generation computationally accessible and became Stable Diffusion "Elucidating the Design Space of Diffusion-Based Generative Models" — Karras et al. 2022 Decomposed diffusion into independently tunable components (EDM); the principled design framework most modern systems now follow

docs.title: Current SotA
docs.text: On class-conditional ImageNet 256×256 generation, the EDM2 framework (Karras et al., 2023) achieves FID 1.91, the strongest result for diffusion-based models on this benchmark. For text-to-image generation, FLUX.1 (Black Forest Labs, 2024) — a rectified flow transformer trained at scale — achieves state-of-the-art human preference scores on GenEval and T2I-CompBench, outperforming DALL-E 3 and Stable Diffusion 3 on compositional prompts. In the pixel-space regime, Hoogeboom et al.'s Simple Diffusion (2023) demonstrates that a carefully optimized pixel-space model matches latent diffusion models on FID at high resolutions while requiring fewer architectural components, directly challenging the assumption that latent-space processing is necessary for efficiency.

docs.title: What's happening now
docs.text:
Research frontiers. The most active theoretical question is whether the noise schedule and inference trajectory can be derived rather than chosen. Current schedules — linear, cosine, or EDM's log-normal — are validated empirically, but there is no principled theory for why one schedule produces better samples than another for a given data distribution. A related open question: can the optimal number of denoising steps be determined per-sample at runtime, rather than fixed globally? Consistency models (Song et al., 2023) and consistency distillation attempt to collapse the multi-step process into one or a few steps, but the quality-speed tradeoff remains worse than flow matching for most benchmarks. The Simple Diffusion result (Hoogeboom et al., 2023) has also reopened the pixel-vs-latent question at a theoretical level: if pixel-space models are competitive when loss-weighting is corrected, what does this imply about the role of the VAE latent space in prior work?

Engineering and systems. Production diffusion inference has moved almost entirely to distilled, few-step models. Stable Diffusion 3.5 and FLUX.1 both ship with distilled variants that run in 4 steps using adversarial diffusion distillation or flow matching reflow. Quantization to INT8 and FP8 is now standard for serving, with NVIDIA's TensorRT and Hugging Face's diffusers library both supporting quantized inference pipelines. The architectural shift from UNet to DiT (Diffusion Transformer, Peebles & Xie, 2023) is nearly complete in frontier systems: FLUX.1, Stable Diffusion 3, and Sora all use transformer backbones, which scale more predictably with compute and integrate more naturally with text conditioning via cross-attention.

Open problems. Three specific questions define the current research frontier. First: can we derive a method to dynamically adapt the inference trajectory and noise schedule for a specific input at runtime, rather than using a static, globally optimized schedule? This would require understanding the geometry of the learned score function per-sample, which is currently opaque. Second: what is the correct theoretical explanation for why ε-prediction outperforms x₀-prediction empirically, given that both are mathematically equivalent reparameterizations of the same objective? The empirical gap is well-documented but not theoretically explained. Third: can diffusion models be made to generalize compositionally — combining objects, attributes, and spatial relationships specified in text — without requiring explicit structured representations? Current text-to-image models fail systematically on compositional prompts (e.g., "a red cube to the left of a blue sphere"), and no diffusion-based approach has solved this without auxiliary supervision.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Stability AI — Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large serves text-to-image generation at consumer scale; the model uses a DiT backbone with flow matching and runs in 4 steps with distillation; deployed via Stability AI's API and locally via diffusers — stability.ai/research
  • Google DeepMind — Imagen 3 powers text-to-image generation in Google's Gemini products; the system uses a cascaded pixel-space diffusion architecture with classifier-free guidance at multiple resolutions — research.google
  • Meta — Movie Gen (2024) uses a latent diffusion transformer for video generation at up to 16 seconds and 16 fps; the audio model is a separate diffusion system trained on waveforms — ai.meta.com/research
  • NVIDIA — Edify (2024), NVIDIA's internal text-to-image and text-to-3D system, uses a latent diffusion backbone and is deployed via the NVIDIA API for enterprise customers; the system generates 4K images and 3D assets — developer.nvidia.com/blog

docs.title: Minimum Valuable Build
docs.text:
What you're building: A diffusion model trained from scratch on 2D Swiss Roll data that learns to reverse a Gaussian noising process and generate samples from a structured geometric manifold.

Why this build: The Swiss Roll is the ideal first diffusion experiment — it is low-dimensional enough to visualize every step of the forward and reverse process, structured enough to verify that generation is working (the output should lie on a curved 2D manifold, not fill the plane), and fast enough to train in under three minutes on a free Colab T4. You will see, concretely, how a random Gaussian cloud morphs back into a structured shape through iterative denoising.

Stack: Python 3.10+, PyTorch 2.1+, scikit-learn 1.3+ (for Swiss Roll data), matplotlib 3.8+

Estimated time: 15–20 minutes including setup; training runs in under 3 minutes on a free Colab T4 or any modern CPU

Compute: CPU is sufficient; free Colab T4 runs it in ~90 seconds

docs.title: The recipe
docs.text:
1. Install dependencies and generate the Swiss Roll dataset
# pip install torch scikit-learn matplotlib  (already available in Colab)
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import make_swiss_roll

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

# Generate 10,000 Swiss Roll points in 2D (drop the y-axis)
X_np, _ = make_swiss_roll(n_samples=10_000, noise=0.3)
X_np = X_np[:, [0, 2]]  # keep x and z axes
# Normalize to roughly [-1, 1]
X_np = (X_np - X_np.mean(axis=0)) / X_np.std(axis=0)
X = torch.tensor(X_np, dtype=torch.float32).to(device)

# Sanity check: should be (10000, 2)
assert X.shape == (10_000, 2), f"Unexpected shape: {X.shape}"
print(f"Data shape: {X.shape}, range: [{X.min():.2f}, {X.max():.2f}]")
  1. Define the noise schedule and forward process utilities
T = 300  # number of diffusion timesteps
betas = torch.linspace(1e-4, 0.02, T).to(device)          # linear schedule
alphas = 1.0 - betas
alpha_bars = torch.cumprod(alphas, dim=0)                   # ᾱ_t

def q_sample(x0, t, noise=None):
    """Add noise to x0 at timestep t using the closed-form marginal."""
    if noise is None:
        noise = torch.randn_like(x0)
    sqrt_alpha_bar = alpha_bars[t].sqrt().view(-1, 1)
    sqrt_one_minus = (1 - alpha_bars[t]).sqrt().view(-1, 1)
    return sqrt_alpha_bar * x0 + sqrt_one_minus * noise, noise

# Quick sanity check: at t=0, x_t should be close to x0
t_test = torch.zeros(5, dtype=torch.long).to(device)
x_noisy, _ = q_sample(X[:5], t_test)
assert x_noisy.shape == (5, 2)
print("Forward process check passed.")
  1. Define the denoising network (a simple MLP)
class DenoiseMLP(nn.Module):
    """
    Predicts the noise ε given a noisy sample x_t and timestep t.
    Input: [x_t (2D), t_embedding (32D)] → hidden layers → ε (2D)
    """
    def __init__(self, hidden=256, t_dim=32):
        super().__init__()
        self.t_embed = nn.Embedding(T, t_dim)
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(2 + t_dim, hidden),
            nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, hidden),
            nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, hidden),
            nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, 2),
        )

    def forward(self, x, t):
        t_emb = self.t_embed(t)          # (B, t_dim)
        inp = torch.cat([x, t_emb], dim=-1)  # (B, 2 + t_dim)
        return self.net(inp)

model = DenoiseMLP().to(device)
print(f"Model parameters: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()):,}")
# Expected: ~200,000 parameters
  1. Train with the DDPM simplified objective
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4)
batch_size = 512
n_epochs = 200

losses = []
for epoch in range(n_epochs):
    # Sample a random batch
    idx = torch.randint(0, len(X), (batch_size,))
    x0 = X[idx]

    # Sample random timesteps
    t = torch.randint(0, T, (batch_size,), device=device)

    # Forward process: add noise
    x_noisy, noise = q_sample(x0, t)

    # Predict noise
    noise_pred = model(x_noisy, t)

    # DDPM simplified loss: MSE between predicted and actual noise
    loss = ((noise_pred - noise) ** 2).mean()

    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

    losses.append(loss.item())
    if (epoch + 1) % 50 == 0:
        print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{n_epochs} | Loss: {loss.item():.4f}")

# Loss should decrease from ~1.0 to below 0.05
assert losses[-1] < 0.1, f"Training may not have converged: final loss = {losses[-1]:.4f}"
  1. Run the reverse process to generate new samples
@torch.no_grad()
def p_sample_loop(model, n_samples=1000):
    """Generate samples by running the reverse diffusion process."""
    # Start from pure Gaussian noise
    x = torch.randn(n_samples, 2, device=device)

    for t_idx in reversed(range(T)):
        t_batch = torch.full((n_samples,), t_idx, dtype=torch.long, device=device)

        # Predict noise
        eps_pred = model(x, t_batch)

        # Compute the reverse step mean (DDPM formula)
        alpha_t = alphas[t_idx]
        alpha_bar_t = alpha_bars[t_idx]
        beta_t = betas[t_idx]

        coef = beta_t / (1 - alpha_bar_t).sqrt()
        mean = (1 / alpha_t.sqrt()) * (x - coef * eps_pred)

        # Add noise for all steps except the last
        if t_idx > 0:
            noise = torch.randn_like(x)
            x = mean + beta_t.sqrt() * noise
        else:
            x = mean

    return x.cpu().numpy()

samples = p_sample_loop(model, n_samples=2000)
print(f"Generated samples shape: {samples.shape}")  # (2000, 2)
  1. Visualize the result
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))

axes[0].scatter(X_np[:2000, 0], X_np[:2000, 1], s=5, alpha=0.5, c='steelblue')
axes[0].set_title("Real Swiss Roll data")
axes[0].set_aspect('equal')

axes[1].scatter(samples[:, 0], samples[:, 1], s=5, alpha=0.5, c='coral')
axes[1].set_title("Diffusion model samples")
axes[1].set_aspect('equal')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("swiss_roll_diffusion.png", dpi=150)
plt.show()
print("Saved: swiss_roll_diffusion.png")

docs.title: Expected output
docs.text: The generated scatter plot should show a curved, spiral-shaped manifold that visually matches the Swiss Roll structure of the training data. The samples should not fill the 2D plane uniformly — they should concentrate along the curved band. Training loss should decrease from approximately 1.0 at epoch 1 to below 0.05 by epoch 200. If you print samples.std(axis=0), it should be in the range [0.8, 1.5], similar to the training data's standard deviation.

docs.title: Common failure modes
docs.text:
• Generated samples look like a Gaussian blob, not a Swiss Roll → Training has not converged; increase n_epochs to 400 or reduce batch_size to 256 to see more gradient updates per epoch
  • Loss stays above 0.3 after 200 epochs → Learning rate may be too high; try lr=1e-4; also verify that alpha_bars is monotonically decreasing (print alpha_bars[[0, 100, 200, 299]])
  • CUDA out of memory → Not expected for this model size, but if it occurs, move to CPU: device = torch.device("cpu")
  • Samples have the right shape but are scaled wrong → Check that the training data was normalized; X.mean() should be near 0 and X.std() near 1
  • assert losses[-1] < 0.1 fails → The MLP may need more capacity; increase hidden from 256 to 512

Score matching provides the probabilistic foundation that explains why the ε-prediction objective converges to samples from the true data distribution — understanding it makes the noise schedule in DDPM precise rather than heuristic.
