docs.title: Flow Matching
docs.text: TL;DR: A simulation-free training framework for continuous normalizing flows that learns straight-line vector fields from noise to data — achieving diffusion-quality generation in 8–20 inference steps instead of 50–1000, now powering FLUX, AlphaFold 3, and Voicebox.

docs.title: For your reader type
docs.text: I am... Start here Goal MS/applied practitioner Key algorithms → MVB Train a flow matching model and understand why it's faster than diffusion Curious generalist What it is → Why it matters Understand what "flow matching" means and why it displaced diffusion Math/theory student Core concepts → Mathematical foundations Derive the CFM objective and understand why OT paths are optimal Researcher / frontier Current SotA → What's happening now Know the open problems: path singularities, discrete flow matching, scaling

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Imagine two cities connected by a road network. A diffusion model is like navigating that network during rush hour — every particle takes a winding, congested route through high-dimensional space, doubling back, merging with other particles, and requiring hundreds of small steps to arrive at the destination. Flow matching is the highway bypass: it draws a straight line between where you start (a sample from Gaussian noise) and where you need to go (a data point), then trains a neural network to follow that line. The result is a generative model that can produce high-fidelity samples in a fraction of the steps.

More precisely, flow matching trains a neural network \(v_\theta(x, t)\) to represent a vector field — a function that, at every point in space and every moment in time, says "move in this direction." Integrating this vector field as an ordinary differential equation (ODE) from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 1\) transports a noise sample into a data sample. The critical insight from Lipman et al. (2022) is that training this vector field does not require simulating the ODE at all. Instead, you construct a simple, analytically tractable conditional vector field between individual noise-data pairs — the straight line \(u_t(x \mid x_0, x_1) = x_1 - x_0\) — and regress against it directly. The marginal vector field that the model learns, averaged over all pairs, is provably consistent with the data distribution.

This is what separates flow matching from earlier continuous normalizing flow (CNF) methods: those methods required integrating the ODE during training to compute the log-likelihood, which was computationally prohibitive. Flow matching bypasses this entirely. The training objective is a simple mean-squared error between the network's predicted vector field and the analytically computed conditional target. The consequence is that flow matching trains as cheaply as a standard diffusion model but produces straighter trajectories that require far fewer ODE steps to integrate accurately at inference time.

docs.title: Why it matters at the frontier
docs.text:
The practical impact of flow matching became undeniable in 2024. Black Forest Labs released FLUX.1, an open-weight image generation model built on Rectified Flow (a flow matching variant) that outperformed DALL-E 3 and Stable Diffusion 3 on human preference benchmarks while running inference in 20–28 steps. AlphaFold 3 adopted a flow matching-like diffusion module as its structure prediction head, replacing the score-based diffusion used in earlier protein structure work. Meta's Voicebox and AudioBox use flow matching for zero-shot speech synthesis and audio generation. The convergence is not coincidental: flow matching's straighter paths translate directly into fewer neural function evaluations (NFEs) at inference, which is the dominant cost in production deployment.

The theoretical significance runs deeper than engineering efficiency. Flow matching, score matching, and denoising diffusion probabilistic models are all instances of the same underlying framework — learning to transport one probability distribution to another. Flow matching makes this transport explicit and geometrically interpretable: the learned vector field is a velocity field on the space of probability measures, and the quality of generation is directly tied to the curvature of the learned paths. This geometric view has opened new research directions in optimal transport, Riemannian flow matching for non-Euclidean data, and discrete flow matching for language and protein sequences. Frontier labs are actively working on all three, and the theoretical tools are maturing fast enough that practical improvements are following within months of theoretical results.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
• Continuous Normalizing Flow (CNF) — a generative model defined by an ODE \(\dot{x} = v_\theta(x, t)\) whose solution maps a simple source distribution to a complex target distribution; the flow is invertible by construction.
  • Vector field — a function \(v: \mathbb{R}^d \times [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}^d\) that assigns a velocity to every point in space at every time; integrating it defines a trajectory (flow) through space.
  • Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) — the training objective that regresses the network against analytically computable per-sample conditional vector fields, avoiding ODE simulation during training.
  • Probability path — a time-indexed family of distributions \(p_t\) interpolating between the source \(p_0\) and target \(p_1\); the vector field generates this path by transporting mass continuously.
  • Optimal Transport (OT) coupling — a joint distribution over (noise, data) pairs that minimizes the expected squared distance \(\mathbb{E}[\|x_1 - x_0\|^2]\); using OT couplings instead of independent pairs straightens the learned trajectories.
  • Rectified Flow — a flow matching variant (Liu et al., 2022) that iteratively "reflows" trajectories by re-pairing noise and data using the model's own transport map, progressively straightening paths.
  • Neural Function Evaluations (NFEs) — the number of times the network \(v_\theta\) is called during ODE integration at inference; straighter paths require fewer NFEs for the same accuracy.
  • Interpolant — the time-indexed path \(x_t = \alpha_t x_1 + \sigma_t x_0\) connecting a noise sample \(x_0\) and a data sample \(x_1\); the choice of \(\alpha_t\) and \(\sigma_t\) determines path geometry and is a design choice.

docs.title: Mathematical foundations
docs.text:
The flow matching training objective starts from the marginal flow matching loss, which is intractable directly but can be replaced by the conditional flow matching loss without changing the gradient:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t,\, x_0 \sim p_0,\, x_1 \sim p_1} \left\| v_\theta(x_t, t) - u_t(x_t \mid x_0, x_1) \right\|^2 \]

where \(v_\theta(x_t, t)\) is the neural network's predicted vector field evaluated at the interpolated point \(x_t\) and time \(t\), \(u_t(x_t \mid x_0, x_1)\) is the analytically known conditional target vector field for the specific pair \((x_0, x_1)\), \(x_0 \sim p_0\) is a noise sample drawn from the source distribution (typically \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\)), \(x_1 \sim p_1\) is a data sample drawn from the target distribution, and \(t \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1]\) is a time uniformly sampled from the unit interval. This equation says that training is pure regression: at each step, sample a noise-data pair, interpolate to get \(x_t\), compute the analytic target velocity, and minimize the squared error.

The linear interpolant (the simplest and most common choice) defines the interpolated point and its conditional target velocity as:

\[ x_t = (1 - t)\, x_0 + t\, x_1, \qquad u_t(x_t \mid x_0, x_1) = x_1 - x_0 \]

where \(x_t \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is the point at time \(t \in [0,1]\) along the straight line from \(x_0\) to \(x_1\), \(x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is the noise sample, \(x_1 \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is the data sample, and \(u_t = x_1 - x_0\) is the constant displacement velocity along that line — independent of \(t\). This equation says that the conditional target is simply the displacement vector: constant along the path, the same at every timestep. The model learns to predict this displacement, averaged over all pairs in the dataset.

The OT-CFM objective replaces independent sampling of \((x_0, x_1)\) with a minibatch OT coupling \(\pi^*(x_0, x_1)\) that minimizes expected squared displacement:

\[ \pi^* = \arg\min_{\pi \in \Pi(p_0, p_1)} \mathbb{E}_{(x_0, x_1) \sim \pi} \left[ \|x_1 - x_0\|^2 \right] \]

where \(\Pi(p_0, p_1)\) is the set of all joint distributions whose marginals are \(p_0\) and \(p_1\) respectively, \(\pi\) is a candidate coupling (joint distribution over noise-data pairs), and \(\pi^*\) is the optimal transport plan that pairs each noise sample with the data point it is geometrically closest to in expectation. This equation says that OT coupling minimizes the average path length, which in turn minimizes trajectory curvature and reduces the NFEs needed at inference.

The continuity equation is the PDE that any valid probability path must satisfy:

\[ \frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (p_t\, v_t) = 0 \]

where \(p_t : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\) is the probability density at time \(t\), \(v_t : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d\) is the vector field generating the flow at time \(t\), and \(\nabla \cdot\) denotes the divergence operator over the spatial coordinates. This equation says that probability mass is conserved: the vector field cannot create or destroy probability, only transport it. Flow matching implicitly satisfies this constraint by construction — the learned vector field generates a valid probability path by design.

docs.title: Key algorithms / techniques
docs.text:
• Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) — Lipman et al. (2022); the foundational algorithm that replaces the intractable marginal flow matching objective with a tractable conditional regression loss, enabling simulation-free training of CNFs.
  • OT-CFM (Optimal Transport CFM) — Tong et al. (2023); augments CFM with minibatch OT couplings to straighten trajectories, reducing NFEs at inference without changing the training architecture.
  • Rectified Flow — Liu et al. (2022); independently derived flow matching with linear interpolants, plus the "reflow" procedure that iteratively re-pairs noise and data using the trained model to further straighten paths.
  • Multisample Flow Matching — Pooladian et al. (2023); uses minibatch OT couplings across multiple samples simultaneously to construct straighter flows, with theoretical guarantees on trajectory straightness.
  • Optimal Flow Matching — Kornilov et al. (2024); constructs displacement interpolants that provably minimize path curvature, achieving near-one-step generation on standard benchmarks.
  • Riemannian Flow Matching — Chen & Lipman (2023); extends CFM to Riemannian manifolds (spheres, tori, SO(3)) using geodesic interpolants, enabling flow matching on protein backbone angles and other non-Euclidean data.
  • Discrete Flow Matching — Campbell et al. (2024); adapts the CFM framework to discrete state spaces (tokens, graphs) by defining flows over categorical distributions, enabling flow-based language and protein sequence generation.
  • Carré du Champ Flow Matching — Bamberger et al. (2025); introduces geometry-aware anisotropic noise schedules derived from the carré du champ operator, resolving the quality-generalization tradeoff and preventing memorization on complex data manifolds.

docs.title: Current SotA
docs.text: FLUX.1-dev (Black Forest Labs, 2024), built on Rectified Flow, achieves a human preference win rate of 69% against DALL-E 3 on the GenAI-Bench benchmark and generates 1024×1024 images in 20–28 NFEs. On the ImageNet 256×256 class-conditional generation benchmark, flow matching models reach FID scores below 2.0 with 10–20 function evaluations, compared to 50–1000 for DDPM-class models at equivalent quality. For protein structure generation, AlphaFold 3's flow matching module achieves a median TM-score of 0.85 on CAMEO blind prediction targets (2024), surpassing all prior single-sequence methods.

docs.title: What's happening now
docs.text:
Research frontiers. The most active theoretical direction is extending flow matching to non-Euclidean and discrete spaces. Riemannian Flow Matching (Chen & Lipman, 2023) handles smooth manifolds like protein backbone torsion angles, but the extension to combinatorial spaces — graphs, token sequences, molecular graphs with variable topology — requires fundamentally different interpolant constructions. Discrete Flow Matching (Campbell et al., 2024) and related masked diffusion approaches are converging on a shared framework, but the theoretical guarantees available for continuous flows (path straightness, OT optimality) do not yet transfer cleanly. Bamberger et al. (2025) introduced the carré du champ operator as a tool for constructing geometry-aware noise schedules, which opens the question of whether operator-theoretic tools from stochastic analysis can systematically resolve the quality-generalization tradeoff across data modalities.

Engineering and systems. The dominant engineering challenge is reducing the cost of OT coupling computation at training time. Exact OT on a minibatch of size \(n\) costs \(O(n^3)\) with the Hungarian algorithm or \(O(n^2 / \epsilon)\) with Sinkhorn, which becomes a bottleneck at large batch sizes. Current practice uses approximate minibatch OT with Sinkhorn regularization (\(\epsilon \approx 0.05\)) and batch sizes of 256–1024, which is fast enough for image generation but may not scale to the trillion-token batches used in language model training. Several groups are exploring learned couplings — using a small auxiliary network to propose pairings — as a way to amortize the OT cost. On the inference side, consistency distillation applied to flow matching models (as in Stable Diffusion 3's distilled variants) can reduce NFEs to 4–8 with minimal quality loss, and this is now standard practice in production deployments.

Open problems. The central unresolved question is: Can we mathematically guarantee and dynamically enforce that learned vector fields do not develop crossing paths or singularities when scaling to high-dimensional, hybrid discrete-continuous spaces, without incurring prohibitive OT matching costs at training time? Path crossings — where two trajectories from different data points pass through the same location at the same time — are provably impossible under exact OT couplings in continuous spaces, but the guarantees break down under minibatch approximations, in discrete spaces, and when the source and target distributions have overlapping support in complex ways. A related open question is whether there exists a principled way to choose the noise schedule (the interpolant \(\alpha_t, \sigma_t\)) for a given data modality without exhaustive empirical search — current choices (linear, cosine, learned) are largely heuristic and the sensitivity to this choice is poorly understood theoretically.

docs.text:

  • Meta AI — Voicebox (2023) and AudioBox (2024), zero-shot speech synthesis and audio generation at production scale; flow matching over mel-spectrogram representations with masked conditioning — https://ai.meta.com/research/publications/voicebox-text-guided-multilingual-universal-speech-generation-at-scale/

docs.title: Minimum Valuable Build
docs.text:
What you're building: A from-scratch PyTorch implementation of Conditional Flow Matching with OT paths, trained on a 2D double-moon dataset, with real-time visualization of the learned vector field.

Why this build: The double-moon dataset makes the vector field visually interpretable — you can literally watch the network learn to draw straight lines from noise to data, and see what happens when paths are not straight. This is the fastest way to develop intuition for why OT couplings matter.

Stack: Python 3.10+, PyTorch 2.1+, matplotlib 3.7+, scipy 1.11+ (for OT coupling), numpy 1.24+. No GPU required — runs on free Colab CPU in under 2 minutes.

Estimated time: 25–35 minutes end-to-end.

docs.title: The recipe
docs.text:
1. Install dependencies and generate the dataset
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.spatial.distance import cdist
from scipy.optimize import linear_sum_assignment

# Generate double-moon data (target distribution p_1)
def make_moons(n=2000, noise=0.05):
    n_half = n // 2
    theta0 = np.linspace(0, np.pi, n_half)
    theta1 = np.linspace(0, np.pi, n_half)
    x0 = np.stack([np.cos(theta0), np.sin(theta0)], axis=1)
    x1 = np.stack([1 - np.cos(theta1), 1 - np.sin(theta1) - 0.5], axis=1)
    X = np.concatenate([x0, x1], axis=0)
    X += np.random.randn(*X.shape) * noise
    return torch.tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32)

data = make_moons(n=4000)
print(f"Data shape: {data.shape}")  # (4000, 2)
assert data.shape == (4000, 2)
  1. Define the vector field network
class VectorField(nn.Module):
    """MLP that maps (x, t) -> velocity in R^2."""
    def __init__(self, hidden=256):
        super().__init__()
        # Input: 2D position + 1D time = 3 dims
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(3, hidden),
            nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, hidden),
            nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, hidden),
            nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, 2),
        )

    def forward(self, x, t):
        # x: (B, 2), t: (B,) or scalar
        if t.dim() == 0:
            t = t.expand(x.shape[0])
        t_emb = t.unsqueeze(-1)  # (B, 1)
        xt = torch.cat([x, t_emb], dim=-1)  # (B, 3)
        return self.net(xt)

model = VectorField(hidden=256)
print(f"Parameters: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()):,}")
  1. Implement minibatch OT coupling
def ot_coupling(x0, x1):
    """
    Compute optimal transport coupling between minibatches x0 and x1.
    Returns reordered x0 such that (x0[i], x1[i]) are OT-paired.
    Cost matrix: squared Euclidean distance.
    """
    C = cdist(x0.numpy(), x1.numpy(), metric='sqeuclidean')
    row_ind, col_ind = linear_sum_assignment(C)
    return x0[row_ind], x1[col_ind]

# Sanity check: OT cost should be <= independent pairing cost
x0_test = torch.randn(64, 2)
x1_test = data[:64]
x0_ot, x1_ot = ot_coupling(x0_test, x1_test)
cost_ot = ((x1_ot - x0_ot) ** 2).sum(dim=-1).mean().item()
cost_ind = ((x1_test - x0_test) ** 2).sum(dim=-1).mean().item()
assert cost_ot <= cost_ind + 1e-4, "OT cost should not exceed independent cost"
print(f"OT cost: {cost_ot:.4f} vs independent: {cost_ind:.4f}")
  1. Write the CFM training loop
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4)
batch_size = 256
n_steps = 5000
losses = []

for step in range(n_steps):
    # Sample noise (source distribution p_0)
    x0 = torch.randn(batch_size, 2)

    # Sample data (target distribution p_1)
    idx = torch.randint(0, len(data), (batch_size,))
    x1 = data[idx]

    # OT coupling: pair x0 with nearest x1 in transport sense
    x0_paired, x1_paired = ot_coupling(x0, x1)

    # Sample time uniformly in [0, 1]
    t = torch.rand(batch_size)

    # Linear interpolant: x_t = (1-t)*x0 + t*x1
    t_col = t.unsqueeze(-1)  # (B, 1) for broadcasting
    xt = (1 - t_col) * x0_paired + t_col * x1_paired

    # Conditional target velocity: u_t = x1 - x0 (constant along path)
    ut = x1_paired - x0_paired

    # Predict velocity and compute MSE loss
    vt_pred = model(xt, t)
    loss = ((vt_pred - ut) ** 2).mean()

    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

    losses.append(loss.item())
    if step % 500 == 0:
        print(f"Step {step:5d} | Loss: {loss.item():.6f}")

print("Training complete.")
  1. Generate samples by integrating the learned ODE
@torch.no_grad()
def generate(model, n_samples=1000, n_steps=20):
    """
    Euler integration of dx/dt = v_theta(x, t) from t=0 to t=1.
    n_steps=20 is sufficient for well-trained flow matching models.
    """
    x = torch.randn(n_samples, 2)
    dt = 1.0 / n_steps
    for i in range(n_steps):
        t = torch.full((n_samples,), i * dt)
        v = model(x, t)
        x = x + v * dt
    return x

samples = generate(model, n_samples=2000, n_steps=20)
print(f"Generated samples shape: {samples.shape}")  # (2000, 2)
  1. Visualize the vector field and generated samples
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4))

# Panel 1: Training data
axes[0].scatter(data[:, 0], data[:, 1], s=2, alpha=0.3, c='steelblue')
axes[0].set_title("Training data (double moon)")
axes[0].set_xlim(-2.5, 3.5); axes[0].set_ylim(-2, 2.5)

# Panel 2: Generated samples
axes[1].scatter(samples[:, 0], samples[:, 1], s=2, alpha=0.3, c='coral')
axes[1].set_title("Generated samples (20 Euler steps)")
axes[1].set_xlim(-2.5, 3.5); axes[1].set_ylim(-2, 2.5)

# Panel 3: Learned vector field at t=0.5
grid_x = np.linspace(-2.5, 3.5, 20)
grid_y = np.linspace(-2, 2.5, 20)
gx, gy = np.meshgrid(grid_x, grid_y)
grid_pts = torch.tensor(
    np.stack([gx.ravel(), gy.ravel()], axis=1), dtype=torch.float32
)
t_mid = torch.full((grid_pts.shape[0],), 0.5)
with torch.no_grad():
    vf = model(grid_pts, t_mid).numpy()
axes[2].quiver(
    grid_pts[:, 0], grid_pts[:, 1],
    vf[:, 0], vf[:, 1],
    alpha=0.7, scale=30, color='darkgreen'
)
axes[2].set_title("Learned vector field at t=0.5")
axes[2].set_xlim(-2.5, 3.5); axes[2].set_ylim(-2, 2.5)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("flow_matching_result.png", dpi=150)
plt.show()
print("Saved: flow_matching_result.png")

docs.title: Expected output
docs.text: After 5000 training steps (roughly 90 seconds on CPU), the loss should drop from approximately 0.8–1.2 to below 0.05. The generated samples panel should show two clear crescent shapes matching the training data. The vector field panel at \(t = 0.5\) should show arrows pointing roughly from the center of the noise distribution toward the two moon clusters — visibly straighter than the curved fields you would see from a score-based model. If you reduce n_steps in generate() to 5, the samples should still be recognizable as double moons, demonstrating the efficiency of straight-path flow matching.

docs.title: Common failure modes
docs.text:
• Loss plateaus above 0.2 after 2000 steps → The OT coupling on CPU with linear_sum_assignment is exact but slow for batch_size > 256; reduce to 128 or switch to Sinkhorn with scipy.sparse.csgraph.min_weight_full_bipartite_matching.
  • Generated samples form a single blob, not two moons → The network is underfitting; increase hidden dimension to 512 or add a fourth hidden layer.
  • AssertionError in OT sanity check → Floating point edge case; the tolerance 1e-4 handles this, but if it fires, check that x0_test and x1_test have the same batch size.
  • Quiver plot arrows all point the same direction → The model has not converged; run for more steps or check that t is being passed correctly (must be a 1D tensor of shape (B,), not a scalar).
  • Samples look good at 20 steps but noisy at 5 steps → OT coupling was not used or batch size was too small; verify the ot_coupling function is being called in the training loop.

If this build worked for you — a ⭐ on GitHub is the only signal we collect.

docs.title: What comes next
docs.text:
Score matching and flow matching are complementary views of the same transport problem — score matching estimates the gradient of the log-density, while flow matching estimates the velocity field directly; understanding both makes the connection to diffusion models precise.

  • [[score-matching]] — the probabilistic foundation that flow matching generalizes; the score function \(\nabla_x \log p_t(x)\) is recoverable from the flow matching vector field via the Fokker-Planck equation.
  • [[diffusion-models]] — the predecessor framework that flow matching largely supersedes for new architectures; the DDPM noise schedule is a special case of the flow matching interpolant with a specific \(\alpha_t, \sigma_t\) choice.
  • [[normalizing-flows]] — the model class that flow matching trains; understanding the change-of-variables formula and the continuous-time limit clarifies why simulation-free training is non-trivial.

docs.title: Connected topics
docs.text:
• [[diffusion-models]] — Flow matching generalizes diffusion models by training continuous-time normalizing flows with straight paths.
  • [[score-matching]] — Flow matching is a simulation-free training method closely related to path-based score matching.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Lipman et al. (2022) — "Flow Matching for Generative Modeling" — https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02747 — the original CFM paper; the appendix contains the proof that the conditional and marginal flow matching objectives have identical gradients, which is the theoretical core of the method.
  • Pooladian et al. (2023) — "Multisample Flow Matching: Straightening Flows with Minibatch Couplings" — https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14772 — derives the theoretical relationship between OT coupling quality and trajectory curvature, with quantitative bounds on NFE reduction.
  • Kornilov et al. (2024) — "Optimal Flow Matching: Learning Straight Trajectories in Just One Step" — https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13117 — the clearest exposition of why displacement interpolants minimize curvature and how to construct them in practice.
  • Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden (2022) — "Building Normalizing Flows with Stochastic Interpolants" — https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.15571 — establishes the stochastic interpolant framework that unifies flow matching, score matching, and diffusion under a single theoretical umbrella.
  • Lilian Weng's survey on flow-based deep generative models (lil'log, 2018, updated 2021) — https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2018-10-13-flow-based-deep-learning/ — provides the normalizing flow background that makes the CNF connection precise; read before the Lipman et al. paper if CNFs are unfamiliar.
  • Chen & Lipman (2023) — "Riemannian Flow Matching on General Geometries" — https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.03660 — extends CFM to non-Euclidean manifolds; essential reading for anyone applying flow matching to molecular or structural biology data.

docs.title: Score Matching
docs.text: TL;DR: Score matching trains a model to predict the gradient of the log-density — the score function — rather than the density itself, eliminating the intractable normalizing constant and providing the probabilistic foundation on which every modern diffusion model is built.

docs.title: For your reader type
docs.text: I am... Start here Goal MS/applied practitioner Key algorithms → Code & implementations Understand the objective underlying every diffusion model you deploy Curious generalist What it is → Why it matters Understand why diffusion models work without knowing the partition function Math/theory student Core concepts → Mathematical foundations Derive the integration-by-parts trick and the denoising equivalence Researcher / frontier Current SotA → What's happening now Find open questions on variance reduction and unified score estimators

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Imagine trying to calculate the exact volume under an incredibly complex, high-dimensional probability landscape — such as the space of all possible 256×256 images — just to ensure your model's distribution integrates to one. This intractable integration is the normalizing constant, or partition function, and it makes standard maximum likelihood estimation impossible for energy-based models: you cannot evaluate the likelihood of a single data point without first solving a global integral over every conceivable input. The insight that breaks this deadlock is geometric rather than probabilistic: if you know the slope of the landscape at every point — the direction and steepness of the gradient — you can reconstruct the shape of the landscape without ever measuring its total volume. Score matching is the formalization of that insight. Instead of learning the density \(p(x)\) directly, it learns the score function \( abla_x \log p(x)\), the gradient of the log-density with respect to the data, and matches it to the model's predicted score at every point in the data distribution.

The computational payoff is immediate and decisive. Given an unnormalized energy-based model \(p_ heta(x) \propto \exp(-f_ heta(x))\), the log-density is \(\log p_ heta(x) = -f_ heta(x) - \log Z_ heta\), where \(Z_ heta\) is the partition function. Because \(Z_ heta\) is a constant with respect to \(x\), it vanishes under differentiation: \( abla_x \log p_ heta(x) = - abla_x f_ heta(x)\). A global integration problem collapses into a local differentiation problem that autograd handles in milliseconds. The remaining challenge is that the true data score \( abla_x \log p_{ ext{data}}(x)\) is also unknown — we only have samples. Hyvärinen (2005) resolved this with an integration-by-parts argument showing that the expected squared difference between model and data scores can be rewritten entirely in terms of quantities computable from the model alone, without ever querying the true score. Vincent (2011) then showed that this objective is equivalent to training a denoising autoencoder, making score matching scalable to the high-dimensional settings where it matters most.

The consequence of these two results is that score matching is not merely a theoretical curiosity: it is the training objective that underlies every modern diffusion model. When a DDPM or a flow-matching model learns to predict noise, it is learning the score of a noise-perturbed data distribution. The architecture, the noise schedule, the sampling procedure — all of these are engineering choices layered on top of the core score-matching objective. Understanding score matching at the level of its derivation is therefore the prerequisite for understanding why any of those engineering choices work, and for knowing when they can be improved.

docs.title: Why it matters at the frontier
docs.text:
Every major generative modeling lab — DeepMind, Google Brain, OpenAI, Stability AI — has converged on score-based or flow-based models as the foundation for their image, audio, and video generation systems. The reason is not aesthetic: it is that score matching is the only known training objective that scales to high-dimensional continuous data without requiring either an explicit likelihood (as in normalizing flows) or a discrete latent space (as in VQ-VAEs). The connection runs deep: Song et al. (2020) showed that the forward noising process of DDPM defines a stochastic differential equation whose reverse is governed by the score of the noised distribution, unifying score matching, diffusion models, and stochastic optimal control into a single framework. This unification is what makes score matching a live research topic rather than a settled one — the framework is powerful enough that improvements to the score estimator propagate directly into better generation quality, faster sampling, and more stable training.

The open frontier concerns variance and efficiency. The original Hyvärinen objective requires computing the trace of the Jacobian of the score network, which costs \(O(d)\) backward passes for \(d\)-dimensional data — prohibitive for images. Denoising score matching sidesteps this by perturbing data and regressing to the noise, but introduces a bias that depends on the noise level. Sliced score matching (Song & Ermon, 2019) uses random projections to estimate the trace cheaply, but adds its own variance. The deeper question — how to construct a score estimator that is simultaneously unbiased, low-variance, and computationally cheap across all noise scales — remains open, and its resolution would directly improve the training efficiency of every diffusion model in production today.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
• Score function — the gradient of the log-density with respect to the data, \( abla_x \log p(x)\), which points in the direction of steepest increase in log-probability at each point \(x\).
  • Partition function — the normalizing constant \(Z = \int \exp(-f(x))\, dx\) that makes an energy function a valid probability density; it is intractable in high dimensions and vanishes under differentiation with respect to \(x\).
  • Energy-based model (EBM) — a model of the form \(p_ heta(x) \propto \exp(-f_ heta(x))\) where \(f_ heta\) is a neural network; the score is \(- abla_x f_ heta(x)\), computable without \(Z\).
  • Fisher divergence — the expected squared \(\ell_2\) distance between the model score and the data score, \(\mathbb{E}_{p_{ ext{data}}}\left[\| abla_x \log p_ heta(x) - abla_x \log p_{ ext{data}}(x)\|^2 ight]\); minimizing this is the score matching objective.
  • Integration-by-parts trick — the algebraic manipulation (Hyvärinen, 2005) that rewrites the Fisher divergence into an expectation involving only the model's score and its Jacobian diagonal, eliminating the unknown data score from the objective.
  • Denoising score matching (DSM) — the reformulation (Vincent, 2011) showing that matching the score of a noise-perturbed distribution \(q_\sigma( ilde{x} \mid x)\) is equivalent to training a denoising function, making the objective scalable and free of explicit Jacobian computation.
  • Sliced score matching — the approximation (Song & Ermon, 2019) that estimates the Jacobian trace using random projections \(\mathbf{v}^ op abla_x s_ heta(x) \mathbf{v}\), reducing the cost from \(O(d)\) to \(O(1)\) backward passes per sample.
  • Noise-conditional score network (NCSN) — a score network \(s_ heta(x, \sigma)\) trained simultaneously across a geometric sequence of noise levels \(\sigma_1 > \sigma_2 > \cdots > \sigma_L\), enabling annealed Langevin dynamics sampling.

docs.title: Mathematical foundations
docs.text:
The score matching objective. The Fisher divergence between model and data is:

\[ J( heta) = \mathbb{E}_{p_{ ext{data}}(x)}\!\left[ rac{1}{2}\left\|s_ heta(x) - abla_x \log p_{ ext{data}}(x) ight\|^2 ight] \]

where \(s_ heta(x)\) is the model's predicted score (a neural network mapping \(\mathbb{R}^d o \mathbb{R}^d\)), \( abla_x \log p_{ ext{data}}(x)\) is the true data score (unknown), and the expectation is over data samples. Minimizing \(J( heta)\) forces the model's score to match the data's score in the \(\ell_2\) sense, averaged over the data distribution.

The integration-by-parts reformulation (Hyvärinen, 2005) shows that \(J( heta)\) equals, up to a constant independent of \( heta\):

\[ J_{ ext{ISM}}( heta) = \mathbb{E}_{p_{ ext{data}}(x)}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{d} \partial_{x_i} s_{ heta,i}(x) + rac{1}{2}\left\|s_ heta(x) ight\|^2 ight] \]

where \(s_{ heta,i}(x)\) is the \(i\)-th component of the score network output, \(\partial_{x_i} s_{ heta,i}(x)\) is the \(i\)-th diagonal entry of the Jacobian of \(s_ heta\) (requiring one backward pass per dimension), and \(d\) is the data dimensionality. The true data score has been eliminated entirely — the objective is computable from the model alone, given only data samples. The cost is the Jacobian diagonal, which requires \(O(d)\) backward passes and is prohibitive for image-scale data.

The denoising equivalence (Vincent, 2011). Define a noised sample \( ilde{x} = x + \epsilon\) where \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)\). The denoising score matching objective is:

\[ J_{ ext{DSM}}( heta) = \mathbb{E}_{p_{ ext{data}}(x)}\,\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2 I)}\!\left[\left\|s_ heta( ilde{x}) - abla_{ ilde{x}} \log q_\sigma( ilde{x} \mid x) ight\|^2 ight] \]

where \(q_\sigma( ilde{x} \mid x) = \mathcal{N}( ilde{x}; x, \sigma^2 I)\) is the Gaussian noise kernel, \( abla_{ ilde{x}} \log q_\sigma( ilde{x} \mid x) = -( ilde{x} - x)/\sigma^2\) is the score of the kernel (the direction pointing from the noisy sample back to the clean sample), and \(\sigma\) is the noise standard deviation. Training a score network to predict \(-( ilde{x} - x)/\sigma^2\) — equivalently, to denoise — is identical to minimizing the Fisher divergence with respect to the noised distribution, with no Jacobian computation required.

The multi-scale objective (Song & Ermon, 2019). For a geometric sequence of noise levels \(\{\sigma_i\}_{i=1}^{L}\) with \(\sigma_1 > \sigma_2 > \cdots > \sigma_L\), the NCSN objective is:

\[ \mathcal{L}( heta) = rac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^{L} \lambda(\sigma_i)\,\mathbb{E}_{p_{ ext{data}}(x)}\,\mathbb{E}_{ ilde{x} \sim q_{\sigma_i}(\cdot \mid x)}\!\left[\left\|\sigma_i\, s_ heta( ilde{x}, \sigma_i) + rac{ ilde{x} - x}{\sigma_i} ight\|^2 ight] \]

where \(\lambda(\sigma_i) = \sigma_i^2\) is a weighting function that equalizes the magnitude of the score across noise levels, \(s_ heta( ilde{x}, \sigma_i)\) is the noise-conditional score network evaluated at noise level \(\sigma_i\), and \(L\) is the total number of noise levels. A single network learns the score at every noise scale simultaneously, enabling annealed Langevin sampling from coarse to fine.

docs.title: Key algorithms / techniques
docs.text:
• Implicit Score Matching (ISM) (Hyvärinen, 2005) — the original formulation that uses integration by parts to eliminate the data score from the objective, at the cost of computing the diagonal of the score Jacobian (\(O(d)\) backward passes).
  • Denoising Score Matching (DSM) (Vincent, 2011) — replaces the Jacobian computation with a regression target derived from the noise kernel score, making the objective \(O(1)\) in compute and scaling to high-dimensional data; the direct ancestor of DDPM's training objective.
  • Sliced Score Matching (SSM) (Song & Ermon, 2019) — approximates the Jacobian trace using random unit vectors \(\mathbf{v}\) via \(\mathbf{v}^\top (\nabla_x s_\theta(x))\mathbf{v}\), reducing cost to a small constant number of backward passes regardless of dimension.
  • Noise-Conditional Score Networks (NCSN / NCSNv2) (Song & Ermon, 2019; Song et al., 2020) — trains a single score network conditioned on noise level across a geometric schedule, enabling annealed Langevin dynamics that navigate from a tractable noisy distribution to the data distribution.
  • Score-based SDE framework (Song et al., 2020) — unifies DDPM and NCSN by showing that any forward noising process defines an SDE whose reverse is governed by the score, enabling continuous-time score matching and deterministic ODE sampling.
  • Tweedie's formula — a closed-form relationship between the score and the posterior mean of the clean data given a noisy observation, \(\mathbb{E}[x \mid \tilde{x}] = \tilde{x} + \sigma^2 \nabla_{\tilde{x}} \log q_\sigma(\tilde{x})\), used to convert score estimates into direct denoising predictions.

docs.text: Paper Year Authors Why essential "Estimation of Non-Normalized Statistical Models by Score Matching" 2005 Hyvärinen Introduces score matching and the integration-by-parts trick; the foundational paper "A Connection Between Score Matching and Denoising Autoencoders" 2011 Vincent Proves DSM equivalence; makes score matching scalable and connects it to denoising "Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution" 2019 Song & Ermon Introduces NCSN and multi-scale score matching; the direct precursor to DDPM "Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations" 2020 Song et al. Unifies all score-based methods under a continuous SDE framework; defines the modern field

docs.title: Seminal papers & test-of-time
docs.text: Paper Year Key contribution Hyvärinen, "Estimation of Non-Normalized Statistical Models by Score Matching" 2005 Proved that Fisher divergence can be minimized without knowing the data score; enabled EBM training without MCMC Vincent, "A Connection Between Score Matching and Denoising Autoencoders" 2011 Showed denoising and score matching are the same objective; unlocked scalable score estimation Song & Ermon, "Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution" 2019 First high-quality image generation via score matching + Langevin dynamics; introduced NCSN Ho et al., "Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models" 2020 Reframed DSM as a variational bound; achieved state-of-the-art image quality and triggered the diffusion era Song et al., "Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations" 2020 Continuous-time unification of DDPM and NCSN; introduced probability flow ODEs for deterministic sampling

docs.title: Current SotA
docs.text: Score matching as a training objective underlies the highest-performing generative models across modalities. On class-conditional ImageNet 256×256, EDM2 (Karras et al., 2024) achieves FID 1.58 using an improved score-parameterization and preconditioning scheme, surpassing the previous best of 1.79 from DiT-XL/2. On text-to-image generation, FLUX.1 (Black Forest Labs, 2024) — built on a rectified flow objective that is a continuous-time variant of score matching — achieves state-of-the-art human preference scores on the GenAI-Bench benchmark, outperforming DALL-E 3 and Stable Diffusion 3 on prompt alignment. For audio, Voicebox (Le et al., Meta, 2023) applies continuous-time score matching to speech synthesis, achieving a word error rate of 1.9% on LibriSpeech test-clean with zero-shot voice cloning.

docs.title: What's happening now
docs.text:
Research frontiers. The most active theoretical direction is understanding the variance structure of different score estimators across noise scales. DSM is unbiased at a fixed noise level but the optimal weighting across levels — the \(\lambda(\sigma)\) function in the NCSN objective — is not analytically known and is typically set heuristically. Karras et al. (2022, "Elucidating the Design Space of Diffusion-Based Generative Models," arXiv:2206.00364) showed that the choice of noise schedule, score parameterization, and sampler interact in non-obvious ways, and that principled choices yield large quality improvements without architectural changes. More recently, Kingma & Gao (2023, "Understanding Diffusion Objectives as the ELBO with Simple Data Augmentation," arXiv:2303.00848) proved that the weighted DSM objective is equivalent to a variational lower bound with a specific data augmentation, providing a principled justification for the weighting schemes used in practice and opening the door to tighter bounds.

Engineering and systems. The dominant engineering challenge is reducing the number of score function evaluations required at inference time. Standard Langevin dynamics requires hundreds to thousands of steps; DDIM (Song et al., 2020) reduced this to 50 deterministic steps by treating the score network as defining a probability flow ODE. Consistency models (Song et al., 2023, arXiv:2303.01469) go further by training a network to map any noisy sample directly to the clean data in a single step, achieving FID 2.06 on CIFAR-10 with one network evaluation. The engineering question is how to train consistency models stably at scale — the distillation procedure is sensitive to the teacher score network's quality, and direct consistency training (without a pretrained teacher) remains less stable than distillation-based approaches.

Open problems. The central unresolved question is: Can we construct a score estimator that is simultaneously unbiased, low-variance, and \(O(1)\) in compute across all noise scales, without requiring a pretrained teacher or a fixed noise schedule? ISM is unbiased but \(O(d)\) in compute. DSM is \(O(1)\) but introduces a noise-level-dependent bias. SSM is \(O(1)\) but adds projection variance. A unified estimator that analytically controls the bias-variance tradeoff across scales — perhaps by combining energy-based and data-driven score components — would directly improve training efficiency for every diffusion model in production. A second open question is whether score matching can be extended to discrete or mixed continuous-discrete spaces without approximation, which would unlock score-based training for language models and structured data.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Stability AI — Stable Diffusion 3 and SDXL use a latent diffusion model trained with a continuous-time score matching objective (EDM-style preconditioning); deployed at scale via the Stability AI API serving millions of requests per day — https://stability.ai/research/scaling-rectified-flow-transformers-high-resolution-image-synthesis
  • Black Forest Labs — FLUX.1 uses a rectified flow objective (a continuous-time score matching variant) with a transformer backbone; FLUX.1 [dev] and [schnell] are publicly available on Hugging Face and power several commercial image generation products — https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev
  • Meta AI — Voicebox applies continuous-time score matching to non-autoregressive speech synthesis; achieves 1.9% WER on LibriSpeech with zero-shot voice cloning at production quality — https://ai.meta.com/blog/voicebox-generative-ai-model-speech/
  • Google DeepMind — Imagen Video and Lumiere use cascaded diffusion models trained with DSM objectives for text-to-video generation; Lumiere generates 80-frame, 5-second clips at 1024×1024 resolution — https://research.google/blog/lumiere-a-space-time-diffusion-model-for-video-generation/
  • NVIDIA — EDM2 (Karras et al., 2024) is the reference score-parameterization used in NVIDIA's generative research stack; achieves FID 1.58 on ImageNet 256×256 and is the basis for ongoing work on consistency distillation at scale — https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/elucidating-the-design-space-of-diffusion-based-generative-models/

docs.title: Code & implementations
docs.text:
• NCSNv2 (official) — Song & Ermon's reference implementation of Noise-Conditional Score Networks in PyTorch: https://github.com/ermongroup/ncsnv2
  • score_sde (official) — Song et al.'s score-based SDE framework, covering VP-SDE, VE-SDE, and sub-VP-SDE with Langevin and ODE samplers: https://github.com/yang-song/score_sde_pytorch
  • EDM (NVIDIA) — Karras et al.'s elucidated diffusion model with principled score preconditioning, achieving FID 1.58 on ImageNet: https://github.com/NVlabs/edm
  • Consistency Models (official) — Song et al.'s single-step distillation of score networks: https://github.com/openai/consistency_models
  • HuggingFace Diffusers — Production-grade implementations of DDPM, DDIM, and score-based samplers with pretrained checkpoints: https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers

For a hands-on build with this concept, see the MVB on [[denoising-diffusion-probabilistic-models]].

docs.title: What comes next
docs.text:
Score matching provides the probabilistic foundation — the training objective — that DDPM and NCSN are built on. Understanding it at the derivation level makes the noise schedule, the loss weighting, and the sampler design in those models precise rather than heuristic.

  • [[denoising-diffusion-probabilistic-models]] — DDPM is the discrete-time training procedure that operationalizes DSM at scale; the connection between the ELBO and the DSM objective is the key link.
  • [[score-based-sde]] — the continuous-time generalization that unifies DDPM and NCSN under a single SDE framework, enabling probability flow ODE sampling and exact likelihood computation.
  • [[energy-based-models]] — score matching was originally developed as a training method for EBMs; understanding EBMs clarifies why the partition function is intractable and what score matching is actually bypassing.
  • [[flow-matching]] — flow matching generalizes the score-based training idea by directly regressing vector fields rather than score functions, removing the need for a fixed noise schedule entirely.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Hyvärinen, A. (2005). "Estimation of Non-Normalized Statistical Models by Score Matching." Journal of Machine Learning Research, 6, 695–709. https://jmlr.org/papers/v6/hyvarinen05a.html — The original paper; the integration-by-parts derivation in Section 2 is the essential read.
  • Song, Y. & Ermon, S. (2019). "Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution." arXiv:1907.05600. https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.05600 — Introduces NCSN and annealed Langevin dynamics; the experiments section shows the first high-quality score-based image generation.
  • Song, Y. et al. (2020). "Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations." arXiv:2011.13456. https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.13456 — The unification paper; Appendix B contains the proof that the reverse SDE is governed by the score, which is the theoretical core of the modern diffusion literature.
  • Karras, T. et al. (2022). "Elucidating the Design Space of Diffusion-Based Generative Models." arXiv:2206.00364. https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.00364 — A systematic empirical study of how score parameterization, noise schedule, and sampler interact; the most practically useful paper for anyone training a diffusion model.
  • Lilian Weng, "What are Diffusion Models?" (lil'log, 2021). https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2021-07-11-diffusion-models/ — A detailed walkthrough connecting score matching, DDPM, and NCSN with annotated equations; useful as a companion to the original papers.
  • Kingma, D. & Gao, R. (2023). "Understanding Diffusion Objectives as the ELBO with Simple Data Augmentation." arXiv:2303.00848. https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.00848 — Proves that the weighted DSM objective is a variational lower bound, providing a principled justification for loss weighting schemes used in practice.

# Variational Autoencoders
> **TL;DR:** Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are generative models that learn a latent representation of data, allowing for the generation of new, similar data points by sampling from that latent space.

---

## What it is
Imagine you're trying to build a system that can generate realistic images of cats, but instead of just memorizing existing pictures, it can create entirely new ones. Or, consider a medical imaging system that can reconstruct 3D models from limited scan data. These tasks require a model that can understand the underlying structure of data and generate new instances. Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are a key technology for this.

VAEs are a type of generative model that learn a compressed, latent representation of input data. Unlike standard autoencoders that learn a deterministic mapping, VAEs learn a probability distribution in the latent space. This probabilistic approach allows us to sample from the latent space and generate new data points that resemble the training data. The VAE architecture consists of two main components: an encoder, which maps the input data to a latent distribution, and a decoder, which maps samples from the latent distribution back to the original data space.

The key innovation in VAEs is the use of variational inference to train the model. Because the true posterior distribution over the latent variables is often intractable, VAEs approximate it using a simpler, tractable distribution, typically a Gaussian. The model is trained by maximizing a lower bound on the marginal likelihood of the data, known as the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO). This ELBO balances the reconstruction accuracy of the decoder with the similarity between the approximate posterior and a prior distribution over the latent space, encouraging the latent space to be well-structured and continuous.

## Why it matters at the frontier
VAEs are crucial for addressing several open problems in generative modeling. One major challenge is generating high-fidelity, diverse samples from complex, multi-modal data. VAEs offer a framework for learning disentangled representations, where different latent dimensions capture independent factors of variation in the data. This disentanglement can enable more controllable generation, where specific attributes of the generated data can be manipulated by modifying the corresponding latent dimensions.

Frontier labs are actively exploring VAEs for various applications, including image and video generation, anomaly detection, and representation learning. Researchers are also investigating novel VAE architectures and training techniques to improve the quality and diversity of generated samples. For example, researchers are exploring ways to mitigate common artifacts in VAE training, such as blurry reconstructions and mode collapse (Li et al., 2025). The ability to generate realistic and diverse data is critical for advancing research in areas such as computer vision, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning.

## Core concepts
- **Encoder** — A neural network that maps input data to parameters of a latent distribution, typically the mean and variance of a Gaussian.
- **Decoder** — A neural network that maps samples from the latent distribution back to the original data space, generating a reconstruction of the input.
- **Latent Space** — A lower-dimensional space that captures the underlying structure and essential features of the data.
- **Variational Inference** — A technique used to approximate intractable posterior distributions by optimizing a tractable approximation.
- **Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO)** — A lower bound on the marginal likelihood of the data, used as the objective function for training VAEs.
- **Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence** — A measure of the difference between two probability distributions, used to regularize the latent space in VAEs.
- **Reparameterization Trick** — A technique that allows gradients to be backpropagated through stochastic nodes, enabling end-to-end training of VAEs.

## Mathematical foundations
\[\mathcal{L}_{VAE} = \mathbb{E}_{q(z|x)}[\log p(x|z)] - D_{KL}(q(z|x) || p(z))\]

where \(\mathcal{L}_{VAE}\) is the evidence lower bound (ELBO), \(x\) is the input data, \(z\) is the latent variable, \(q(z|x)\) is the approximate posterior, \(p(x|z)\) is the likelihood, \(p(z)\) is the prior, and \(D_{KL}\) is the Kullback-Leibler divergence.
This is the fundamental loss function for Variational Autoencoders, balancing reconstruction accuracy and regularization of the latent space.

\[D_{KL}(q(z|x) || p(z)) = \int q(z|x) \log \frac{q(z|x)}{p(z)} dz\]

where \(q(z|x)\) is the approximate posterior distribution of the latent variable \(z\) given input \(x\), and \(p(z)\) is the prior distribution of the latent variable \(z\).
This equation defines the Kullback-Leibler divergence, which measures the difference between the approximate posterior and the prior, encouraging the latent space to be regularized.

\[\text{ELBO} = \mathbb{E}_{q(z|x)}[\log p(x|z)] - \mathbb{E}_{q(z|x)}[\log q(z|x)] + \mathbb{E}_{q(z|x)}[\log p(z)]\]

where ELBO is the Evidence Lower Bound, \(x\) is the input data, \(z\) is the latent variable, \(q(z|x)\) is the approximate posterior, and \(p(x|z)\) is the likelihood, \(p(z)\) is the prior.
This is an alternative formulation of the ELBO, which is the objective function that VAEs aim to maximize during training.

## Key algorithms / techniques
- **Reparameterization Trick (Kingma & Welling, 2013)** — Enables gradient-based optimization of VAEs by expressing the latent variable as a deterministic function of the parameters of the approximate posterior and a noise variable.
- **Variational Inference (Jordan et al., 1999)** — Approximates the intractable posterior distribution over latent variables by optimizing a tractable variational distribution.
- **Adversarial Training (Goodfellow et al., 2014)** — Combines VAEs with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to improve the quality and realism of generated samples.

## Current SotA
Dora-VAE achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction quality for 3D shapes by using a sharp edge sampling strategy and a dual cross-attention mechanism (Rui Chen et al., 2024). VIVAT (Li et al., 2025) provides a systematic approach to mitigating common artifacts in KL-VAE training, enhancing the overall quality of generated samples. Jian et al. (2025) introduces FAE (Foundation Auto-Encoders), a foundation generative-AI model for anomaly detection in time-series data, based on Variational Auto-Encoders (VAEs).

## What's happening now
Research on VAEs is currently focused on improving the quality, diversity, and controllability of generated samples. New architectures, such as incorporating attention mechanisms and normalizing flows, are being explored to enhance the representational capacity of VAEs and reduce artifacts in generated data. Additionally, researchers are investigating methods for disentangling latent representations, allowing for more fine-grained control over the generated outputs.

Engineering efforts are focused on deploying VAEs in real-world applications, such as anomaly detection, image generation, and data compression. Companies are leveraging cloud platforms like Amazon SageMaker to scale VAE training and inference, enabling the processing of large datasets and the deployment of VAE models in production environments. Optimizations for inference speed and memory usage are also critical for deploying VAEs on resource-constrained devices.

A key open problem is developing VAE architectures that can effectively learn and generate high-fidelity, diverse, and controllable outputs from complex, multi-modal data sources, while also being computationally efficient and robust to noisy data. This requires addressing challenges such as mode collapse, blurry reconstructions, and the difficulty of learning disentangled representations. Further research is needed to develop novel training techniques and architectural innovations that can overcome these limitations.

## Minimum Valuable Build
**What you're building:** A simple convolutional VAE that generates images of handwritten digits from the MNIST dataset.
**Why this build:** This build demonstrates the core principles of VAEs: encoding data into a latent space, and decoding latent vectors back into images.
**Stack:** PyTorch 2.0.0, torchvision 0.15.0
**Estimated time:** 2-3 hours

### The recipe

1. **Set up the environment:**
   ```python
   import torch
   import torch.nn as nn
   import torch.optim as optim
   from torchvision import datasets, transforms
   from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
   import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
   import numpy as np

   device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
   print(f"Using device: {device}")
   ```

2. **Define the VAE architecture:**
   ```python
   class VAE(nn.Module):
       def __init__(self, latent_dim):
           super(VAE, self).__init__()

           # Encoder
           self.encoder = nn.Sequential(
               nn.Conv2d(1, 32, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1),  # 28x28 -> 14x14
               nn.ReLU(),
               nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1), # 14x14 -> 7x7
               nn.ReLU(),
               nn.Flatten(),
               nn.Linear(64 * 7 * 7, 256),
               nn.ReLU()
           )
           self.fc_mu = nn.Linear(256, latent_dim)
           self.fc_logvar = nn.Linear(256, latent_dim)

           # Decoder
           self.decoder = nn.Sequential(
               nn.Linear(latent_dim, 256),
               nn.ReLU(),
               nn.Linear(256, 64 * 7 * 7),
               nn.ReLU(),
               nn.Unflatten(dim=1, unflattened_size=(64, 7, 7)),
               nn.ConvTranspose2d(64, 32, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1, output_padding=1), # 7x7 -> 14x14
               nn.ReLU(),
               nn.ConvTranspose2d(32, 1, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1, output_padding=1), # 14x14 -> 28x28
               nn.Sigmoid()
           )

       def encode(self, x):
           x = self.encoder(x)
           mu = self.fc_mu(x)
           logvar = self.fc_logvar(x)
           return mu, logvar

       def reparameterize(self, mu, logvar):
           std = torch.exp(0.5 * logvar)
           eps = torch.randn_like(std)
           return mu + eps * std

       def decode(self, z):
           x_hat = self.decoder(z)
           return x_hat

       def forward(self, x):
           mu, logvar = self.encode(x)
           z = self.reparameterize(mu, logvar)
           x_hat = self.decode(z)
           return x_hat, mu, logvar
   ```

3. **Define the loss function:**
   ```python
   def loss_function(x_hat, x, mu, logvar):
       reconstruction_loss = nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy(x_hat, x, reduction='sum')
       kl_divergence = -0.5 * torch.sum(1 + logvar - mu.pow(2) - logvar.exp())
       return reconstruction_loss + kl_divergence
   ```

4. **Load the MNIST dataset:**
   ```python
   transform = transforms.Compose([
       transforms.ToTensor()
   ])

   train_dataset = datasets.MNIST(root='./data', train=True, download=True, transform=transform)
   test_dataset = datasets.MNIST(root='./data', train=False, download=True, transform=transform)

   batch_size = 64
   train_loader = DataLoader(train_dataset, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True)
   test_loader = DataLoader(test_dataset, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=False)
   ```

5. **Train the VAE:**
   ```python
   latent_dim = 20
   model = VAE(latent_dim).to(device)
   optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

   epochs = 10
   for epoch in range(epochs):
       model.train()
       train_loss = 0
       for batch_idx, (data, _) in enumerate(train_loader):
           data = data.to(device)
           optimizer.zero_grad()
           x_hat, mu, logvar = model(data)
           loss = loss_function(x_hat, data, mu, logvar)
           loss.backward()
           train_loss += loss.item()
           optimizer.step()

           if batch_idx % 100 == 0:
               print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs}, Batch {batch_idx}/{len(train_loader)}, Loss: {loss.item() / len(data)}")

       print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs}, Average Loss: {train_loss / len(train_loader.dataset)}")
   ```

6. **Generate new images:**
   ```python
   model.eval()
   with torch.no_grad():
       # Sample from the latent space
       num_samples = 16
       z = torch.randn(num_samples, latent_dim).to(device)
       generated_images = model.decode(z)

       # Display the generated images
       fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 4, figsize=(8, 8))
       for i, ax in enumerate(axes.flatten()):
           img = generated_images[i].cpu().squeeze().numpy()
           ax.imshow(img, cmap='gray')
           ax.axis('off')
       plt.show()
   ```

### Expected output
After training, the code will display 16 generated images of handwritten digits. The images will not be perfect, but they should resemble digits from the MNIST dataset. You should also see the loss decreasing during training.

### Common failure modes
- **Loss not decreasing:** Reduce the learning rate or increase the number of epochs. → Try reducing the learning rate to 1e-4 or increasing the number of epochs to 20.
- **Generated images are blurry:** Increase the capacity of the encoder and decoder networks. → Add more convolutional layers or increase the number of channels in the existing layers.
- **CUDA out of memory error:** Reduce the batch size. → Try reducing the batch size to 32 or 16.

docs.text:
Learning structure from data without labels: self-supervised objectives, contrastive methods, and the geometry of learned representations.

What makes a good representation? This is one of the most fundamental questions in deep learning. Representation learning asks how to extract structure from raw data — without relying on expensive human labels — and how to build representations that transfer, generalize, and compose.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Imagine teaching someone what a "guitar" is — not by handing them a dictionary definition, but by showing them an acoustic guitar and an electric guitar side by side ("these are the same kind of thing") while contrasting both against a violin ("this is different"). No labels required. The learner builds an internal model of "guitar-ness" purely from the structure of comparisons. This is the core intuition behind contrastive learning: rather than predicting absolute categories, a model learns by mapping relative semantic distances. Things that belong together should land close in the model's internal space; things that don't belong together should land far apart.

The practical consequence of this framing is enormous. Supervised learning requires a human to assign a label to every training example — a bottleneck that limits scale. Contrastive learning sidesteps this by constructing its own supervision signal from the data itself. Two crops of the same image, a sentence and its translation, a photo and its caption — these are "positive pairs" that the model should map to nearby points. Everything else in the batch is a "negative" the model should push away. This self-supervised signal can be generated automatically at internet scale, which is why contrastive methods have become the dominant pre-training strategy for vision, language, and multimodal systems.

What makes contrastive learning work in practice is the geometry it imposes on the learned space. A well-trained contrastive encoder doesn't just cluster positives together — it distributes representations uniformly across the hypersphere, preventing the model from collapsing to a trivial solution where everything maps to the same point. This balance between alignment (positives close) and uniformity (representations spread out) is the central tension the field has spent the last five years learning to control.

docs.title: Why it matters at the frontier
docs.text:
Contrastive learning is the mechanism that made large-scale multimodal foundation models possible. CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) demonstrated that training a vision encoder and a text encoder jointly with a contrastive objective on 400 million web-scraped image-caption pairs produces visual representations that transfer to dozens of downstream tasks without any task-specific fine-tuning. That result reframed the entire question of visual pre-training: the bottleneck was never model capacity, it was the supervision signal. Contrastive learning at scale provides a supervision signal that is effectively unlimited, which is why every major vision-language model — from ALIGN to SigLIP to the vision towers inside LLaVA — uses some variant of this approach.

The open problems that remain are not incremental. Contrastive learning still struggles with dimensional collapse — the tendency for representations to concentrate in a low-dimensional subspace of the embedding space, wasting capacity and degrading transfer. It also struggles with hard negatives: when a batch contains two images of different guitars, the model is penalized for treating them as dissimilar, even though they are semantically close. And as systems scale beyond two modalities (image + text + audio + depth + video), the pairwise cosine similarity that underlies InfoNCE becomes geometrically inadequate — a problem that recent work on Gramian-based alignment (2025) is beginning to address. These are the questions that determine whether contrastive representations can serve as the universal substrate for multimodal AI.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
• Positive pair — two views of the same underlying semantic content (e.g., two augmented crops of one image, or an image and its caption) that the model is trained to map to nearby points in embedding space.
  • Negative pair — two examples from different semantic categories that the model is trained to push apart; in practice, all other examples in the batch serve as negatives.
  • Embedding space / latent space — the high-dimensional vector space (typically \(\mathbb{R}^{128}\) to \(\mathbb{R}^{1024}\)) where encoders map inputs; contrastive training shapes the geometry of this space.
  • InfoNCE loss — the standard contrastive objective, derived from noise-contrastive estimation, that trains the model to identify the true positive among \(N-1\) negatives in a batch.
  • Temperature parameter \(\tau\) — a scalar that controls the sharpness of the similarity distribution; low \(\tau\) makes the model focus on hard negatives, high \(\tau\) smooths the gradient signal.
  • Alignment — the property that positive pairs have high cosine similarity; a necessary condition for useful representations but not sufficient on its own.
  • Uniformity — the property that representations are spread uniformly across the unit hypersphere; prevents dimensional collapse and ensures the embedding space is used efficiently.
  • Dimensional collapse — the failure mode where representations span only a low-dimensional subspace despite the encoder having high capacity; a central unsolved problem in contrastive learning.

docs.title: Mathematical foundations
docs.text:
The core contrastive objective is the InfoNCE loss. For a batch of \(N\) image-text pairs, the loss for a single image \(i\) is:

\[ \mathcal{L}_i = -\log \frac{\exp(\text{sim}(z_i^I, z_i^T) / \tau)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} \exp(\text{sim}(z_i^I, z_j^T) / \tau)} \]

where \(z_i^I \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is the \(\ell_2\)-normalized image embedding for example \(i\), \(z_i^T \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is the \(\ell_2\)-normalized text embedding for the same example, \(z_j^T\) ranges over all \(N\) text embeddings in the batch (including the true positive at \(j = i\)), \(\text{sim}(\cdot, \cdot)\) is cosine similarity, and \(\tau > 0\) is the temperature hyperparameter. This equation says that the model is solving an \(N\)-way classification problem: given image \(i\), identify which of the \(N\) text embeddings is its true match. The loss is minimized when the true positive scores higher than all negatives.

The full symmetric CLIP loss averages the image-to-text and text-to-image directions:

\[ \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left( \mathcal{L}_i^{I \to T} + \mathcal{L}_i^{T \to I} \right) \]

where \(\mathcal{L}_i^{I \to T}\) is the per-example loss for identifying the correct text given image \(i\) — computed as the InfoNCE expression above — and \(\mathcal{L}_i^{T \to I}\) is the symmetric counterpart: the loss for identifying the correct image given text \(i\), computed by transposing the similarity matrix and applying the same softmax-cross-entropy. The factor \(\frac{1}{2N}\) averages over both directions and all examples in the batch. This symmetry ensures that both encoders receive gradient signal from both directions simultaneously.

Wang and Isola (2020) decomposed the contrastive objective into two interpretable terms. The alignment loss is:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{align}} = \mathbb{E}_{(x, x^+) \sim p_{\text{pos}}} \left[ \| f(x) - f(x^+) \|^2 \right] \]

where \(f(x) \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is the \(\ell_2\)-normalized embedding of input \(x\), \(x^+\) is a positive view drawn from the positive pair distribution \(p_{\text{pos}}\), and \(\|\cdot\|^2\) is squared Euclidean distance on the unit hypersphere. This term says that the model should minimize the distance between positive pairs — it measures how well the encoder aligns semantically equivalent inputs.

The uniformity loss is:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{uniform}} = \log \mathbb{E}_{x, y \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} p_{\text{data}}} \left[ e^{-2\|f(x) - f(y)\|^2} \right] \]

where \(x\) and \(y\) are two independently sampled data points from the marginal data distribution \(p_{\text{data}}\), and \(f(\cdot)\) is again the \(\ell_2\)-normalized encoder. This term is minimized when representations are maximally spread across the unit hypersphere — it penalizes representations that cluster together regardless of semantics. The tension between these two terms is the fundamental trade-off contrastive learning must navigate: perfect alignment would collapse all positives to a single point, while perfect uniformity would push all points apart regardless of semantics.

docs.title: Key algorithms / techniques
docs.text:
• SimCLR (Chen et al., 2020) — trains a single vision encoder using two random augmentations of each image as positives; introduced the projection head (a small MLP applied before the loss) and showed that large batch sizes (4096+) are critical for performance.
  • MoCo / MoCo v2 / MoCo v3 (He et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020, 2021) — uses a momentum encoder (an exponential moving average of the online encoder) and a memory queue to decouple batch size from the number of negatives, enabling contrastive training on single-GPU hardware.
  • CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) — trains a vision encoder and a text encoder jointly with symmetric InfoNCE on 400M web-scraped image-caption pairs; the resulting embeddings enable zero-shot classification by comparing image embeddings to text embeddings of class names.
  • ALIGN (Jia et al., 2021) — scales CLIP-style training to 1.8 billion noisy image-text pairs without aggressive data cleaning, showing that scale compensates for noise.
  • BYOL (Grill et al., 2020) — eliminates explicit negatives entirely by using an online/target network asymmetry with a stop-gradient operation; demonstrated that uniformity can be maintained without negative pairs, challenging the assumption that negatives are necessary.
  • SimSiam (Chen & He, 2021) — further simplified BYOL by removing the momentum encoder, showing that stop-gradient alone prevents collapse; provided theoretical grounding for why asymmetric architectures avoid trivial solutions.
  • SigLIP (Zhai et al., 2023) — replaces the softmax-based InfoNCE with a sigmoid loss that treats each pair independently, removing the dependency on large batch sizes and enabling more stable training at scale.
  • GRAM (2025) — extends contrastive alignment beyond pairwise cosine similarity to \(k > 2\) modalities using Gramian volume as the alignment metric, enabling geometrically principled multi-modal pre-training.
