Provides the first systematic empirical study of reward hacking as a function of KL divergence, establishing the quantitative relationship between policy-reference distance and reward model exploitation

docs.title: Seminal papers & test-of-time
docs.text: Paper Year Key contribution Learning to summarize with human feedback (Stiennon et al.) 2020 First large-scale demonstration that RLHF improves LLM outputs on a concrete task (summarization), establishing the empirical viability of the pipeline Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms (Schulman et al.) 2017 Introduced PPO, which became the default RL optimizer for RLHF due to its stability and simplicity relative to TRPO Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences (Christiano et al.) 2017 Pioneered the use of human preference comparisons (rather than explicit reward functions) to train RL agents; the conceptual origin of modern RLHF Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model (Rafailov et al.) 2023 Showed that the RLHF objective can be optimized directly from preference data without an explicit RL loop, spawning an entire family of offline alignment methods

docs.title: Current SotA
docs.text: The strongest publicly documented RLHF-trained systems are GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024) and Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Anthropic, 2024), both of which achieve human-preference win rates above 70% against their predecessor models on internal evaluations, though neither lab publishes full training details. On open benchmarks, DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek, 2025) achieves 79.8% on MATH-500 and 97.3% on AIME 2024 using GRPO-based RL training without supervised fine-tuning on chain-of-thought data — demonstrating that online RL alone can elicit complex reasoning. Among open-weight models with documented RLHF pipelines, Llama 3.1 (Meta, 2024) reports that its 70B instruction model achieves a 57.1% win rate against GPT-4 on MT-Bench using iterative RLHF with rejection sampling.

docs.title: What's happening now
docs.text:
Research frontiers. The most active theoretical question in RLHF research is whether KL-divergence regularization is the right tool for preventing reward hacking. Work on "catastrophic Goodhart" (2024) has shown formally that when reward model errors are heavy-tailed — which is the realistic case, since human preference data is noisy and inconsistent at the extremes — standard KL penalties fail to bound the policy's exploitation of those errors. This has pushed researchers toward alternative regularization schemes, including reward model ensembles for uncertainty estimation, constrained optimization formulations that treat reward hacking as a hard constraint rather than a soft penalty, and process reward models that score reasoning steps rather than final outputs. The open question is precise: Can we derive a regularization scheme that provides a formal guarantee against reward hacking when the reward model's error distribution has heavy tails, without sacrificing the policy improvement that makes RLHF useful?

Engineering and systems. The dominant engineering trend is reducing the memory footprint of online RLHF. Traditional PPO-based RLHF requires four models in GPU memory simultaneously — the policy, the reference model, the reward model, and the critic — making it inaccessible without multi-GPU infrastructure. RLOO (Ahmadian et al. 2024) eliminates the critic, and implementations in HuggingFace TRL now make single-GPU RLHF on 7B-class models feasible on consumer hardware. Separately, the rise of GRPO (used in DeepSeek-R1) has demonstrated that group-normalized reward signals can replace both the critic and the reference model's KL computation in certain settings, further reducing overhead. The practical consequence is that RLHF is rapidly becoming accessible to practitioners without datacenter-scale compute.

Open problems. Three specific questions define the frontier. First: how does reward model quality scale with the size of the preference dataset, and is there a point of diminishing returns beyond which more human labels stop improving alignment? Gao et al. (2023) established the KL-vs-reward tradeoff empirically, but the data-scaling law for reward models remains poorly characterized. Second: can generative reward models (LLMs prompted to evaluate outputs) replace trained Bradley-Terry reward models without introducing new failure modes from the evaluator model's own biases? Third: does RLHF training on reasoning tasks (math, code) transfer to alignment properties (honesty, refusal), or are these orthogonal axes that require separate optimization?

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• OpenAI — ChatGPT / GPT-4 — RLHF with PPO is the documented post-training method for InstructGPT and its successors; OpenAI reports that RLHF-trained models are preferred by human raters over SFT-only models 85% of the time at the scale of millions of daily users — https://openai.com/research/instruction-following
  • Anthropic — Claude — Uses Constitutional AI (RLAIF), a variant of RLHF where AI-generated critiques replace a portion of human preference labels, enabling preference data generation at scale without proportional annotation cost; documented in the Constitutional AI paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08073
  • Meta — Llama 3 — Uses iterative RLHF with rejection sampling fine-tuning (SFT on high-reward outputs) followed by PPO; the 405B model's post-training pipeline is documented in the Llama 3 technical report — https://ai.meta.com/research/publications/the-llama-3-herd-of-models/
  • Google DeepMind — Gemini — Applies RLHF across modalities (text, image, code) with reward models trained on human preference data collected from internal raters; Gemini 1.5 Pro achieves top scores on MMLU and HumanEval after RLHF post-training — https://research.google/blog/gemini-a-family-of-highly-capable-multimodal-models/

docs.title: Minimum Valuable Build
docs.text:
What you're building: A working online RLHF pipeline that aligns a EleutherAI/pythia-1b language model on human preference data using the RLOO trainer in HuggingFace TRL, producing a reward-optimized checkpoint you can query directly.

Why this build: RLOO eliminates the critic network that makes PPO inaccessible on consumer hardware, making this the first RLHF recipe that runs end-to-end on a free Colab T4 (16GB VRAM). The build demonstrates the full three-stage pipeline — SFT, reward modeling, and RL — in a single session.

Stack: trl>=0.12.0, transformers>=4.40.0, datasets>=2.18.0, accelerate>=0.28.0, torch>=2.2.0. Model: EleutherAI/pythia-1b. Dataset: trl-lib/ultrafeedback_binarized.

Estimated time: 60–90 minutes on a free Colab T4 GPU.

docs.title: The recipe
docs.text:
1. Install dependencies and verify GPU
!pip install -q trl>=0.12.0 transformers>=4.40.0 datasets>=2.18.0 accelerate>=0.28.0

import torch
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
print(f"Device: {device}")
print(f"VRAM available: {torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0).total_memory / 1e9:.1f} GB")
# Expected: Device: cuda, VRAM: ~15.7 GB on Colab T4
  1. Load the preference dataset
from datasets import load_dataset

dataset = load_dataset("trl-lib/ultrafeedback_binarized", split="train[:5000]")
eval_dataset = load_dataset("trl-lib/ultrafeedback_binarized", split="test[:500]")

# Inspect the structure
print(dataset[0].keys())
# Expected keys: prompt, chosen, rejected (each is a list of chat messages)
print(f"Train size: {len(dataset)}, Eval size: {len(eval_dataset)}")
  1. Load the base model and tokenizer
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoModelForSequenceClassification

model_id = "EleutherAI/pythia-1b"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token
tokenizer.padding_side = "left"  # Required for causal LM generation

# Load the policy model (will be fine-tuned)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    device_map="auto"
)
print(f"Policy model parameters: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) / 1e9:.2f}B")
# Expected: ~1.0B parameters
  1. Train a reward model on the preference data
from trl import RewardTrainer, RewardConfig

reward_model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    num_labels=1,
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    device_map="auto"
)
reward_model.config.pad_token_id = tokenizer.pad_token_id

reward_config = RewardConfig(
    output_dir="./reward_model",
    num_train_epochs=1,
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
    learning_rate=1e-5,
    max_length=512,
    logging_steps=50,
    save_steps=500,
    bf16=True,
    remove_unused_columns=False,
)

reward_trainer = RewardTrainer(
    model=reward_model,
    args=reward_config,
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    train_dataset=dataset,
    eval_dataset=eval_dataset,
)

reward_trainer.train()
reward_trainer.save_model("./reward_model_final")
print("Reward model training complete.")
  1. Run RLOO alignment on the policy
from trl import RLOOTrainer, RLOOConfig
from transformers import pipeline

# Load the trained reward model as a pipeline for scoring
reward_pipeline = pipeline(
    "text-classification",
    model="./reward_model_final",
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    device=0,
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    truncation=True,
    max_length=512,
)

rloo_config = RLOOConfig(
    output_dir="./rloo_policy",
    num_train_epochs=1,
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
    learning_rate=3e-6,
    kl_coef=0.05,           # beta: KL penalty coefficient
    rloo_k=4,               # number of responses sampled per prompt
    max_new_tokens=128,
    logging_steps=25,
    save_steps=200,
    bf16=True,
)

rloo_trainer = RLOOTrainer(
    config=rloo_config,
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    policy=model,
    reward_model=reward_pipeline,
    train_dataset=dataset,
    eval_dataset=eval_dataset,
)

rloo_trainer.train()
rloo_trainer.save_model("./rloo_policy_final")
print("RLOO alignment complete.")
  1. Evaluate the aligned model
from transformers import pipeline as hf_pipeline

aligned_pipeline = hf_pipeline(
    "text-generation",
    model="./rloo_policy_final",
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    device=0,
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)

test_prompts = [
    "Explain the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning.",
    "What is the capital of France?",
    "Write a short poem about the ocean.",
]

for prompt in test_prompts:
    output = aligned_pipeline(
        prompt,
        max_new_tokens=100,
        do_sample=True,
        temperature=0.7,
        pad_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id,
    )
    print(f"Prompt: {prompt}")
    print(f"Response: {output[0]['generated_text'][len(prompt):]}")
    print("---")
  1. Sanity-check: compare reward scores before and after alignment
# Score a sample response with the reward model to verify improvement
test_response = "Supervised learning uses labeled data to train models, while unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabeled data."

score = reward_pipeline(test_response)
print(f"Reward score for test response: {score[0]['score']:.4f}")
# A higher score after RLOO training vs. the base model indicates successful alignment

docs.title: Expected output
docs.text: After reward model training (~20 minutes), the reward model loss should decrease from approximately 0.69 (random) to below 0.55 on the eval set. After RLOO training (~40 minutes), the mean reward score on eval prompts should increase by 0.1–0.3 points relative to the SFT baseline, and the KL divergence from the reference model should stabilize between 2 and 8 nats. The aligned model's responses to the test prompts should be noticeably more structured and on-topic than the base Pythia-1B outputs.

docs.title: Common failure modes
docs.text:
• CUDA out of memory during RLOO → Reduce rloo_k from 4 to 2, or reduce max_new_tokens from 128 to 64; RLOO's memory scales linearly with k.
  • Reward model outputs NaN scores → Ensure tokenizer.pad_token_id is set before loading the reward model; Pythia's tokenizer has no default pad token.
  • KL divergence explodes after 100 steps → Increase kl_coef from 0.05 to 0.1; the policy is drifting too far from the reference model.
  • Reward score does not improve → Check that the reward pipeline is receiving the full response (prompt + completion), not just the completion; the reward model was trained on full sequences.
  • RewardTrainer raises shape mismatch → Set remove_unused_columns=False in RewardConfig; the trainer needs the raw chosen and rejected columns.

If this build worked for you — a ⭐ on GitHub is the only signal we collect.

docs.title: What comes next
docs.text:
RLHF's KL-penalized objective has a closed-form solution that connects directly to the theory of optimal transport and energy-based models — understanding that connection makes the DPO reparameterization precise rather than surprising.

  • [[direct-preference-optimization]] — DPO reparameterizes the RLHF objective to eliminate the explicit RL loop, making the reward model implicit in the policy itself; the relationship is exact, not approximate.
  • [[proximal-policy-optimization]] — PPO is the RL algorithm that makes the RLHF training loop stable; understanding its clipping mechanism explains why RLOO can replace the critic but not the clipping.
  • [[reward-modeling]] — the reward model is the weakest link in the RLHF pipeline; this page covers Bradley-Terry training, reward model ensembles, and the scaling laws for reward model quality.

docs.title: Connected topics
docs.text:
• [[transformer-architecture]] — RLHF post-training is applied almost exclusively to Transformer-based language models; the attention mechanism's capacity for in-context learning is what makes the SFT stage effective.
  • [[diffusion-models]] — RLHF-style preference optimization has been adapted for image generation, where reward models trained on human aesthetic judgments fine-tune diffusion policies using the same KL-penalized objective.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Ouyang et al. (2022) — "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback" — https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155 — the primary source for the three-stage RLHF pipeline; reading the appendix reveals the annotation guidelines and inter-annotator agreement statistics that are omitted from most summaries.
  • Ahmadian et al. (2024) — "Back to Basics: Revisiting REINFORCE-Style Optimization for Learning from Human Feedback" — https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14740 — the RLOO paper; includes ablations comparing RLOO to PPO on reward score, KL divergence, and wall-clock time that are essential for practitioners choosing an RL algorithm.
  • Gao et al. (2023) — "Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization" — https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.10760 — the first systematic empirical study of reward hacking as a function of KL divergence; establishes the quantitative relationship between policy-reference distance and proxy reward exploitation that every RLHF practitioner should internalize.
  • Rafailov et al. (2023) — "Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model" — https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290 — shows that the RLHF objective has a closed-form solution expressible entirely in terms of the policy, eliminating the need for explicit RL; the derivation is the clearest exposition of why the KL-penalized objective has the structure it does.
  • Lilian Weng — "Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback" (lil'log, 2023) — https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2023-01-27-the-transformer-family-v2/ — provides an intuitive walkthrough of the Bradley-Terry derivation and the reward hacking taxonomy that complements the mathematical treatment on this page.
  • Christiano et al. (2017) — "Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences" — https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03741 — the conceptual origin of modern RLHF; demonstrates preference-based reward learning in Atari and MuJoCo environments, establishing the pairwise comparison framework that all subsequent work inherits.

docs.title: Track 07 · Language Models, Transformers & Multimodal AI
docs.text:
The architecture of modern AI: self-attention, transformers, large language models, multimodal systems, and the frontier of machine reasoning.

This track covers the dominant computational paradigm in modern AI — the transformer and its descendants — together with the language models and multimodal systems built on top of it. It spans architecture (how attention works) to system scale (how LLMs are trained) to behavior (how they reason).

docs.title: State Space Models
docs.text: TL;DR: State Space Models (SSMs) offer a computationally efficient alternative to Transformers for modeling sequential data, particularly excelling in tasks with long-range dependencies.

docs.title: For your reader type
docs.text: I am... Start here Goal MS/applied practitioner Key algorithms → In production Understand where SSMs are used Curious generalist What it is → Why it matters Build intuition Math/theory student Core concepts → Mathematical foundations Understand the mechanics Researcher / frontier Current SotA → Seminal papers Know where the open problems are

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Imagine you're trying to predict the stock market, or the next word in a sentence. Traditional methods struggle with the long-range dependencies inherent in these tasks. State space models offer a fresh approach, drawing on control theory to model sequential data more effectively. They represent a system's "state" and how it changes over time, allowing for more efficient processing of long sequences.

State space models (SSMs) are a class of models that describe the evolution of a system's internal state over time, based on inputs and previous states. Unlike recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or Transformers, SSMs often exhibit linear computational complexity with respect to sequence length, making them particularly appealing for handling long sequences. This efficiency stems from their ability to represent the entire history of a sequence in a compressed state vector, which is updated iteratively.

SSMs have seen a resurgence in deep learning, offering a compelling alternative to attention-based models for sequence modeling. They provide a structured way to capture temporal dependencies and have shown promising results in various applications, including language modeling, time series forecasting, and audio processing. Their ability to handle long sequences efficiently makes them a valuable tool in scenarios where Transformers become computationally prohibitive.

docs.title: Why it matters at the frontier
docs.text:
State space models are gaining traction at the frontier due to their potential to overcome the limitations of Transformers, especially in handling long-range dependencies and reducing computational costs. Research labs are actively exploring novel SSM architectures and training techniques to improve their performance and scalability. The ability to process long sequences efficiently opens up new possibilities for modeling complex systems and making accurate predictions in various domains.

One of the key open problems in the field is how to design SSM architectures that dynamically adapt their internal representations to the specific characteristics of different input sequences, optimizing both performance and computational efficiency across a wide range of tasks. Addressing this challenge could lead to more robust and versatile SSMs that can effectively handle diverse sequential data. Further research is also focused on improving the interpretability of SSMs, making them more transparent and understandable for practitioners.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
• State Vector — A representation of the system's internal state at a given time, encapsulating relevant information about its past and present.
  • State Transition Matrix — A matrix that defines how the state vector evolves from one time step to the next, based on the current state and input.
  • Input Matrix — A matrix that maps the input to the state vector, determining how the input influences the system's internal state.
  • Output Matrix — A matrix that maps the state vector to the output, determining how the system's internal state is translated into observable outputs.
  • Feedforward Matrix — A matrix that directly maps the input to the output, bypassing the state vector.
  • Impulse Response — The system's output when presented with a brief input signal (an impulse), characterizing the system's dynamic behavior.
  • Linear Time-Invariance (LTI) — A property of systems where the system's response to an input does not depend on when the input was applied.

docs.title: Mathematical foundations
docs.text:
State space models can be described by a set of equations that define the evolution of the system's state and output over time. In continuous time, the state-space representation is given by:

\[ \dot{x}(t) = A x(t) + B u(t) \]

where \(\dot{x}(t)\) is the time derivative of the state vector \(x(t)\), \(A\) is the state matrix, \(B\) is the input matrix, and \(u(t)\) is the input. This equation describes how the internal state evolves over time.

\[ y(t) = C x(t) + D u(t) \]

where \(y(t)\) is the output, \(C\) is the output matrix, \(x(t)\) is the state vector, \(D\) is the feedforward matrix, and \(u(t)\) is the input. This equation describes how the output is generated from the state and input.

The impulse response \(H\) of the system is given by:

\[ H = CA + D \]

where \(H\) is the impulse response, \(C\) is the output matrix, \(A\) is the state matrix, and \(D\) is the feedforward matrix. The impulse response is a key property in understanding the system's behavior.

In discrete time, the state-space representation is given by:

\[ x_{k+1} = A x_k + B u_k \]

where \(x_{k+1}\) is the state at the next time step, \(x_k\) is the state at the current time step, \(A\) is the state matrix, \(B\) is the input matrix, and \(u_k\) is the input at the current time step. This equation describes how the state evolves in discrete time steps.

\[ y_k = C x_k + D u_k \]

where \(y_k\) is the output at the current time step, \(C\) is the output matrix, \(x_k\) is the state at the current time step, \(D\) is the feedforward matrix, and \(u_k\) is the input at the current time step. This equation describes how the output is generated in discrete time steps.

docs.title: Key algorithms / techniques
docs.text:
• Mamba (2023) — A selective state space model that dynamically adjusts its internal state based on the input, improving performance and efficiency for long sequences.
  • Structured State Space Sequence (S4) (2021) — A class of SSMs designed to efficiently model long-range dependencies in sequential data by leveraging structured matrices.
  • HiPPO (2020) — A family of continuous-time memory models that use high-order polynomial projections to approximate ideal memory dynamics.

docs.title: Essential reading
docs.text: Paper Year Authors Why essential Efficient Hybrid Language Model Compression through Group-Aware SSM Pruning 2025 Li et al. Showcases state-of-the-art hybrid models and the benefits of compression. SDE: A Simplified and Disentangled Dependency Encoding Framework for State Space Models in Time Series Forecasting 2024 Weng et al. Highlights the application of SSMs in time series forecasting. docs.title: What's happening now
docs.text: Research frontiers are focused on developing novel SSM architectures that can dynamically adapt to different input sequences, optimizing both performance and computational efficiency. Engineering and systems efforts are centered around integrating SSMs into existing deep learning frameworks and developing efficient implementations for large-scale deployment. A key open problem is how to develop state space models that effectively capture both long-range dependencies and complex, structured relationships within time series data, while maintaining computational efficiency and interpretability.

docs.title: Transformer Architecture
docs.text: TL;DR: The transformer replaced sequential recurrence with parallel token-to-token routing via self-attention — now the universal backbone for language, vision, and multimodal AI, and the subject of active research into whether its quadratic inference cost can be eliminated without sacrificing its expressive power.

docs.title: For your reader type
docs.text: I am... Start here Goal MS/applied practitioner Key algorithms → MVB Build a hybrid Mamba-Transformer block and train it on text Curious generalist What it is → Why it matters Understand why transformers displaced every prior architecture Math/theory student Core concepts → Mathematical foundations Derive multi-head attention and understand the residual stream Researcher / frontier Current SotA → What's happening now Know where attention is being challenged and why

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Imagine translating a novel where the only tool available is a single sticky note passed from word to word. Each word reads the note, scribbles an update, and hands it forward. By chapter three, the note is a smeared palimpsest — the opening sentence has been overwritten so many times it is unrecognizable. This is the fundamental bottleneck of LSTMs and GRUs: a fixed-size hidden state that must compress the entire history of a sequence into a single vector, then pass it forward one step at a time. The further apart two relevant tokens are, the more that signal degrades. The transformer shattered this constraint by giving every token a direct, high-bandwidth connection to every other token simultaneously — not a telephone game, but a conference call where every participant can hear every other participant at once, regardless of how far apart they are seated.

The mechanism that enables this is self-attention. For each token, the model computes three vectors — a query, a key, and a value — by projecting the token's embedding through learned weight matrices. The query of one token is compared against the keys of all other tokens to produce attention weights, which then determine how much of each token's value vector to mix into the output. Because this comparison happens in parallel across all token pairs, the entire operation reduces to a matrix multiplication — fast on modern accelerators, and free of the sequential dependency that made RNNs slow to train. Stack this attention mechanism with a position-wise feedforward network, wrap both in residual connections and layer normalization, and repeat the block N times: that is a transformer.

What makes the transformer more than an engineering convenience is that it reframes sequence modeling as a spatial routing problem. Rather than asking "what happened before this token?", it asks "which tokens are most relevant to this token, and by how much?" The feedforward sublayer then acts as a per-token memory lookup — research by Geva et al. (2021) showed that FFN layers function as key-value stores, retrieving factual associations independently of position. Together, the attention and feedforward sublayers form a residual stream: a shared information highway that each layer reads from and writes to, accumulating increasingly abstract representations as depth increases.

docs.title: Why it matters at the frontier
docs.text:
The transformer's dominance is not accidental — it is a consequence of hardware alignment. Self-attention and feedforward projections are dense matrix multiplications, which map almost perfectly onto the parallelism of modern GPUs and TPUs. This alignment allowed transformers to scale in ways that RNNs structurally could not: more data, more parameters, more compute, reliably producing better models. The scaling laws documented by Kaplan et al. (2020) and later refined by Hoffmann et al. (2022) are transformer-specific observations, and they have driven every major lab's infrastructure investment for the past five years. GPT-4, Gemini Ultra, Claude 3, and Llama 3 are all transformer-based, and the engineering ecosystems — vLLM, FlashAttention, tensor parallelism — are built around the transformer's computational profile.

The frontier tension is now the quadratic cost of attention. As context windows grow from 4K to 128K to 1M tokens, the memory and compute required for full self-attention scales as \(O(n^2)\) in sequence length, making long-context inference increasingly expensive. This has made the transformer's own success a pressure point: the architecture that enabled scaling is now the bottleneck to further scaling. The response from frontier labs has been a wave of hybrid architectures — Mamba, RWKV, RetNet, and most recently NVIDIA's Nemotron-H — that interleave attention layers with linear-time state-space or recurrent layers, preserving the reasoning capability of attention while reducing its cost at long contexts. Whether these hybrids can match pure transformers on all tasks, or whether some capability is intrinsically tied to full quadratic attention, is the central open question driving architecture research in 2025.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
• Token embedding — a learned mapping from discrete vocabulary indices to dense vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), where \(d\) is the model dimension; the input representation before any attention is applied.
  • Query, Key, Value (QKV) projections — three learned linear transformations applied to each token's embedding to produce the vectors used in attention score computation.
  • Scaled dot-product attention — the core operation: dot-product similarity between queries and keys, scaled by \(\sqrt{d_k}\), softmaxed to produce weights, then applied to values.
  • Multi-head attention — running \(h\) independent attention operations in parallel on lower-dimensional projections, then concatenating and projecting the results; allows the model to attend to different aspects of the sequence simultaneously.
  • Positional encoding — information injected into token embeddings (or attention scores) to give the model awareness of token order, since self-attention is permutation-invariant by default.
  • Residual stream — the shared vector that flows through the network; each sublayer (attention, FFN) reads from it and adds its output back to it, enabling gradient flow and interpretable layer-wise decomposition.
  • Feedforward sublayer — a two-layer MLP applied independently to each token position after attention; functions as a position-wise memory lookup with a typical expansion ratio of 4×.
  • Causal masking — in decoder-only models, a mask applied to attention weights that prevents each token from attending to future tokens, enforcing autoregressive generation.

docs.title: Mathematical foundations
docs.text:
The core attention operation for a single head is:

\[ \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V \]

where \(Q \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k}\) is the matrix of query vectors for all \(n\) tokens, \(K \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k}\) is the matrix of key vectors, \(V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_v}\) is the matrix of value vectors, and \(d_k\) is the dimension of the key vectors used for scaling. The scaling by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) prevents the dot products from growing large in magnitude as \(d_k\) increases, which would push the softmax into regions of near-zero gradient.

Multi-head attention concatenates \(h\) such operations run on separate linear projections:

\[ \text{MultiHead}(X) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_h)\,W^O \] \[ \text{head}_i = \text{Attention}(XW_i^Q,\; XW_i^K,\; XW_i^V) \]

where \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) is the input sequence, \(W_i^Q, W_i^K \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_k}\) and \(W_i^V \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_v}\) are the per-head projection matrices, and \(W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{hd_v \times d}\) is the output projection that maps the concatenated heads back to the model dimension. This equation says that each head learns a different subspace in which to measure token relevance, and the output projection mixes those subspace-specific signals back into a single representation.

Shaw et al. (2018) extended the attention score to incorporate relative position information:

\[ e_{ij} = \frac{(x_i W^Q)(x_j W^K + a_{ij}^K)^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} \]

where \(x_i, x_j \in \mathbb{R}^d\) are the input embeddings at positions \(i\) and \(j\), \(W^Q\) and \(W^K\) are the query and key projection matrices, \(a_{ij}^K \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}\) is a learned relative position representation (a parameter vector) encoding the directed distance from position \(i\) to position \(j\), and \(d_k\) is the key dimension. This equation says that the relevance between two tokens depends not only on their content but on how far apart they are and in which direction — injecting sequence order dynamically into the attention score rather than adding a fixed offset to the input embedding.

The full transformer block update for layer \(\ell\) is:

[ x' = x + \text{MultiHead}(\text{LN}(x)) ] [ x^{\ell+1} = x' + \text{FFN}(\text{LN}(x')) ]

where \(x \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) is the residual stream entering the block, \(\text{LN}\) denotes layer normalization (pre-norm formulation), \(\text{MultiHead}\) is the multi-head attention sublayer, and \(\text{FFN}\) is the position-wise feedforward sublayer. The additive residual structure means each layer's output is a correction to the previous representation rather than a full rewrite, which stabilizes gradient flow and allows the residual stream to be interpreted as a shared information bus.

docs.title: Key algorithms / techniques
docs.text:
• Scaled dot-product attention (Vaswani et al., 2017) — the foundational QKV mechanism; computes pairwise token relevance via dot products scaled by \(\sqrt{d_k}\), enabling parallel sequence processing.
  • Multi-head attention (Vaswani et al., 2017) — runs \(h\) attention heads in parallel on projected subspaces, then concatenates; allows simultaneous attention to syntactic, semantic, and positional patterns.
  • Relative position representations (Shaw et al., 2018) — replaces fixed sinusoidal position embeddings with learned per-distance vectors added directly to attention logits, making position encoding dynamic and generalizable to unseen lengths.
  • Rotary Position Embedding / RoPE (Su et al., 2021) — encodes position by rotating query and key vectors in complex space; preserves relative position information through the dot product and has become the default in most modern LLMs including Llama and Mistral.
  • FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022; v2 2023) — a hardware-aware exact attention algorithm that tiles the computation to avoid materializing the full \(n \times n\) attention matrix in HBM, reducing memory from \(O(n^2)\) to \(O(n)\) and achieving 2–4× wall-clock speedup.
  • Grouped Query Attention / GQA (Ainslie et al., 2023) — shares key and value heads across groups of query heads, reducing KV cache memory at inference by a factor of \(h/g\) where \(g\) is the number of groups; used in Llama 3 and Mistral.
  • Sliding window attention (Beltagy et al., 2020; Longformer) — restricts each token to attend only to a local window of size \(w\), reducing complexity to \(O(nw)\); used in combination with global attention tokens for long-document tasks.
  • Hybrid attention + SSM layers (Gu & Dao, 2023; NVIDIA, 2025) — interleaves full self-attention layers with Mamba state-space layers that process tokens in \(O(n)\) time, achieving near-transformer quality at a fraction of the inference cost for long sequences.

docs.text: Paper Year Key contribution "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al.) 2017 Established the transformer as a complete sequence model without recurrence or convolution; introduced scaled dot-product and multi-head attention "BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers" (Devlin et al.) 2018 Showed that bidirectional transformer pre-training on masked language modeling transfers to virtually every NLP task via fine-tuning "Language Models are Few-Shot Learners" (Brown et al.) 2020 Demonstrated that scaling decoder-only transformers to 175B parameters produces emergent in-context learning without any gradient updates "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" (Kaplan et al.) 2020 Established power-law relationships between model size, data, compute, and loss — the empirical foundation for every subsequent scaling decision "Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models" (Hoffmann et al.) 2022 Revised Kaplan's scaling laws to show data and model size should scale equally; produced Chinchilla, which matched GPT-3 at 4× fewer parameters "FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness" (Dao et al.) 2022 Made long-context transformers practical by eliminating the memory bottleneck of materializing the attention matrix; now standard in every production training stack

docs.title: Current SotA
docs.text: As of mid-2025, the strongest publicly benchmarked language models remain transformer-based or transformer-hybrid. Meta's Llama 3.1 405B achieves 88.6 on MMLU and 73.0 on HumanEval. Google's Gemini 1.5 Pro extends the context window to 1M tokens using a mixture of full and sliding-window attention layers, achieving state-of-the-art on long-document retrieval benchmarks. NVIDIA's Nemotron-H 56B, a hybrid model with roughly 90% Mamba layers and 10% attention layers, matches or exceeds comparably-sized pure-transformer models on standard benchmarks while reducing inference-time KV cache memory by over 40% at 128K context length — the most concrete demonstration to date that hybrid architectures can close the quality gap.

docs.title: What's happening now
docs.text:
Research frontiers. The dominant research question is no longer how to make transformers better in isolation, but how to replace or augment attention with sub-quadratic alternatives without losing capability. Mamba 2 (Dao & Gu, 2024) unified state-space models with linear attention under a single structured state-space duality framework, providing theoretical grounding for why SSMs can approximate attention in many settings. RWKV-6 and RetNet have similarly shown that linear-recurrent architectures can match transformer perplexity on language modeling at moderate context lengths. The open question is whether any of these alternatives preserve the full in-context learning and multi-step reasoning capabilities that emerge in large transformers — capabilities that may depend on the quadratic all-pairs interaction that linear methods approximate away.

Engineering and systems. The engineering response to the quadratic bottleneck has been aggressive. FlashAttention-3 (2024) exploits NVIDIA H100 tensor core asynchrony to achieve near-theoretical peak utilization on attention, reducing the practical cost of full attention at long contexts. Speculative decoding, now deployed in production at Google and Meta, uses a small draft model to propose token sequences that the large transformer verifies in parallel, achieving 2–3× throughput improvements without changing model quality. KV cache quantization (INT8 and INT4 keys/values) has become standard practice for long-context serving, reducing memory pressure at the cost of minor quality degradation that is acceptable in most production settings. The vLLM project's PagedAttention manages KV cache memory with OS-style virtual paging, enabling high-throughput batched inference that was previously impossible due to memory fragmentation.

Open problems. The central unresolved question is precise and consequential: What is the mathematically optimal ratio and interleaving pattern of self-attention layers to state-space layers that preserves full Turing-complete reasoning while minimizing quadratic inference costs? Nemotron-H uses a roughly 10% attention / 90% Mamba ratio chosen empirically, but there is no theoretical framework for predicting which tasks require full attention and how many attention layers are sufficient. A related open problem is whether positional encoding is a fundamental limitation: current long-context models degrade significantly beyond their training context length, and it is unclear whether this is a property of attention itself or of the position encoding schemes layered on top of it. Finally, the mechanistic basis for in-context learning — the ability of large transformers to implement new algorithms from examples in the prompt without gradient updates — remains poorly understood, with competing theories (gradient descent in the forward pass, Bayesian inference, associative memory retrieval) each supported by partial evidence.

docs.title: Minimum Valuable Build
docs.text:
What you're building: A single hybrid Mamba-Transformer block in PyTorch — one self-attention layer interleaved with one Mamba SSM layer — trained as a character-level language model on TinyShakespeare.

Why this build: This is the architecture pattern driving frontier hybrid models like Nemotron-H. Building it from scratch makes the trade-off concrete: the attention layer handles long-range dependency; the Mamba layer handles local sequential structure in \(O(n)\) time. Seeing both in one forward pass is more instructive than reading about either in isolation.

Stack: Python 3.10+, PyTorch 2.2+, mamba-ssm 1.2.0 (requires CUDA), einops 0.7.0. Runs on a free Colab T4 (16GB VRAM) or any RTX 3080/3090.

Estimated time: 45–60 minutes end-to-end (15 min setup, 20 min training, rest for experimentation).

docs.title: The recipe
docs.text:
1. Install dependencies
# In a Colab cell or terminal
!pip install torch==2.2.0 mamba-ssm==1.2.0 einops==0.7.0 --quiet
  1. Download TinyShakespeare and build the character tokenizer
import urllib.request, torch

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/char-rnn/master/data/tinyshakespeare/input.txt"
urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, "input.txt")

text = open("input.txt").read()
chars = sorted(set(text))
vocab_size = len(chars)                        # 65 for TinyShakespeare
stoi = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(chars)}
itos = {i: c for i, c in enumerate(chars)}
encode = lambda s: [stoi[c] for c in s]
decode = lambda l: "".join([itos[i] for i in l])

data = torch.tensor(encode(text), dtype=torch.long)
n = int(0.9 * len(data))
train_data, val_data = data[:n], data[n:]

print(f"Vocab size: {vocab_size}, Train tokens: {len(train_data):,}")
# Expected: Vocab size: 65, Train tokens: 1,003,854
  1. Define the hybrid block: one attention layer + one Mamba layer
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from einops import rearrange
from mamba_ssm import Mamba

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, block_size):
        super().__init__()
        assert d_model % n_heads == 0
        self.n_heads = n_heads
        self.d_head = d_model // n_heads
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model, bias=False)
        self.proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
        # Causal mask: lower-triangular
        self.register_buffer(
            "mask",
            torch.tril(torch.ones(block_size, block_size)).view(1, 1, block_size, block_size)
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).split(C, dim=2)
        # Reshape to (B, n_heads, T, d_head)
        q = rearrange(q, "b t (h d) -> b h t d", h=self.n_heads)
        k = rearrange(k, "b t (h d) -> b h t d", h=self.n_heads)
        v = rearrange(v, "b t (h d) -> b h t d", h=self.n_heads)
        # Scaled dot-product attention with causal mask
        scale = self.d_head ** -0.5
        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) * scale
        att = att.masked_fill(self.mask[:, :, :T, :T] == 0, float("-inf"))
        att = F.softmax(att, dim=-1)
        y = att @ v
        y = rearrange(y, "b h t d -> b t (h d)")
        return self.proj(y)


class HybridBlock(nn.Module):
    """One attention sublayer + one Mamba sublayer, each with pre-norm and residual."""
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, block_size, d_state=16, d_conv=4, expand=2):
        super().__init__()
        self.ln1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.attn = CausalSelfAttention(d_model, n_heads, block_size)
        self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        # Mamba SSM: processes the sequence in O(n) time
        self.mamba = Mamba(
            d_model=d_model,
            d_state=d_state,    # SSM state expansion factor
            d_conv=d_conv,      # local convolution width
            expand=expand,      # block expansion factor
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attn(self.ln1(x))   # attention residual
        x = x + self.mamba(self.ln2(x))  # Mamba residual
        return x


class HybridLM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, d_model, n_heads, block_size, n_layers):
        super().__init__()
        self.embed = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)
        self.pos_embed = nn.Embedding(block_size, d_model)
        self.blocks = nn.Sequential(*[
            HybridBlock(d_model, n_heads, block_size) for _ in range(n_layers)
        ])
        self.ln_f = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.head = nn.Linear(d_model, vocab_size, bias=False)
        self.block_size = block_size

    def forward(self, idx, targets=None):
        B, T = idx.shape
        assert T <= self.block_size
        tok = self.embed(idx)
        pos = self.pos_embed(torch.arange(T, device=idx.device))
        x = tok + pos
        x = self.blocks(x)
        x = self.ln_f(x)
        logits = self.head(x)
        loss = None
        if targets is not None:
            loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, logits.size(-1)), targets.view(-1))
        return logits, loss
  1. Instantiate the model and verify parameter count
BLOCK_SIZE = 256
D_MODEL    = 256
N_HEADS    = 8
N_LAYERS   = 4   # 4 hybrid blocks = 4 attention + 4 Mamba layers

model = HybridLM(
    vocab_size=vocab_size,
    d_model=D_MODEL,
    n_heads=N_HEADS,
    block_size=BLOCK_SIZE,
    n_layers=N_LAYERS,
).to(device)

n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"Parameters: {n_params/1e6:.2f}M")
# Expected: ~6–8M parameters

# Sanity check: one forward pass
dummy = torch.zeros(2, BLOCK_SIZE, dtype=torch.long, device=device)
logits, _ = model(dummy)
assert logits.shape == (2, BLOCK_SIZE, vocab_size), f"Unexpected shape: {logits.shape}"
print("Forward pass shape check passed.")
  1. Write the training loop
def get_batch(split, batch_size=32):
    data = train_data if split == "train" else val_data
    ix = torch.randint(len(data) - BLOCK_SIZE, (batch_size,))
    x = torch.stack([data[i : i + BLOCK_SIZE] for i in ix]).to(device)
    y = torch.stack([data[i + 1 : i + BLOCK_SIZE + 1] for i in ix]).to(device)
    return x, y

optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4, weight_decay=0.1)
scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(optimizer, T_max=3000)

@torch.no_grad()
def estimate_loss(eval_iters=100):
    model.eval()
    out = {}
    for split in ["train", "val"]:
        losses = []
        for _ in range(eval_iters):
            xb, yb = get_batch(split)
            _, loss = model(xb, yb)
            losses.append(loss.item())
        out[split] = sum(losses) / len(losses)
    model.train()
    return out

model.train()
for step in range(3001):
    xb, yb = get_batch("train")
    _, loss = model(xb, yb)
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
    optimizer.step()
    scheduler.step()

    if step % 500 == 0:
        metrics = estimate_loss()
        print(f"Step {step:4d} | train loss {metrics['train']:.4f} | val loss {metrics['val']:.4f}")
  1. Generate text from the trained model
@torch.no_grad()
def generate(model, prompt, max_new_tokens=200, temperature=0.8):
    model.eval()
    idx = torch.tensor(encode(prompt), dtype=torch.long, device=device).unsqueeze(0)
    for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
        idx_cond = idx[:, -BLOCK_SIZE:]
        logits, _ = model(idx_cond)
        logits = logits[:, -1, :] / temperature
        probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
        next_tok = torch.multinomial(probs, num_samples=1)
        idx = torch.cat([idx, next_tok], dim=1)
    return decode(idx[0].tolist())

print(generate(model, prompt="\n", max_new_tokens=300))

docs.title: Expected output
docs.text:
Training for 3000 steps on a T4 GPU takes approximately 8–12 minutes. Expected loss trajectory:

  • Step 0: train loss ~4.17, val loss ~4.17 (near random for 65-class vocab: \(\ln 65 \approx 4.17\))
  • Step 500: train loss ~2.0–2.2, val loss ~2.1–2.3
  • Step 1500: train loss ~1.6–1.8, val loss ~1.7–1.9
  • Step 3000: train loss ~1.4–1.6, val loss ~1.5–1.7

Generated text at step 3000 will be recognizably Shakespearean in structure — consistent meter, character-name prefixes, plausible dialogue — though not semantically coherent. The key observation to make: the Mamba layers handle local character n-gram patterns efficiently, while the attention layers handle longer-range structural patterns like matching an opening speech tag to its closing line.

docs.title: Common failure modes
docs.text:
• ImportError: mamba_ssm not found → Mamba requires CUDA; run in Colab with GPU runtime enabled (Runtime → Change runtime type → T4 GPU). CPU-only environments will not work.
  • CUDA out of memory → Reduce batch_size from 32 to 16, or reduce BLOCK_SIZE from 256 to 128. The model itself is small; the batch is usually the culprit.
  • Loss stays at ~4.17 after 500 steps → Check that targets are shifted by one position (i.e., y = data[i+1:i+BLOCK_SIZE+1]); a common bug is passing x == y which makes the task trivial but produces no learning signal.
  • AssertionError on forward pass shape → Ensure d_model % n_heads == 0; with D_MODEL=256 and N_HEADS=8, each head has dimension 32, which is valid.
  • Mamba layer produces NaN after a few steps → Add gradient clipping (clip_grad_norm_ with max norm 1.0) before optimizer.step(); Mamba's selective scan can produce large gradients early in training.

If this build worked for you — a ⭐ on GitHub is the only signal we collect.

docs.title: Code & implementations
docs.text:
• Original Transformer (Vaswani et al.) — Harvard NLP's annotated implementation: https://nlp.seas.harvard.edu/annotated-transformer/
  • nanoGPT (Karpathy) — minimal decoder-only transformer in ~300 lines, the cleanest reference for the GPT architecture: https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT
  • Mamba official repository (Gu & Dao) — includes mamba-ssm PyPI package and reference SSM kernels; find via the arXiv paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752
  • FlashAttention (Dao et al.) — now integrated into PyTorch 2.0+ via F.scaled_dot_product_attention; official documentation at https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html
  • Hugging Face Transformers — production implementations of every major transformer variant with pretrained weights: https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers
  • Nemotron-H model weights — NVIDIA's hybrid Mamba-Transformer family on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Nemotron-H-56B-Base

docs.title: What comes next
docs.text:
Self-attention is the mechanism inside each transformer block; understanding its mathematical structure — how queries, keys, and values interact and what the attention matrix actually represents — makes the transformer's behavior interpretable rather than opaque.

  • [[self-attention]] — the atomic operation inside every transformer block; understanding its geometry explains why transformers generalize across modalities.
  • [[positional-encoding]] — the mechanism that breaks the transformer's permutation invariance; RoPE and ALiBi are the current production standards and connect directly to long-context generalization.
  • [[state-space-models]] — the linear-time alternative to attention that Mamba implements; understanding SSMs makes the hybrid architecture in the MVB above precise rather than a black box.

docs.title: Connected topics
docs.text:
• [[rlhf]] — RLHF is the standard procedure for aligning transformer-based large language models with human preferences after pretraining.
  • [[diffusion-models]] — modern diffusion models increasingly adopt transformer architectures (DiT, Stable Diffusion 3) as their primary denoising backbone.
  • [[flow-matching]] — flow matching formulations frequently utilize transformer backbones, with the same attention and feedforward structure applied to continuous generative modeling.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Vaswani et al. (2017) — "Attention Is All You Need" — https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762 — the original paper; reading the architecture section alongside the annotated implementation is the most efficient path to understanding the full model.
  • Shaw et al. (2018) — "Self-Attention with Relative Position Representations" — https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.02155 — explains why absolute position embeddings are limiting and how relative position representations fix the problem; the conceptual ancestor of RoPE.
  • Dao et al. (2022) — "FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness" — https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135 — explains the hardware-level reason attention was slow and how tiling solves it; essential for anyone deploying transformers at scale.
  • Lilian Weng — "The Transformer Family Version 2.0" (lil'log, 2023) — https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2023-01-27-the-transformer-family-v2/ — a comprehensive survey of transformer variants through 2023, covering sparse attention, linear attention, and positional encoding schemes with consistent notation.
  • Elhage et al. (2021) — "A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits" — https://transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework/index.html — introduces the residual stream perspective and shows how attention heads compose; the foundation of mechanistic interpretability research on transformers.
  • NVIDIA (2025) — "Nemotron-H: A Family of Accurate and Efficient Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Models" — available via the Hugging Face model card at https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Nemotron-H-56B-Base — the most detailed public analysis of how to optimally mix attention and SSM layers, with ablations on layer ratio, interleaving pattern, and task-specific performance.

docs.text:

# Vision Language Models
> **TL;DR:** Vision Language Models (VLMs) bridge the gap between visual and textual information, enabling machines to understand and reason about the world in a way that mirrors human comprehension.

---

## For your reader type

| I am... | Start here | Goal |
|---|---|---|
| MS/applied practitioner | [Key algorithms](#key-algorithms--techniques) → [Code & implementations](#code--implementations) | Build something that works |
| Curious generalist | [What it is](#what-it-is) → [Why it matters](#why-it-matters-at-the-frontier) | Build intuition |
| Math/theory student | [Core concepts](#core-concepts) → [Mathematical foundations](#mathematical-foundations) | Understand the mechanics |
| Researcher / frontier | [Current SotA](#current-sota) → [Seminal papers](#seminal-papers--test-of-time) | Know where the open problems are |

---

## What it is

Imagine you're trying to find a specific outfit online, but the product descriptions are vague and the images don't quite capture the details you need. Or, consider the challenge of summarizing a complex scientific paper that includes both text and figures. Vision language models are designed to solve these problems by combining the power of image understanding with the ability to process and generate human language. These models can "see" and "understand" the visual world, allowing them to answer questions, generate descriptions, and perform tasks that require both visual and textual information.

Vision language models (VLMs) are a class of deep learning models that process and understand both images and text. They leverage the power of neural networks, particularly transformers, to extract meaningful representations from visual and textual data and align them in a shared embedding space. This alignment enables the model to perform a variety of tasks, such as image captioning, visual question answering, and multimodal reasoning.

VLMs typically consist of two main components: a visual encoder (e.g., a convolutional neural network or a vision transformer) and a language model (e.g., a transformer-based language model). The visual encoder processes the image and extracts relevant features, while the language model processes the text and generates the desired output. The key challenge is to effectively fuse these two modalities, allowing the model to reason about the relationships between visual and textual information.

## Why it matters at the frontier

Vision language models are at the forefront of AI research because they enable machines to interact with the world in a more human-like way. By combining visual and textual understanding, VLMs can perform tasks that were previously impossible for machines, such as understanding the context of a scene, answering questions about images, and generating creative content based on visual prompts. This opens up new possibilities for AI in a wide range of applications, from healthcare to education to entertainment.

The development of robust and generalizable VLMs is a key priority for many research labs. One major open problem is how to develop VLMs that are truly robust to variations in visual input (e.g., lighting, occlusion, viewpoint) and that can generalize effectively to novel tasks and domains without requiring extensive fine-tuning. Addressing this challenge will require new architectures, training methods, and datasets that can capture the complexity and diversity of the real world.

## Core concepts

- **Visual Encoder** — A neural network (e.g., CNN or Vision Transformer) that extracts features from an image.
- **Language Model** — A neural network (e.g., Transformer) that processes and generates text.
- **Multimodal Embedding Space** — A shared representation space where visual and textual features are aligned.
- **Attention Mechanism** — A mechanism that allows the model to focus on the most relevant parts of the input (both image and text) when making predictions.
- **Cross-Modal Attention** — An attention mechanism that allows the model to attend to both visual and textual features simultaneously.
- **Contrastive Learning** — A training method that encourages the model to learn similar representations for semantically related images and text.
- **Image Captioning** — The task of generating a textual description of an image.
- **Visual Question Answering (VQA)** — The task of answering questions about an image.

## Mathematical foundations

\[
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V
\]

where \(Q\) is the query matrix, \(K\) is the key matrix, \(V\) is the value matrix, and \(d_k\) is the dimension of the key vectors.
This equation defines the core self-attention mechanism, calculating the weighted sum of the values based on the similarity between queries and keys.

\[
MultiHead(Q, K, V) = Concat(head_1, ..., head_h)W^O
\]

where \(head_i = Attention(QW_i^Q, KW_i^K, VW_i^V)\), where \(W_i^Q\), \(W_i^K\), \(W_i^V\) are weight matrices, and \(W^O\) is the output weight matrix.
This equation describes multi-head attention, where the attention mechanism is performed multiple times in parallel with different learned linear projections of the queries, keys, and values.

\[
LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x))
\]

where \(x\) is the input to the sublayer, and \(Sublayer(x)\) is the output of the sublayer (e.g., self-attention or feed-forward network).
This equation represents the residual connection and layer normalization, which are crucial for training deep neural networks.

\[
\text{Cross-Entropy Loss} = -\sum_{i=1}^{C} y_i \log(\hat{y}_i)
\]

where \(C\) is the number of classes, \(y_i\) is the true label (one-hot encoded), and \(\hat{y}_i\) is the predicted probability for class \(i\).
This equation is used to calculate the loss during training, measuring the difference between the predicted and actual outputs.

## Key algorithms / techniques

- **Attention Mechanism (Vaswani et al., 2017)** — Allows the model to focus on the most relevant parts of the input when making predictions.
- **Cross-Modal Attention** — Enables the model to attend to both visual and textual features simultaneously, facilitating interaction between the two modalities.
- **Contrastive Learning** — Encourages the model to learn similar representations for semantically related images and text, improving the alignment of visual and textual features.
- **Transformer Architecture** — A powerful neural network architecture that has become the foundation for many VLMs, enabling them to process and generate both images and text effectively.

## Essential reading

| Paper | Year | Authors | Why essential |
|---|---|---|---|
| Attention Is All You Need | 2017 | Vaswani et al. | This foundational paper introduced the Transformer architecture, which uses self-attention mechanisms to process sequential data, revolutionizing the field of natural language processing and influencing the development of vision language models. |
| What matters when building vision-language models? | 2024 | Li et al. | This paper investigates critical design decisions in vision-language models, such as pre-trained models, architecture, data, and training methods, and introduces Idefics2. |
| Gemini 1.5: Unlocking multimodal understanding across millions of tokens of context | 2024 | Gemini Team | This paper introduces the Gemini 1.5 family of models, which can recall and reason over fine-grained information from millions of tokens of context, including multiple long documents and hours of video and audio. |

## Seminal papers & test-of-time

| Paper | Year | Key contribution |
|---|---|---|
| Attention Is All You Need | 2017 | Introduced the Transformer architecture, which has become the foundation for many VLMs. |

## Current SotA

Gemini 1.5 achieves state-of-the-art performance on a variety of multimodal tasks, including visual question answering and image captioning (2024). Command A Vision demonstrates leading multimodal performance with open weights (2025). Idefics2 showcases competitive performance with parameter-efficient architectures across diverse tasks (2024).

## What's happening now

Research in VLMs is currently focused on improving their robustness, generalization ability, and efficiency. New architectures, training methods, and datasets are being developed to address these challenges. For example, Duvvuri et al. (2026) introduced Interleaved Head Attention, a novel approach to improve the efficiency and performance of attention mechanisms in large language models. Klein et al. (2026) introduced Tucker Attention, a generalization of approximate attention mechanisms to reduce the memory footprint of self-attention.

Engineering efforts are focused on deploying VLMs in real-world applications, such as healthcare, education, and entertainment. This involves optimizing the models for deployment on various hardware platforms, as well as developing user-friendly interfaces that allow people to interact with the models easily. AWS is actively working on fine-tuning and deploying Meta Llama 3.2 Vision for web automation at scale.

A key open problem is how to develop VLMs that can reason about the world in a more human-like way. This requires the models to understand the context of a scene, make inferences based on visual and textual information, and generate creative content that is both informative and engaging. How can we develop VLMs that are truly robust to variations in visual input and that can generalize effectively to novel tasks and domains without requiring extensive fine-tuning?

## In production

- AWS — Generating fashion product descriptions — Scalable production workflow — [https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/generating-fashion-product-descriptions-by-fine-tuning-a-vision-language-model-with-sagemaker-and-amazon-bedrock/]
- NVIDIA — VILA (Visual Language Model) — Designed for production deployment from edge to cloud — [https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/visual-language-models-on-nvidia-hardware-with-vila/]
- AWS — Fine-tuning and deploying Meta Llama 3.2 Vision for web automation — Production-oriented workflow for web automation at scale — [https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/fine-tune-and-deploy-meta-llama-3-2-vision-for-generative-ai-powered-web-automation-using-aws-dlcs-amazon-eks-and-amazon-bedrock/]

docs.title: Track 08 · Causal & Statistical Inference
docs.text:
Moving from correlation to causation: structural causal models, the do-calculus, counterfactual reasoning, and causal representation learning.

Statistical inference tells you what is associated. Causal inference tells you what would happen if you intervened. This distinction — correlation vs. causation — is one of the deepest ideas in science and increasingly central to frontier AI research.

docs.text:

  • The Do-Calculus — interventions, Pearl's do operator, identification
  • Counterfactual Reasoning — potential outcomes, counterfactual worlds, abduction-action-prediction

docs.title: Counterfactuals
docs.text: TL;DR: Counterfactuals answer "what would have happened to this specific individual under a different treatment?" — a question that population-level statistics cannot resolve, and that structural causal models make computationally precise.

docs.title: For your reader type
docs.text: I am... What you get Go to MS/applied practitioner A runnable Pyro recipe for Pearl's three-step counterfactual algorithm on synthetic patient data Key algorithms → MVB Curious generalist An intuitive explanation of why "what if?" questions are fundamentally different from "what causes?" questions What it is → Why it matters Math/theory student The formal SCM definition, the abduction-action-prediction equations, and the non-identifiability conditions Core concepts → Mathematical foundations Researcher / frontier Bounds under partial observability, diffusion-based counterfactual trajectory models, and the open scaling question Current SotA → What's happening now

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A patient is admitted to a hospital, given Drug A, and dies. The attending physician is left with a question that haunts clinical practice: would this patient have survived if they had received Drug B instead? This is not a question about populations — it is a question about a single individual, in a specific physiological state, at a specific moment. No randomized trial can answer it, because the trial would need to observe the same patient in two parallel realities simultaneously. This impossibility is what Judea Pearl calls the fundamental problem of causal inference, and it is precisely the problem that counterfactual reasoning is designed to address.

Counterfactuals occupy the highest rung of Pearl's causal hierarchy — above association ("what is correlated with survival?") and above intervention ("what happens to survival rates if we prescribe Drug B to everyone?"). A counterfactual query asks: given that we observed a specific individual receive treatment \(X = x\) and outcome \(Y = y\), what would \(Y\) have been had \(X\) been set to \(x'\) instead? The key word is given — the individual's observed history is evidence that constrains the space of possible worlds we reason over. Standard A/B testing and do-calculus interventions operate on populations and cannot condition on an individual's realized outcome; counterfactuals can, because they combine the observational record with a structural model of the data-generating process.

The machinery that makes this tractable is the Structural Causal Model (SCM). An SCM specifies, for each variable, a deterministic function of its parents and an exogenous noise term. The noise terms encode everything about the individual that the model does not explicitly represent — their genetics, their immune response, their unmeasured comorbidities. When we observe that a patient died under Drug A, we learn something about the likely values of those noise terms. Pearl's three-step algorithm — Abduction, Action, Prediction — formalizes this: first infer the noise distribution from the observation, then surgically replace the treatment in the model, then propagate forward to compute the counterfactual outcome. The result is a distribution over what would have happened, grounded in what did happen.

docs.title: Why it matters at the frontier
docs.text:
The practical stakes of counterfactual reasoning are highest wherever decisions are made about individuals rather than populations. In clinical medicine, counterfactuals underpin individualized treatment rules — the question is not "does Drug B help patients on average?" but "would Drug B have helped this patient, given everything we observed about them?" In algorithmic fairness, counterfactuals formalize the notion of discrimination: a decision is counterfactually unfair if it would have differed had the individual's protected attribute been different while everything causally upstream remained fixed. In reinforcement learning, off-policy evaluation is a counterfactual problem — estimating what return a new policy would have achieved on trajectories generated by a different policy. Frontier labs at DeepMind, Meta AI, and Microsoft Research are actively investing in counterfactual methods precisely because the move from population-level models to individual-level decisions is where the hardest unsolved problems live.

The current research frontier is defined by two tensions. The first is identifiability: counterfactuals are generally not identifiable from observational data alone without strong assumptions about the functional form of the SCM or the independence of noise terms. In non-parametric settings, the best one can do is compute sharp bounds on the counterfactual probability — a result that is theoretically clean but computationally expensive in high dimensions. The second tension is scalability: the abduction step requires posterior inference over the exogenous noise variables, which is tractable in linear-Gaussian or discrete models but becomes a hard variational inference problem in deep, continuous SCMs. Recent work on causal diffusion models and robust counterfactual bounds in Markov Decision Processes represents the field's attempt to resolve both tensions simultaneously, and neither problem is close to solved.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
• Structural Causal Model (SCM) — a tuple \(\mathcal{M} = \langle \mathbf{U}, \mathbf{V}, \mathcal{F}, P(\mathbf{U}) \rangle\) where \(\mathbf{U}\) are exogenous noise variables, \(\mathbf{V}\) are endogenous observed variables, \(\mathcal{F}\) is a set of structural equations \(V_i = f_i(\text{Pa}(V_i), U_i)\), and \(P(\mathbf{U})\) is a joint distribution over the noise.
  • Potential outcome — the value \(Y(x)\) that variable \(Y\) would take if \(X\) were set to \(x\) by intervention; in SCM terms, this is the solution to the modified model \(\mathcal{M}_x\) obtained by replacing the equation for \(X\) with the constant \(x\).
  • Abduction — the first step of Pearl's algorithm: use the observed evidence \(\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{e}\) to update the prior \(P(\mathbf{U})\) to the posterior \(P(\mathbf{U} \mid \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{e})\), capturing everything the observation tells us about the individual's latent characteristics.
  • Action — the second step: modify the SCM by replacing the structural equation for the intervened variable with a constant, producing the submodel \(\mathcal{M}_{x'}\), which represents the hypothetical world where \(X\) was set to \(x'\).
  • Prediction — the third step: propagate the posterior noise distribution \(P(\mathbf{U} \mid \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{e})\) through the modified submodel \(\mathcal{M}_{x'}\) to compute the counterfactual distribution \(P(Y_{x'} \mid \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{e})\).
  • Counterfactual identifiability — the property that the counterfactual distribution \(P(Y_x \mid \mathbf{e})\) can be uniquely computed from the observational distribution \(P(\mathbf{V})\) and the causal graph; this fails in general for non-Markovian models with hidden confounders.
  • Probability of necessity (PN) — the probability that the actual cause \(X = x\) was necessary for the observed outcome \(Y = y\), defined as \(P(Y_{x'} = y' \mid X = x, Y = y)\); a key quantity in legal and medical attribution.
  • Counterfactual bounds — tight intervals \([P^-, P^+]\) on a counterfactual probability when the SCM is not fully specified; computed using linear programming over the space of compatible joint distributions on potential outcomes.

docs.title: Mathematical foundations
docs.text:
The counterfactual quantity of interest is the distribution of \(Y\) in a world where \(X\) was set to \(x'\), conditioned on having observed \(\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{e}\):

\[ P(Y_{x'} = y \mid \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{e}) = \int P(Y = y \mid \mathbf{U} = \mathbf{u}, \text{do}(X = x')) \, dP(\mathbf{U} = \mathbf{u} \mid \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{e}) \]

where \(Y_{x'}\) is the potential outcome of \(Y\) under intervention \(\text{do}(X = x')\), \(\mathbf{U}\) is the vector of exogenous noise variables, \(\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{e}\) is the observed evidence for this individual, and \(P(\mathbf{U} \mid \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{e})\) is the posterior over noise after conditioning on the observation. This equation says that the counterfactual distribution is a mixture of deterministic model outputs, averaged over the posterior uncertainty about the individual's latent characteristics.

The abduction step computes the posterior noise distribution using Bayes' rule applied to the SCM:

\[ P(\mathbf{U} = \mathbf{u} \mid \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{e}) = \frac{P(\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{e} \mid \mathbf{U} = \mathbf{u}) \, P(\mathbf{U} = \mathbf{u})}{P(\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{e})} \]

where \(P(\mathbf{U} = \mathbf{u})\) is the prior over exogenous noise, \(P(\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{e} \mid \mathbf{U} = \mathbf{u})\) is the likelihood of the observed evidence given a specific noise realization (which is deterministic in a fully specified SCM — it is 1 if the structural equations produce \(\mathbf{e}\) from \(\mathbf{u}\) and 0 otherwise), and the denominator is the marginal likelihood. This equation says that observing an individual's outcome pins down which noise realizations are consistent with their history.

The Probability of Necessity (PN) — the probability that the actual treatment was necessary for the observed outcome — is:

\[ \text{PN} = P(Y_{x'} \neq y \mid X = x, Y = y) \]

where \(Y_{x'}\) is the counterfactual outcome under the alternative treatment \(x'\), \(X = x\) is the treatment that was actually administered, and \(Y = y\) is the outcome that was actually observed. This equation says that PN measures how often, among individuals who received \(x\) and experienced \(y\), the outcome would have been different under \(x'\) — a direct formalization of "but for" causation in law and medicine.

When the SCM is not fully identified, the sharp lower and upper bounds on a counterfactual probability \(P(Y_x = y)\) are obtained by solving:

\[ P^- = \min_{\pi \in \Pi} \sum_{\mathbf{u}} \mathbf{1}[f(\mathbf{u}, x) = y] \, \pi(\mathbf{u}), \quad P^+ = \max_{\pi \in \Pi} \sum_{\mathbf{u}} \mathbf{1}[f(\mathbf{u}, x) = y] \, \pi(\mathbf{u}) \]

where \(\pi(\mathbf{u})\) is a distribution over noise realizations, \(\Pi\) is the set of distributions consistent with the observed marginals, \(f(\mathbf{u}, x)\) is the structural equation evaluated at noise \(\mathbf{u}\) and treatment \(x\), and the indicator \(\mathbf{1}[\cdot]\) selects noise realizations that produce outcome \(y\). This equation says that the tightest possible bounds are obtained by optimizing over all noise distributions that are compatible with what we can observe, without committing to a specific parametric form.

docs.title: Key algorithms / techniques
docs.text:
• Pearl's Abduction-Action-Prediction (AAP) algorithm (Pearl, 2000) — the canonical three-step procedure for computing counterfactuals in a fully specified SCM: update the noise posterior from observations, modify the structural equations to reflect the hypothetical intervention, then propagate the posterior noise through the modified model.
  • Linear programming bounds (Balke & Pearl, 1994) — computes sharp non-parametric bounds on counterfactual probabilities by formulating the space of compatible noise distributions as a linear program; exact but exponential in the number of binary variables.
  • Variational counterfactual inference — approximates the abduction posterior \(P(\mathbf{U} \mid \mathbf{E})\) using amortized variational inference (e.g., a learned encoder), enabling counterfactual queries in deep SCMs where exact posterior computation is intractable.
  • Causal normalizing flows — parameterizes each structural equation as an invertible neural network, making abduction exact via the inverse pass and enabling gradient-based counterfactual optimization; used in models such as CAREFL (Khemakhem et al., 2021).
  • Counterfactual data augmentation (CDA) — generates counterfactual training examples by intervening on sensitive attributes in an SCM, used to debias classifiers without requiring access to a held-out counterfactual dataset.
  • Robust counterfactual bounds in MDPs — extends non-parametric bounding to sequential decision-making by computing tight intervals on counterfactual returns under model uncertainty, without assuming a specific transition model; see Buesing et al. (2019) for the foundational treatment and the 2025 extension at https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13731.
  • Causal diffusion models — uses score-based generative models to represent the joint distribution of factual and counterfactual trajectories, enabling counterfactual inference in continuous, high-dimensional, and heavily confounded time-series settings; see Sanchez et al. (2022), "Diffusion Causal Models for Counterfactual Estimation," https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.10166.
  • Potential outcome rankings (Kawakami, 2025) — frames counterfactual decision-making as a ranking problem over potential outcomes, enabling treatment selection under partial identifiability without committing to point estimates of counterfactual values; https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10776.
