docs.title: Seminal papers & test-of-time
docs.text: Paper Year Key contribution "Causality: Models, Reasoning, and Inference" (Pearl) 2000 Introduced the SCM framework and the three-rung causal hierarchy; defined counterfactuals formally within the do-calculus "Identification of Joint Interventional Distributions in Recursive Semi-Markovian Causal Models" (Shpitser & Pearl) 2006 Proved complete identification conditions for interventional and counterfactual distributions in non-Markovian graphs "Bounds on Treatment Effects from Studies with Imperfect Compliance" (Balke & Pearl) 1997 Introduced linear programming as a tool for computing sharp non-parametric counterfactual bounds; foundational for partial identification "Counterfactual Fairness" (Kusner et al.) 2017 Applied counterfactual reasoning to algorithmic fairness, defining a decision as fair iff it is invariant to counterfactual changes in protected attributes "Causal Effect Inference with Deep Latent-Variable Models" (Louizos et al.) 2017 Combined variational autoencoders with causal graphs to perform counterfactual inference from observational data with hidden confounders

docs.title: Current SotA
docs.text: The strongest results on individual-level counterfactual estimation currently come from deep SCM approaches. CAREFL (Khemakhem et al., 2021) achieves near-exact counterfactual recovery on synthetic benchmarks where the ground truth is known, using affine coupling flows as structural equations. On the IHDP benchmark for individual treatment effect estimation — a standard proxy for counterfactual accuracy — recent transformer-based causal models achieve \(\sqrt{\epsilon_{\text{PEHE}}} \approx 0.4\), compared to 0.9 for classical BART-based methods. For sequential counterfactual reasoning, the robust MDP bounds framework (see https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13731) produces intervals that are demonstrably tighter than prior Fréchet-based approaches on the standard sepsis treatment simulation benchmark, while remaining valid under arbitrary model misspecification.

docs.title: What's happening now
docs.text:
Research frontiers. The most active theoretical direction is partial identification in high-dimensional SCMs — computing sharp bounds on counterfactual quantities when the causal graph is known but the structural equations are not. Classical LP-based bounding (Balke & Pearl) is exact but scales exponentially with the number of binary variables, making it inapplicable to modern tabular or image-structured data. Recent work is exploring whether neural network function classes can be used to parameterize the space of compatible SCMs and optimize bounds via gradient descent, but convergence guarantees remain elusive. A parallel line of work asks whether large language models can serve as approximate SCMs for text-domain counterfactuals — generating "what if the patient had been younger?" narratives — though the faithfulness of these generations to any underlying causal structure is deeply unclear.

Engineering and systems. The practical bottleneck for deployed counterfactual systems is the abduction step: inferring the posterior over exogenous noise variables requires either exact inference (feasible only in small discrete or linear-Gaussian models) or variational approximation (fast but biased). Libraries such as Pyro and NumPyro have made variational counterfactual inference accessible, and the do-calculus module in causalgraphicalmodels supports exact computation for small discrete SCMs. The emerging pattern in production systems is to pre-train an amortized inference network — an encoder that maps observed individual histories to approximate noise posteriors — so that counterfactual queries at serving time are a single forward pass rather than an optimization loop. This reduces query latency from minutes to milliseconds but introduces a training-time approximation error that is difficult to bound.

Open problems. The central open question is precise: Can counterfactual distributions in non-parametric, partially observed SCMs with continuous variables be bounded in polynomial time in the number of variables, without restricting the function class of the structural equations? Current methods either assume parametric structure (making bounds non-sharp), restrict to discrete variables (making the LP tractable but the model unrealistic), or rely on variational approximations (making bounds invalid rather than conservative). A second open question concerns sequential settings: the framework at https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13731 computes valid bounds in MDPs, but the bounds widen rapidly with horizon length, making long-horizon counterfactual reasoning under uncertainty effectively uninformative. Whether tighter bounds are achievable without additional structural assumptions — such as Markovian noise or known reward structure — is unresolved.

docs.text:

  • Meta AI — applies counterfactual data augmentation in hate speech and misinformation classifiers, generating counterfactual examples by intervening on protected attributes in a learned SCM to reduce spurious correlations — ai.meta.com/research
  • Google — uses counterfactual evaluation in YouTube recommendation to estimate the causal effect of surfacing a video on long-term user satisfaction, distinguishing it from the selection effect of the existing ranker — research.google
  • Uber — employs counterfactual off-policy evaluation to estimate the revenue impact of surge pricing policies on historical trip data, avoiding the need to run live experiments for every pricing variant — eng.uber.com

docs.title: Minimum Valuable Build
docs.text:
What you're building: A Pyro structural causal model that executes Pearl's Abduction-Action-Prediction algorithm on a synthetic patient-treatment dataset, producing a posterior distribution over counterfactual survival outcomes for individual patients.

Why this build: This demonstrates the complete counterfactual pipeline end-to-end — the abduction step (posterior inference over noise), the action step (surgical graph modification), and the prediction step (forward simulation) — in a setting where the ground truth counterfactual is known, so you can verify correctness.

Stack: Python 3.10+, pyro-ppl==1.9.0, torch==2.1.0, numpy, matplotlib. Runs on CPU or free Google Colab T4.

Estimated time: 45–60 minutes.

docs.title: The recipe
docs.text:
1. Install dependencies
# In a Colab cell or terminal
!pip install pyro-ppl==1.9.0 torch==2.1.0 --quiet
  1. Define the structural causal model

The SCM encodes a simple medical scenario: a patient's severity \(S\) affects both treatment assignment \(T\) (confounding) and survival \(Y\). The exogenous noise terms \(U_S, U_T, U_Y\) are the latent individual characteristics.

import torch
import pyro
import pyro.distributions as dist
from pyro import poutine
import numpy as np

pyro.set_rng_seed(42)

def scm(intervene_T=None):
    """
    Structural Causal Model for patient treatment.

    Variables:
      U_S ~ Normal(0, 1)       — latent severity factor
      U_Y ~ Normal(0, 1)       — latent resilience factor
      S = sigmoid(U_S)         — observed severity in [0, 1]
      T ~ Bernoulli(sigmoid(S))— treatment (1=Drug B, 0=Drug A), confounded by S
      Y = sigmoid(2*T - 3*S + U_Y) > 0.5  — survival (1=survived)
    """
    # Exogenous noise variables
    U_S = pyro.sample("U_S", dist.Normal(0., 1.))
    U_Y = pyro.sample("U_Y", dist.Normal(0., 1.))

    # Endogenous variables via structural equations
    S = torch.sigmoid(U_S)
    pyro.deterministic("S", S)

    if intervene_T is None:
        # Observational: T is caused by severity S
        T = pyro.sample("T", dist.Bernoulli(torch.sigmoid(S)))
    else:
        # Interventional: do(T = intervene_T)
        T = pyro.deterministic("T", torch.tensor(float(intervene_T)))

    # Survival outcome — Drug B (T=1) helps, high severity (S) hurts
    survival_prob = torch.sigmoid(2. * T - 3. * S + U_Y)
    Y = pyro.sample("Y", dist.Bernoulli(survival_prob))

    return {"S": S, "T": T, "Y": Y, "U_S": U_S, "U_Y": U_Y}

# Sanity check: run the observational model
trace = poutine.trace(scm).get_trace()
print("Observational sample:", {k: v.value.item() for k, v in trace.nodes.items() 
                                  if k in ["S", "T", "Y"]})
  1. Generate a synthetic patient cohort and observe a specific individual
# Generate 1000 patients under the observational distribution
n_patients = 1000
records = []
for _ in range(n_patients):
    trace = poutine.trace(scm).get_trace()
    records.append({
        "S": trace.nodes["S"]["value"].item(),
        "T": trace.nodes["T"]["value"].item(),
        "Y": trace.nodes["Y"]["value"].item(),
    })

import numpy as np
records = {k: np.array([r[k] for r in records]) for k in ["S", "T", "Y"]}

# Identify a patient who received Drug A (T=0) and died (Y=0)
mask = (records["T"] == 0) & (records["Y"] == 0)
print(f"Patients who received Drug A and died: {mask.sum()}")

# Pick one such patient — this is our observed individual
# We observe their severity S and that they received T=0 and died Y=0
observed_S = float(records["S"][mask][0])
print(f"Observed patient severity: {observed_S:.3f}")
  1. Step 1 — Abduction: infer the posterior over noise given the observation
from pyro.infer import MCMC, NUTS

# Condition the model on the observed individual's data
observed_data = {
    "T": torch.tensor(0.),   # received Drug A
    "Y": torch.tensor(0.),   # died
    "S": torch.tensor(observed_S),
}

# We need to condition on S too — treat it as observed
def conditioned_scm():
    """SCM conditioned on the observed individual's factual data."""
    U_S = pyro.sample("U_S", dist.Normal(0., 1.))
    U_Y = pyro.sample("U_Y", dist.Normal(0., 1.))

    S = torch.sigmoid(U_S)
    # Condition on observed severity
    pyro.factor("S_obs", dist.Normal(S, 0.01).log_prob(observed_data["S"]))

    # Condition on observed treatment T=0 (Drug A)
    T = pyro.sample("T", dist.Bernoulli(torch.sigmoid(S)))
    pyro.factor("T_obs", dist.Bernoulli(torch.sigmoid(S)).log_prob(observed_data["T"]))

    # Condition on observed outcome Y=0 (died)
    survival_prob = torch.sigmoid(2. * T - 3. * S + U_Y)
    pyro.factor("Y_obs", dist.Bernoulli(survival_prob).log_prob(observed_data["Y"]))

# Run NUTS to get posterior samples over (U_S, U_Y)
nuts_kernel = NUTS(conditioned_scm, adapt_step_size=True)
mcmc = MCMC(nuts_kernel, num_samples=500, warmup_steps=200, num_chains=1)
mcmc.run()

posterior_samples = mcmc.get_samples()
print(f"Posterior U_S mean: {posterior_samples['U_S'].mean():.3f}")
print(f"Posterior U_Y mean: {posterior_samples['U_Y'].mean():.3f}")
print(f"Implied posterior severity: {torch.sigmoid(posterior_samples['U_S']).mean():.3f}")
  1. Step 2 — Action: modify the SCM to set do(T = 1) (Drug B)
# The action step is structural: we replace the equation for T with a constant.
# In Pyro, this is done by passing intervene_T=1 to the SCM.
# No code change needed here — the scm() function already supports this via intervene_T.
print("Action step: replacing T's structural equation with do(T=1)")
  1. Step 3 — Prediction: propagate posterior noise through the modified SCM
# For each posterior noise sample (U_S, U_Y), run the intervened SCM
counterfactual_Y = []

for i in range(len(posterior_samples["U_S"])):
    u_s = posterior_samples["U_S"][i]
    u_y = posterior_samples["U_Y"][i]

    # Replay the SCM with fixed noise and do(T=1)
    S_cf = torch.sigmoid(u_s)
    T_cf = torch.tensor(1.)  # do(T=1): Drug B
    survival_prob_cf = torch.sigmoid(2. * T_cf - 3. * S_cf + u_y)
    Y_cf = (survival_prob_cf > 0.5).float()
    counterfactual_Y.append(Y_cf.item())

counterfactual_Y = np.array(counterfactual_Y)
p_survive_drugB = counterfactual_Y.mean()
print(f"\nCounterfactual P(Y=1 | do(T=1), observed T=0, Y=0, S={observed_S:.3f})")
print(f"  = {p_survive_drugB:.3f}")
print(f"\nInterpretation: This patient would have survived with Drug B with probability {p_survive_drugB:.1%}")
  1. Compute the Probability of Necessity and visualize
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# PN = P(Y_drugB = 1 | T=0, Y=0) — already computed above
PN = p_survive_drugB
print(f"Probability of Necessity (PN): {PN:.3f}")
print(f"Drug A was necessary for this patient's death with probability {PN:.1%}")

# Compare: population-level ATE vs individual counterfactual
# ATE: E[Y | do(T=1)] - E[Y | do(T=0)] — computed by Monte Carlo
ate_samples_T1 = []
ate_samples_T0 = []
for _ in range(2000):
    trace1 = poutine.trace(lambda: scm(intervene_T=1)).get_trace()
    trace0 = poutine.trace(lambda: scm(intervene_T=0)).get_trace()
    ate_samples_T1.append(trace1.nodes["Y"]["value"].item())
    ate_samples_T0.append(trace0.nodes["Y"]["value"].item())

ATE = np.mean(ate_samples_T1) - np.mean(ate_samples_T0)
print(f"\nPopulation ATE (Drug B vs Drug A): {ATE:.3f}")
print(f"Individual counterfactual (this patient): {p_survive_drugB:.3f}")
print("→ Population ATE and individual counterfactual can diverge substantially due to confounding.")

# Plot posterior over counterfactual survival probability
survival_probs_cf = []
for i in range(len(posterior_samples["U_S"])):
    u_s = posterior_samples["U_S"][i]
    u_y = posterior_samples["U_Y"][i]
    S_cf = torch.sigmoid(u_s)
    prob = torch.sigmoid(2. * torch.tensor(1.) - 3. * S_cf + u_y).item()
    survival_probs_cf.append(prob)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
plt.hist(survival_probs_cf, bins=30, color="steelblue", edgecolor="white", alpha=0.8)
plt.axvline(np.mean(survival_probs_cf), color="red", linestyle="--", 
            label=f"Mean = {np.mean(survival_probs_cf):.2f}")
plt.xlabel("Counterfactual P(survive | Drug B)")
plt.ylabel("Posterior samples")
plt.title("Individual Counterfactual Distribution: P(Y=1 | do(T=1), observed T=0, Y=0)")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("counterfactual_posterior.png", dpi=120)
plt.show()
print("Saved: counterfactual_posterior.png")

docs.title: Expected output
docs.text:
Running the full script produces: - A printed counterfactual probability, e.g. P(Y=1 | do(T=1), observed T=0, Y=0, S=0.72) = 0.68, meaning this specific patient would have survived with 68% probability under Drug B. - A printed Probability of Necessity, e.g. PN = 0.68. - A printed ATE, typically around 0.35–0.45, demonstrating that the population-level effect and the individual counterfactual diverge substantially for high-severity patients. - A histogram (counterfactual_posterior.png) showing the posterior distribution over the counterfactual survival probability, which should be unimodal and concentrated away from 0.5 for a clearly high-severity patient.

MCMC convergence: R-hat values should be below 1.05 for both U_S and U_Y. If they are not, increase warmup_steps to 500.

docs.title: Common failure modes
docs.text:
• MCMC divergences or very low acceptance rate → The model is poorly conditioned. Add target_accept_prob=0.8 to the NUTS kernel: NUTS(conditioned_scm, adapt_step_size=True, target_accept_prob=0.8).
  • Posterior U_Y is nearly identical to the prior → The observed outcome \(Y\) is not constraining the noise. Check that observed_data["Y"] is set to torch.tensor(0.) (float, not int) and that the pyro.factor call uses the correct log-probability.
  • Counterfactual probability is always near 0.5 → The structural equation for \(Y\) is too weak. Increase the coefficient on \(T\) from 2. to 3. in the survival probability equation to make the treatment effect stronger.
  • ImportError: No module named 'pyro' → Run !pip install pyro-ppl==1.9.0 in a fresh Colab cell and restart the runtime.
  • Slow MCMC (>10 min) → Reduce num_samples to 200 and warmup_steps to 100 for a quick check; restore to 500/200 for final results.

If this build worked for you — a ⭐ on GitHub is the only signal we collect.

docs.title: What comes next
docs.text:
Counterfactual reasoning in a fully specified SCM is tractable; the hard problem is what to do when the SCM is only partially known or the graph itself is uncertain.

  • [[structural-causal-models]] — the formal framework that makes counterfactual computation possible; the structural equations and noise independence assumptions are what distinguish SCM-based counterfactuals from potential outcomes defined without a generative model.
  • [[do-calculus]] — establishes which causal and counterfactual quantities can be computed from observational data alone, and provides the graphical criteria (front-door, back-door) that determine when the abduction step is well-defined.
  • [[partial-identification]] — the natural extension when counterfactuals are not point-identified; the LP-based bounding methods that produce valid intervals rather than point estimates under model uncertainty.

docs.title: Connected topics
docs.text:
• [[bayesian-inference]] — Bayesian inference supplies the posterior update machinery that makes the abduction step tractable; the abduction equation is Bayes' rule applied to the SCM's noise variables.
  • [[reinforcement-learning-off-policy-evaluation]] — off-policy evaluation in RL is a counterfactual problem: estimating what return a new policy would have achieved on trajectories generated by a different policy.
  • [[algorithmic-fairness]] — counterfactual fairness (Kusner et al., 2017) defines discrimination in terms of whether a decision would change under a counterfactual intervention on a protected attribute, connecting SCM formalism directly to fairness auditing.
  • [[causal-representation-learning]] — learns latent SCMs from high-dimensional data, which is a prerequisite for applying counterfactual reasoning to images, text, and time-series without hand-specified structural equations.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Pearl, J. (2009) — Causality: Models, Reasoning, and Inference (2nd ed.), Cambridge University Press — the definitive reference for the SCM framework, counterfactual identifiability theory, and the three-rung causal hierarchy; Chapter 7 covers counterfactuals in full formal detail.
  • Shpitser, I. & Pearl, J. (2007) — "What Counterfactuals Can Be Tested" — https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.5294 — establishes which counterfactual statements are empirically testable from observational data, a prerequisite for any applied counterfactual system.
  • Bareinboim, E. et al. (2022) — "On Pearl's Hierarchy and the Foundations of Causal Inference" — https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.03024 — provides a rigorous modern treatment of the three-rung hierarchy, clarifying the formal separation between associational, interventional, and counterfactual queries and the conditions under which each is computable.
  • Khemakhem, I. et al. (2021) — "Causal Autoregressive Flows" — https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.02268 — introduces normalizing flows as structural equations, enabling exact abduction via invertibility and gradient-based counterfactual optimization in continuous SCMs.
  • Lilian Weng — "Causality in Machine Learning" (lil'log, 2021) — https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2021-12-31-causal-rl/ — surveys the intersection of causal inference and reinforcement learning, with a section on counterfactual off-policy evaluation that connects the SCM formalism to practical RL settings.

docs.title: Do-Calculus
docs.text: TL;DR: Do-calculus is Pearl's complete axiomatic system for transforming interventional queries — "what happens if we force X?" — into estimable statistical formulas using only observational data, making causal effect identification mathematically rigorous and algorithmically decidable.

docs.title: For your reader type
docs.text: I am... What you get Go to MS/applied practitioner A working identification engine using DoWhy that derives adjustment formulas automatically Key algorithms → MVB Curious generalist An intuition for why passive data alone cannot answer causal questions, and how do-calculus bridges that gap What it is → Why it matters Math/theory student The three formal rules with annotated notation, and the completeness theorem that makes them powerful Core concepts → Mathematical foundations Researcher / frontier Open problems in high-dimensional identification, partial observability, and connections to deep learning Current SotA → What's happening now

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Imagine trying to prove that a new lung cancer drug saves lives when you cannot ethically run a randomized controlled trial. Your observational data is hopelessly confounded: only the wealthiest, healthiest patients can afford the drug, so the people who take it would have survived longer anyway. You cannot force anyone to take or avoid the drug — you can only watch. The question is whether there exists any mathematical procedure that lets you extract the causal signal from this biased, passive record. For most of the twentieth century, the honest answer was: not in general, and not without heroic assumptions you cannot verify. Do-calculus is the framework that changed that answer.

Developed by Judea Pearl in the 1990s and formalized in its complete form by 2000, do-calculus introduces a new operator — \(do(X = x)\) — that represents a physical intervention: surgically setting a variable to a value by cutting all incoming causal arrows to it, rather than merely conditioning on observing it. The central problem is that \(P(Y \mid do(X = x))\) — the probability of outcome \(Y\) when we force \(X\) to \(x\) — is not the same as \(P(Y \mid X = x)\), the probability of \(Y\) given we observe \(X = x\). The difference is confounding. Do-calculus provides three inference rules that govern when and how you can legally rewrite expressions involving \(do\) operators into expressions involving only ordinary conditional probabilities, which are estimable from data. The rules are sound — every derivation they produce is correct — and, crucially, they are complete: if a causal effect cannot be identified using these three rules, it cannot be identified at all from the given graph structure.

What makes this practically powerful is that the rules operate on the causal graph, not on the data directly. You encode your assumptions about the data-generating process as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), and the calculus performs algebraic surgery on that graph — deleting edges, conditioning on sets of variables, swapping observations for interventions — until the interventional query is expressed purely in terms of observable distributions. The front-door criterion, the back-door criterion, and the ID algorithm are all special cases or consequences of this framework. The result is a decision procedure: given a causal graph and a query, you can determine mechanically whether the effect is identifiable and, if so, produce the exact formula for estimating it.

docs.title: Why it matters at the frontier
docs.text:
The frontier of machine learning is increasingly confronting questions that observational data alone cannot answer: does this recommendation cause engagement or merely correlate with it? Does this medical treatment cause recovery or do healthier patients self-select into it? Does this policy intervention cause economic growth or is it confounded by pre-existing conditions? These are not statistical questions — they are causal questions, and answering them requires the kind of formal framework that do-calculus provides. Major labs including DeepMind, Microsoft Research, and Amazon Science have active programs in causal machine learning precisely because production systems that optimize for observed correlations routinely fail when deployed in environments where the causal structure shifts. Do-calculus gives those programs a mathematical foundation that is both rigorous and algorithmically tractable.

The deeper frontier tension is between the expressiveness of modern deep learning and the identifiability guarantees of do-calculus. Neural networks can represent arbitrarily complex functions, but they cannot, on their own, distinguish correlation from causation. Recent work on causal representation learning — including work from Schölkopf's group at MPI-IS and Bengio's group at Mila — attempts to embed do-calculus-style reasoning into learned representations, so that models can generalize across interventional distributions rather than collapsing when the data-generating process changes. The open problem is tractability: the ID algorithm that implements do-calculus is polynomial in the number of variables for fixed graph structure, but discovering the graph itself, and scaling identification to graphs with thousands of nodes, remains an active and largely unsolved research challenge.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
• Intervention — the operation \(do(X = x)\) that sets variable \(X\) to value \(x\) by removing all incoming edges to \(X\) in the causal graph, simulating a randomized experiment.
  • Interventional distribution — the joint distribution \(P(V \mid do(X = x))\) over all variables \(V\) in the mutilated graph where \(X\)'s parents are severed; distinct from the observational conditional \(P(V \mid X = x)\).
  • Identifiability — a causal effect \(P(Y \mid do(X))\) is identifiable from a graph \(G\) if it can be uniquely computed from the observational distribution \(P(V)\) for every model consistent with \(G\).
  • Mutilated graph — the graph \(G_{\overline{X}}\) obtained by deleting all arrows into \(X\), representing the post-intervention world where \(X\) is externally controlled.
  • d-separation — a graphical criterion for reading off conditional independence relations from a DAG; the foundation on which all three rules of do-calculus rest.
  • Back-door criterion — a sufficient condition for identifiability: a set \(Z\) blocks all back-door paths from \(X\) to \(Y\) if it contains no descendant of \(X\) and d-separates \(X\) from \(Y\) in \(G_{\overline{X}}\).
  • Front-door criterion — an identifiability condition applicable when direct back-door adjustment is impossible due to unobserved confounders, using a mediating variable set \(M\) that intercepts all directed paths from \(X\) to \(Y\).
  • ID algorithm — the complete, sound algorithm (Shpitser & Pearl, 2006) that decides identifiability and returns the estimand formula for any query expressible in do-calculus.

docs.title: Mathematical foundations
docs.text:
The three rules of do-calculus operate on a causal graph \(G\) and its mutilated variants. Let \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\), and \(W\) be disjoint sets of variables. \(G_{\overline{X}}\) denotes \(G\) with all arrows into \(X\) deleted; \(G_{\underline{X}}\) denotes \(G\) with all arrows out of \(X\) deleted.

Rule 1 — Insertion/deletion of observations:

\[ P(Y \mid do(X), Z, W) = P(Y \mid do(X), W) \quad \text{if } (Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid X, W)_{G_{\overline{X}}} \]

where \(Y\), \(Z\), \(W\), \(X\) are disjoint variable sets, \(G_{\overline{X}}\) is the graph with all incoming edges to \(X\) removed, and \((Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid X, W)_{G_{\overline{X}}}\) denotes d-separation of \(Y\) and \(Z\) given \(X, W\) in that mutilated graph. This rule says that if \(Z\) carries no information about \(Y\) beyond what \(X\) and \(W\) already provide in the post-intervention world, observing \(Z\) can be freely added or dropped.

Rule 2 — Action/observation exchange:

\[ P(Y \mid do(X), do(Z), W) = P(Y \mid do(X), Z, W) \quad \text{if } (Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid X, W)_{G_{\overline{X}\,\underline{Z}}} \]

where \(G_{\overline{X}\,\underline{Z}}\) is the graph with incoming edges to \(X\) deleted and outgoing edges from \(Z\) deleted. This rule says that intervening on \(Z\) is equivalent to merely observing \(Z\) when \(Z\) is d-separated from \(Y\) given \(X, W\) in the doubly mutilated graph — the key step that converts \(do\) operators into ordinary conditionals.

Rule 3 — Insertion/deletion of actions:

\[ P(Y \mid do(X), do(Z), W) = P(Y \mid do(X), W) \quad \text{if } (Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid X, W)_{G_{\overline{X}\,\overline{Z(W)}}} \]

where \(Z(W)\) denotes the nodes of \(Z\) that are not ancestors of any node in \(W\) in \(G_{\overline{X}}\), and \(G_{\overline{X}\,\overline{Z(W)}}\) removes incoming edges to both \(X\) and that subset of \(Z\). This rule says that an intervention on \(Z\) has no effect on \(Y\) — and can be deleted — when \(Z\) is d-separated from \(Y\) in the appropriate mutilated graph.

The front-door formula — the canonical example of a non-trivial do-calculus derivation:

\[ P(Y \mid do(X)) = \sum_{m} P(M = m \mid X) \sum_{x'} P(Y \mid X = x', M = m)\, P(X = x') \]

where \(X\) is the treatment variable, \(Y\) is the outcome, \(M\) is a mediator that intercepts all directed paths from \(X\) to \(Y\), \(m\) indexes values of \(M\), and \(x'\) indexes values of \(X\) in the outer sum. This equation says that the causal effect of \(X\) on \(Y\) can be computed entirely from observational quantities — even when \(X\) and \(Y\) share an unobserved common cause — by routing the estimate through the mediator \(M\).

docs.title: Key algorithms / techniques
docs.text:
• Back-door adjustment — when a set \(Z\) satisfies the back-door criterion, the causal effect is \(P(Y \mid do(X)) = \sum_z P(Y \mid X, Z=z) P(Z=z)\); the simplest and most widely applied identification strategy.
  • Front-door adjustment — applies when unobserved confounders block back-door adjustment but a mediator set \(M\) intercepts all causal paths from \(X\) to \(Y\); derived by applying Rules 2 and 3 of do-calculus in sequence.
  • ID algorithm (Shpitser & Pearl, 2006) — a complete, sound recursive algorithm that takes a causal graph and a query \(P(Y \mid do(X))\) and either returns the unique identifying functional or reports that the effect is not identifiable; runs in polynomial time for fixed graph topology.
  • IDC algorithm (Shpitser & Pearl, 2006) — extends ID to conditional interventional distributions \(P(Y \mid do(X), Z)\), enabling identification of context-specific causal effects.
  • ADMG-based identification (Richardson & Spirtes, 2002; Ilya Shpitser et al.) — reformulates identification in acyclic directed mixed graphs (ADMGs) using fixing operators, providing a cleaner algebraic foundation for do-calculus in the presence of latent variables.
  • Causal effect estimation via propensity scores — when back-door adjustment is applicable, propensity score weighting (\(IPW\)) and doubly robust estimators implement the adjustment formula in finite samples with statistical efficiency guarantees.
  • Generalized adjustment criterion (Perković et al., 2018) — a complete graphical criterion for covariate adjustment that subsumes both back-door and front-door criteria, applicable to a broader class of graphs including those with selection bias.

docs.title: Essential reading
docs.text: Paper Year Authors Why essential "The Do-Calculus Revisited" 2012 Judea Pearl Accessible re-derivation of all three rules with worked examples; the clearest entry point to the formal system "Identification of Joint Interventional Distributions in Recursive Semi-Markovian Causal Models" 2006 Ilya Shpitser, Judea Pearl Proves completeness of do-calculus via the ID algorithm; establishes that non-identifiability is a mathematical fact, not a limitation of technique "Identification in Causal Models Represented as Acyclic Directed Mixed Graphs" 2002 Thomas Richardson, Peter Spirtes Introduces the ADMG framework that handles latent variables cleanly, extending do-calculus beyond fully observed DAGs "Complete Identification Methods for the Causal Hierarchy" 2008 Ilya Shpitser, Judea Pearl Unifies identification across all three rungs of Pearl's causal hierarchy (association, intervention, counterfactual) in a single algorithmic framework

docs.title: Seminal papers & test-of-time
docs.text: Paper Year Key contribution "Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research" — Judea Pearl 1995 Introduced do-notation and the first formal rules for causal inference from DAGs; the paper that launched the modern causal inference framework "Causality: Models, Reasoning, and Inference" — Judea Pearl 2000 Book-length treatment establishing structural causal models, do-calculus, and counterfactual reasoning as a unified theory "Identification of Causal Effects Using Instrumental Variables" — Angrist, Imbens, Rubin 1996 Showed that instrumental variable methods are a special case of the broader identifiability problem; connected econometric and graphical traditions "Equivalence of Causal Models with Latent Variables" — Verma & Pearl 1990 Established the graphical foundations (d-separation, Markov condition) that do-calculus is built on "A General Identification Condition for Causal Effects" — Tian & Pearl 2002 Derived the c-component factorization, a key technical tool used inside the ID algorithm

docs.title: Current SotA
docs.text: The ID algorithm remains the gold standard for exact identification in discrete and linear-Gaussian models, and its implementation in libraries like ananke and dowhy handles graphs with dozens of variables in milliseconds. For high-dimensional settings, Bhattacharya et al. (2022) demonstrated identification in acyclic directed mixed graphs with hundreds of nodes using the fixing operator framework, though empirical scaling beyond ~500 nodes remains an open engineering challenge. In the deep learning setting, Ahuja et al. (2023) showed that identifiability of causal representations from interventional data is achievable under sparse mechanism shift assumptions, connecting do-calculus identifiability theory to the latent variable models used in modern foundation model research.

docs.title: What's happening now
docs.text:
Research frontiers. The most active theoretical direction is extending do-calculus to settings where the causal graph itself is unknown or only partially specified. Mooij et al. and Magliacane et al. have developed methods for causal discovery under interventions, where the graph is learned jointly with the identification procedure. A parallel thread concerns partial identifiability: when a causal effect is not point-identified, can do-calculus be used to derive sharp bounds rather than failing entirely? Work by Balke and Pearl on linear programming bounds, and more recently by Duarte et al. (2023) using algebraic geometry, has made this tractable for small graphs. The deepest open question is whether there exists a complete algorithm for the partial identification problem analogous to ID for point identification.

Engineering and systems. The DoWhy library (Microsoft Research) and the ananke package (University of Pennsylvania) have made do-calculus identification accessible to practitioners without requiring manual derivation of adjustment formulas. DoWhy 0.9+ integrates the ID algorithm with automatic graph parsing from domain-specific languages, and connects identification directly to estimation via EconML's doubly robust and instrumental variable estimators. The engineering bottleneck is graph specification: users must encode causal assumptions as a DAG, and errors in that graph propagate silently into wrong estimates. Active work on sensitivity analysis — quantifying how much the estimate changes if the graph is slightly wrong — is making production deployments more robust.

Open problems. The central unsolved problem is: Can the ID algorithm, or a generalization of it, be made tractable for causal graphs with thousands of variables, where the search space over conditioning sets is exponential? Current implementations enumerate d-separation conditions explicitly, which is feasible for graphs with tens of nodes but breaks down at scale. A second open problem is: How can do-calculus be integrated with neural network function approximators so that the identification guarantees transfer to the estimated causal effect, not just the population formula? The gap between identifying the correct functional form and estimating it accurately from finite data with flexible models is not yet closed in a way that preserves the formal guarantees of the calculus.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Microsoft Research — DoWhy library, used internally for causal analysis of A/B test failures and policy evaluation across Azure and Bing; the library has been downloaded over 1 million times and underpins Microsoft's causal AI platform — https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/project/dowhy/
  • Amazon — CausalML and internal causal inference tooling for marketplace pricing and recommendation systems; Amazon Science has published on using do-calculus-based identification to deconfound recommendation feedback loops at scale — https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/
  • LinkedIn — Causal inference at scale for feed ranking and A/B testing; LinkedIn Engineering has described using back-door adjustment and instrumental variable methods (both derivable from do-calculus) to estimate the causal effect of feed interventions on engagement across 900M+ members — https://engineering.linkedin.com/blog/2023/causal-inference-at-linkedin
  • Uber — CausalML open-source library implements do-calculus-adjacent methods (meta-learners, doubly robust estimators) for heterogeneous treatment effect estimation across ride-pricing experiments — https://developer.uber.com/docs/riders/references/api/v1.2/

docs.title: Minimum Valuable Build
docs.text:
What you're building: A symbolic causal identification engine that takes a user-specified DAG with unobserved confounders, automatically applies the ID algorithm to determine identifiability, and derives the front-door adjustment formula for a synthetic smoking-cancer dataset.

Why this build: It demonstrates the complete pipeline from causal graph specification to estimand derivation to numerical estimation — the exact workflow a practitioner uses when a randomized trial is impossible and back-door adjustment fails due to hidden confounders.

Stack: dowhy==0.11.1, networkx==3.2, pandas==2.1, numpy==1.26, scikit-learn==1.4, Python 3.10. Runs on free Colab T4 or any laptop CPU — no GPU required.

Estimated time: 45 minutes end-to-end.

docs.title: The recipe
docs.text:
1. Install dependencies
!pip install dowhy==0.11.1 econml==0.15.1 networkx pandas numpy scikit-learn --quiet
  1. Generate a synthetic dataset with unobserved confounding

The data-generating process encodes the classic smoking → tar → cancer graph, where an unobserved variable (genetic predisposition) confounds both smoking and cancer directly.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

np.random.seed(42)
n = 5000

# Unobserved confounder: genetic predisposition (never in the dataset)
U = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)

# Treatment: smoking (influenced by U — confounded)
X = (0.6 * U + np.random.normal(0, 0.8, n) > 0).astype(int)

# Mediator: tar deposits (caused only by smoking — no direct path from U)
M = 0.7 * X + np.random.normal(0, 0.3, n)

# Outcome: cancer risk score (caused by tar and directly by U)
Y = 0.5 * M + 0.4 * U + np.random.normal(0, 0.5, n)

df = pd.DataFrame({"smoking": X, "tar": M, "cancer": Y})
print(df.head())
print(df.describe())

# Sanity check: naive regression is biased because U is hidden
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
naive = LinearRegression().fit(df[["smoking"]], df["cancer"])
print(f"\nNaive (biased) estimate of smoking effect: {naive.coef_[0]:.4f}")
# True causal effect is 0.7 * 0.5 = 0.35 (smoking -> tar -> cancer only)
  1. Specify the causal graph with the unobserved confounder
import dowhy
from dowhy import CausalModel

# Graph in GML format: U is the unobserved confounder between smoking and cancer
causal_graph = """
graph [
  directed 1
  node [id "smoking" label "smoking"]
  node [id "tar" label "tar"]
  node [id "cancer" label "cancer"]
  node [id "U" label "U"]
  edge [source "smoking" target "tar"]
  edge [source "tar" target "cancer"]
  edge [source "U" target "smoking"]
  edge [source "U" target "cancer"]
]
"""

model = CausalModel(
    data=df,
    treatment="smoking",
    outcome="cancer",
    graph=causal_graph,
    latent_confounders=["U"]
)

model.view_model()
print("Causal graph loaded successfully.")
  1. Identify the causal effect — let DoWhy apply do-calculus
identified_estimand = model.identify_effect(proceed_when_unidentifiable=False)
print(identified_estimand)
# DoWhy will report the front-door estimand because back-door is blocked by U
# Expected output includes: "Estimand type: nonparametric-nde" or front-door criterion
  1. Estimate the causal effect using the identified estimand
# Use the two-stage regression estimator that implements the front-door formula
estimate = model.estimate_effect(
    identified_estimand,
    method_name="frontdoor.two_stage_regression",
    method_params={
        "first_stage_model": "sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression",
        "second_stage_model": "sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression"
    }
)

print(f"\nFront-door causal effect estimate: {estimate.value:.4f}")
print(f"True causal effect (ground truth): 0.3500")
print(f"Naive (confounded) estimate was:   {naive.coef_[0]:.4f}")
  1. Run a refutation test to validate the estimate
# Placebo treatment refutation: replace treatment with random noise
# A valid causal estimate should collapse to ~0 under placebo
refute_placebo = model.refute_estimate(
    identified_estimand,
    estimate,
    method_name="placebo_treatment_refuter",
    placebo_type="permute",
    num_simulations=20
)
print(refute_placebo)

# Data subset refutation: estimate should be stable across data subsets
refute_subset = model.refute_estimate(
    identified_estimand,
    estimate,
    method_name="data_subset_refuter",
    subset_fraction=0.8,
    num_simulations=20
)
print(refute_subset)

docs.title: Expected output
docs.text: The front-door estimate should land in the range [0.32, 0.38], close to the ground truth of 0.35. The naive regression estimate will be substantially higher (typically 0.55–0.65) due to the unobserved confounder \(U\). The placebo refutation should produce an estimate near 0.00 (within two standard deviations), confirming the estimate is not an artifact of spurious correlation. The data subset refutation should show stability across subsets, with standard deviation below 0.05.

docs.title: Common failure modes
docs.text:
• IdentificationError: Effect is not identifiable → Check that the mediator tar has no direct edge from U in your graph; the front-door criterion requires the mediator to be unconfounded. If you accidentally added U → tar, the effect becomes non-identifiable.
  • KeyError: 'U' during model construction → DoWhy requires latent confounders to appear as nodes in the graph GML but not as columns in the dataframe. Ensure U is listed in latent_confounders and absent from df.
  • Front-door estimate far from 0.35 → Increase n to 10,000+; the two-stage regression estimator has high variance at small sample sizes when the first-stage \(R^2\) is low.
  • ModuleNotFoundError: econml → The two-stage regression method requires EconML. Run pip install econml==0.15.1 and restart the kernel.

If this build worked for you — a ⭐ on GitHub is the only signal we collect.

docs.title: Code & implementations
docs.text:
• DoWhy (Microsoft Research) — the primary library for do-calculus-based identification and estimation in Python; implements the ID algorithm, back-door, front-door, and instrumental variable estimands: https://github.com/py-why/dowhy
  • ananke (University of Pennsylvania, Ilya Shpitser's group) — implements identification in acyclic directed mixed graphs using the fixing operator; more theoretically complete than DoWhy for non-Markovian models: https://ananke.readthedocs.io/
  • causaleffect (R package, Carlos Cinelli) — implements the ID and IDC algorithms exactly as described in Shpitser & Pearl (2006); useful for verifying identification results symbolically: https://cran.r-project.org/package=causaleffect
  • CausalML (Uber) — implements treatment effect estimators (meta-learners, doubly robust) that correspond to back-door-adjusted estimands; production-scale Python library: https://github.com/uber/causalml

docs.title: What comes next
docs.text:
Understanding do-calculus makes the back-door and front-door criteria precise instances of a general identification theory rather than isolated tricks — the natural extension is learning when and how to apply each.

  • Backdoor Criterion — the simplest special case of do-calculus identification, applicable when a sufficient adjustment set blocks all confounding paths without invoking the full three-rule system.
  • Instrumental Variables — identification strategy for settings where neither back-door nor front-door adjustment applies; derivable as a special case of the ID algorithm when a valid instrument exists in the graph.
  • Causal Discovery — the upstream problem of learning the causal graph from data, which must be solved before do-calculus identification can be applied in practice.

docs.title: Connected topics
docs.text:
• Bayesian Inference — Do-calculus transforms causal intervention queries into observational distributions solved via Bayesian inference.
  • Agent Architectures — Do-calculus provides a formal framework for agents to reason about the effects of actions.
  • Cognitive Architectures — Causal reasoning via do-calculus is a fundamental component of human-like cognitive architectures.
  • Classical Planning — Both do-calculus and classical planning model the consequences of actions on a system's state.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Pearl, J. (2012). "The Do-Calculus Revisited." UAI 2012 Keynote. https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.4852 — A self-contained re-derivation of all three rules with worked examples and a discussion of completeness; the most accessible formal treatment of the calculus.
  • Shpitser, I. & Pearl, J. (2006). "Identification of Joint Interventional Distributions in Recursive Semi-Markovian Causal Models." AAAI 2006. https://ftp.cs.ucla.edu/pub/stat_ser/r327.pdf — The completeness proof and ID algorithm; essential for understanding why non-identifiability is a mathematical fact rather than a practical limitation.
  • Bareinboim, E. & Pearl, J. (2016). "Causal Inference and the Data-Fusion Problem." PNAS 113(27). https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1510507113 — Extends do-calculus to the data-fusion setting where multiple datasets from different interventional regimes must be combined; directly relevant to modern multi-environment learning.
  • Ilya Shpitser's lecture notes on identification theory, Johns Hopkins University. https://www.cs.jhu.edu/~ilyas/ — Graduate-level treatment of the ID algorithm, fixing operators, and partial identification; the most rigorous pedagogical resource available outside the original papers.
  • Lilian Weng, "Causal Inference" (lil'log, 2021). https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2021-12-31-causal-inference/ — A survey connecting do-calculus to modern machine learning applications including representation learning and reinforcement learning; useful for situating the calculus within the broader ML research agenda.
  • Cinelli, C., Forney, A., & Pearl, J. (2022). "A Crash Course in Good and Bad Controls." Sociological Methods & Research. https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.12721 — Practical guide to covariate selection using do-calculus principles; directly applicable to practitioners deciding which variables to include in regression or matching analyses.

# Supply Chain Management
> **TL;DR:** Supply Chain Management (SCM) is the strategic oversight of the flow of goods, information, and finances from suppliers to customers, and it's being revolutionized by AI-driven optimization and resilience strategies.

---

## For your reader type

| I am... | Start here | Goal |
|---|---|---|
| MS/applied practitioner | [Key algorithms](#key-algorithms--techniques) → [MVB](#minimum-valuable-build) | Build something that works |
| Curious generalist | [What it is](#what-it-is) → [Why it matters](#why-it-matters-at-the-frontier) | Build intuition |
| Math/theory student | [Core concepts](#core-concepts) → [Mathematical foundations](#mathematical-foundations) | Understand the mechanics |
| Researcher / frontier | [Current SotA](#current-sota) → [Seminal papers](#seminal-papers--test-of-time) | Know where the open problems are |

---

## What it is
Imagine a team of software developers, all working on the same project, but each with their own local copy of the code. Now, picture the chaos when they try to merge their changes, leading to conflicts, lost work, and endless frustration. This is where SCM comes in. SCM systems are essential for managing changes to source code over time.

In a broader sense, Supply Chain Management (SCM) encompasses the planning and management of all activities involved in sourcing and procurement, conversion, and all logistics management activities. It also includes coordination and collaboration with channel partners, which can be suppliers, intermediaries, third-party service providers, and customers. At its core, SCM integrates supply and demand management within and across companies.

The global supply chain is a multi-trillion dollar industry, yet it's often plagued by inefficiencies, vulnerabilities, and a lack of transparency. Think of a company trying to launch a new product: they face immense challenges in coordinating suppliers, manufacturing, distribution, and sales. Effective SCM is crucial for navigating these complexities, ensuring products reach consumers efficiently and cost-effectively.

## Why it matters at the frontier
SCM is no longer just about logistics; it's a strategic imperative for businesses seeking competitive advantage in a rapidly changing world. Frontier labs are focused on leveraging AI and machine learning to optimize supply chain operations, enhance resilience, and improve decision-making. This includes developing advanced forecasting models, automating warehouse operations, and creating more transparent and secure supply chain networks.

The open problem is: How can we design a decentralized, AI-driven SCM system that is resilient to adversarial attacks and can dynamically adapt to unforeseen disruptions, while maintaining data privacy and security across all participants? Addressing this requires innovations in areas like federated learning, blockchain technology, and multi-agent systems, pushing the boundaries of what's possible in SCM.

## Core concepts
- **Demand Forecasting** — Predicting future customer demand to optimize inventory levels and production schedules.
- **Inventory Management** — Balancing the costs of holding inventory with the need to meet customer demand.
- **Logistics Optimization** — Streamlining the movement of goods from suppliers to customers, minimizing costs and delivery times.
- **Supplier Relationship Management (SRM)** — Building and maintaining strong relationships with suppliers to ensure a reliable supply of materials and components.
- **Risk Management** — Identifying and mitigating potential disruptions to the supply chain, such as natural disasters or geopolitical events.
- **Blockchain Technology** — Using a distributed ledger to create a transparent and secure record of transactions across the supply chain.
- **Multi-Agent Systems (MAS)** — Employing autonomous agents to coordinate and optimize various aspects of the supply chain.

## Mathematical foundations
SCM problems often involve optimizing complex systems with multiple constraints. Linear programming, a fundamental optimization technique, can be formulated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Minimize } & c^T x \\
\text{Subject to } & Ax \leq b \\
& x \geq 0
\end{aligned}
$$
where \(c\) is the vector of cost coefficients, \(x\) is the vector of decision variables, \(A\) is the matrix of constraint coefficients, and \(b\) is the vector of constraint limits. This formulation is used to minimize a linear objective function subject to linear equality and inequality constraints.

Inventory management often uses the Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) model, which balances ordering costs and holding costs:

$$
EOQ = \sqrt{\frac{2DS}{H}}
$$
where \(D\) is the annual demand quantity, \(S\) is the cost to place one order, and \(H\) is the annual holding cost per unit. This equation helps determine the optimal order quantity to minimize total inventory costs.

## Key algorithms / techniques
- **Linear Programming (LP)** — A mathematical optimization technique used to find the best solution to a problem with linear constraints, often applied to resource allocation and scheduling in SCM.
- **Dynamic Programming (DP)** — An optimization method that breaks down a complex problem into smaller, overlapping subproblems, commonly used for inventory management and production planning.
- **Agent-Based Modeling (ABM)** — A computational modeling approach that simulates the interactions of autonomous agents to understand the behavior of complex systems, useful for analyzing supply chain dynamics.
- **Reinforcement Learning (RL)** — A machine learning technique where an agent learns to make decisions in an environment to maximize a reward, applicable to optimizing logistics and inventory control.

## Essential reading
| Paper | Year | Authors | Why essential |
|---|---|---|---|
| Communicating Sequential Processes | 1978 | Hoare | Introduces the concept of communicating sequential processes, which is essential for understanding how different actors in a supply chain coordinate. |
| Open-Source LLMs Collaboration Beats Closed-Source LLMs: A Scalable Multi-Agent System | 2025 | Tang et al. | Demonstrates how open-source LLMs can be used to optimize supply chain processes, providing a glimpse into the future of SCM. |

## Seminal papers & test-of-time
| Paper | Year | Key contribution |
|---|---|---|
| A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks | 1970 | Introduces the relational model of data, a cornerstone of database management systems, which is crucial for organizing and managing data in complex systems. |
| The Byzantine Generals Problem | 1982 | Defines the Byzantine Generals Problem, a fundamental challenge in distributed computing concerning fault tolerance and consensus in the presence of malicious actors. |

## Current SotA
Tang et al. (2025) demonstrates that SMACS, a scalable multi-agent collaboration system integrating multiple open-source LLMs, outperforms closed-source LLMs on various benchmarks. Yang et al. (2025) presents HeurAgenix, a two-stage hyper-heuristic framework powered by LLMs for solving combinatorial optimization problems, showing improved performance over existing methods. Lu et al. (2025) introduces SCaSML, a physics-informed framework that refines and debiases scientific machine learning predictions during inference by enforcing physical laws.

## What's happening now
Research frontiers in SCM are rapidly evolving, with a focus on leveraging AI and machine learning to create more resilient, efficient, and transparent supply chains. Recent advancements include the development of sophisticated forecasting models that can predict demand with greater accuracy, as well as the use of reinforcement learning to optimize logistics and inventory control. The integration of physics-informed machine learning, as demonstrated by Lu et al. (2025), is also gaining traction, enabling more reliable predictions in complex supply chain scenarios.

Engineering and systems are being transformed by the adoption of cloud-based platforms and the deployment of AI-powered automation solutions. Companies are increasingly using multi-agent systems to coordinate and optimize various aspects of the supply chain, from supplier selection to delivery route planning. Databricks' coSTAR framework exemplifies this trend, providing a means for shipping AI agents safely and efficiently.

Open problems in SCM include developing decentralized, AI-driven systems that are resilient to adversarial attacks and can dynamically adapt to unforeseen disruptions, while maintaining data privacy and security across all participants. Can we develop a self-supervised, inference-time only framework for automatic MAS design that dynamically adapts agent composition and problem decomposition to improve performance on complex tasks, while maintaining cost-efficiency? Addressing these challenges requires innovations in areas like federated learning, blockchain technology, and secure multi-party computation.

## Minimum Valuable Build
**What you're building:** A simplified agent-based simulation of a supply chain with suppliers, manufacturers, and customers.
**Why this build:** Demonstrates how different SCM strategies impact inventory levels and customer satisfaction.
**Stack:** Python 3.8+, Mesa (Agent-Based Modeling framework), NumPy, and Matplotlib.
**Estimated time:** 2-3 hours

### The recipe

1. **Install Mesa:**
   ```bash
   pip install mesa
   ```
   This installs the Mesa framework, which simplifies the creation of agent-based models.

2. **Create a Supply Chain Model:**
   ```python
   import mesa
   import numpy as np

   class Supplier(mesa.Agent):
       def __init__(self, unique_id, model, production_capacity, lead_time):
           super().__init__(unique_id, model)
           self.production_capacity = production_capacity
           self.lead_time = lead_time
           self.inventory = 0

       def step(self):
           # Replenish inventory based on demand forecast
           demand_forecast = self.model.demand_forecast
           order_quantity = min(self.production_capacity, demand_forecast)
           self.inventory += order_quantity
           print(f"Supplier {self.unique_id} produced {order_quantity}, inventory: {self.inventory}")

   class Manufacturer(mesa.Agent):
       def __init__(self, unique_id, model, processing_capacity, lead_time):
           super().__init__(unique_id, model)
           self.processing_capacity = processing_capacity
           self.lead_time = lead_time
           self.inventory = 0
           self.order_queue = 0

       def step(self):
           # Place order to supplier
           supplier = self.model.suppliers[0] # Assuming one supplier
           self.order_queue += self.model.demand_forecast
           print(f"Manufacturer {self.unique_id} ordered {self.model.demand_forecast}, queue: {self.order_queue}")

           # Process materials if available
           if supplier.inventory >= self.order_queue:
               process_quantity = min(self.processing_capacity, self.order_queue)
               self.inventory += process_quantity
               supplier.inventory -= process_quantity
               self.order_queue -= process_quantity
               print(f"Manufacturer {self.unique_id} processed {process_quantity}, inventory: {self.inventory}")
           else:
               print(f"Manufacturer {self.unique_id} waiting for materials")

   class Customer(mesa.Agent):
       def __init__(self, unique_id, model, demand_rate):
           super().__init__(unique_id, model)
           self.demand_rate = demand_rate
           self.satisfied = True

       def step(self):
           # Attempt to purchase from manufacturer
           manufacturer = self.model.manufacturers[0] # Assuming one manufacturer
           if manufacturer.inventory >= self.demand_rate:
               manufacturer.inventory -= self.demand_rate
               self.satisfied = True
               print(f"Customer {self.unique_id} purchased {self.demand_rate}, manufacturer inventory: {manufacturer.inventory}")
           else:
               self.satisfied = False
               print(f"Customer {self.unique_id} demand not satisfied")

   class SupplyChainModel(mesa.Model):
       def __init__(self, num_suppliers, num_manufacturers, num_customers, demand_forecast):
           self.num_suppliers = num_suppliers
           self.num_manufacturers = num_manufacturers
           self.num_customers = num_customers
           self.demand_forecast = demand_forecast
           self.schedule = mesa.time.SimultaneousActivation(self)

           # Create agents
           self.suppliers = [Supplier(i, self, production_capacity=50, lead_time=2) for i in range(num_suppliers)]
           self.manufacturers = [Manufacturer(i + num_suppliers, self, processing_capacity=30, lead_time=3) for i in range(num_manufacturers)]
           self.customers = [Customer(i + num_suppliers + num_manufacturers, self, demand_rate=10) for i in range(num_customers)]

           # Add agents to scheduler
           for agent in self.suppliers + self.manufacturers + self.customers:
               self.schedule.add(agent)

       def step(self):
           '''Advance the model by one step.'''
           self.schedule.step()

   # Set up the model
   num_suppliers = 1
   num_manufacturers = 1
   num_customers = 5
   demand_forecast = 20 # Example demand forecast

   model = SupplyChainModel(num_suppliers, num_manufacturers, num_customers, demand_forecast)

   # Run the simulation
   for i in range(10):
       print(f"Step {i}:")
       model.step()
   ```
   This code defines the agents (Supplier, Manufacturer, Customer) and the SupplyChainModel. Each agent has specific attributes and behaviors. The model simulates the flow of goods through the supply chain.

3. **Run the Simulation:**
   Execute the Python script. The simulation will run for 10 steps, printing the actions and inventory levels of each agent at each step.

### Expected output
The simulation will print the actions of each agent (Supplier, Manufacturer, and Customer) at each step. You should see the supplier producing goods, the manufacturer ordering and processing materials, and the customers attempting to purchase goods. The output will show how inventory levels change over time and whether customer demand is being satisfied.

### Common failure modes
- **Inventory depletion:** If the supplier's production capacity is too low or the manufacturer's processing capacity is too slow, inventory levels may drop to zero, leading to unmet customer demand. → Increase production/processing capacities or reduce demand.
- **Order queue buildup:** If the manufacturer's order queue becomes too large, it may take a long time to fulfill orders, leading to customer dissatisfaction. → Increase processing capacity or improve demand forecasting.
- **Unsatisfied customer demand:** If the manufacturer's inventory is insufficient to meet customer demand, customers will not be satisfied. → Increase production/processing capacities or improve inventory management.

docs.title: Data Parallelism
docs.text: TL;DR: Data parallelism distributes training batches across multiple GPUs and synchronizes gradients via collective communication — but as compute throughput has outpaced network bandwidth by 3–4×, the central engineering challenge has shifted from correctness to hiding communication latency behind computation.

docs.title: For your reader type
docs.text: I am... What you get Go to MS/applied practitioner A working Ring-AllReduce implementation from scratch, production patterns, FSDP configuration Key algorithms → MVB Curious generalist Why your GPU cluster sits idle half the time and what engineers do about it What it is → Why it matters Math/theory student The convergence proof for synchronous SGD, the AllReduce bandwidth formula, gradient compression bounds Core concepts → Mathematical foundations Researcher / frontier Compiler-automated overlap scheduling, FSDP2, ByteScale at 12,000 GPUs Current SotA → What's happening now

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Between NVIDIA's A100 in 2020 and the B200 in 2024, raw compute throughput grew by more than 7×. Inter-node network bandwidth, constrained by the physics of InfiniBand and Ethernet, roughly doubled over the same period. The consequence is stark: on a naively configured GPU cluster, after every backward pass, every GPU must halt and wait for all other GPUs to exchange gradients before any of them can take an optimizer step. Depending on model size and batch configuration, this synchronization barrier can consume 40–50% of total wall-clock training time. The GPUs are not slow — they are idle, waiting for packets.

Data parallelism is the strategy of splitting a training batch across \(N\) workers, each holding a complete copy of the model, computing gradients independently on their local shard, and then aggregating those gradients so every worker applies an identical parameter update. In the simplest formulation, this is embarrassingly parallel: each worker's forward and backward passes are completely independent, and only the final gradient aggregation requires coordination. The reason this works mathematically is that the gradient of a loss over a full batch is exactly the average of the gradients over each mini-batch shard — so the distributed computation is not an approximation, it is exact. This is what distinguishes data parallelism from model parallelism, where the computation itself is split and workers must exchange intermediate activations mid-forward-pass.

The engineering challenge is that "aggregate the gradients" hides enormous complexity. A naive parameter-server approach — where all workers send gradients to a central node, which averages and broadcasts them back — creates a bandwidth bottleneck at the server and does not scale beyond a few dozen workers. The solution that became standard is the Ring-AllReduce algorithm, which arranges workers in a logical ring and pipelines gradient chunks around the ring in two phases, achieving near-perfect bandwidth utilization that is independent of the number of workers. Modern frameworks like PyTorch's DistributedDataParallel (DDP) and FullyShardedDataParallel (FSDP) implement this under the hood, but understanding the primitive is essential for diagnosing the performance failures that occur at scale.

docs.title: Why it matters at the frontier
docs.text:
Every frontier language model trained in the last three years — GPT-4, Llama 3, Gemini, Mistral — was trained with data parallelism as the outermost parallelism dimension. The reason is structural: data parallelism is the only parallelism strategy that does not require modifying the model's computational graph. Tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism both require the model to be surgically partitioned, which introduces correctness constraints and communication patterns that are tightly coupled to architecture. Data parallelism composes cleanly on top of both, which is why the standard recipe for large-scale training is a 3D parallelism configuration: data parallelism across nodes, tensor parallelism within a node, and pipeline parallelism across pipeline stages. Getting the data-parallel dimension right — specifically, getting gradient synchronization to overlap with the backward pass computation — is what determines whether a cluster runs at 40% or 70% model FLOP utilization (MFU).

The frontier problem is that this overlap is currently achieved through manual developer effort: wrapping modules in DDP buckets, configuring FSDP sharding strategies, writing custom gradient hooks. As models grow more heterogeneous (mixture-of-experts, variable-length sequences, dynamic routing) and clusters grow more heterogeneous (different network topologies between nodes and within nodes), the optimal communication schedule changes dynamically during training. No existing system can synthesize this schedule automatically. This is the gap that compiler-native approaches like SimpleFSDP (2024) and ByteScale (2025) are beginning to close, and it is the central open problem in distributed training systems research.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
• Data parallelism — a distributed training strategy where each worker holds a full model replica and processes a disjoint shard of the mini-batch, with gradients averaged across workers before the optimizer step.
  • Synchronous SGD (SSGD) — the variant where all workers must complete their backward pass and exchange gradients before any worker updates parameters; mathematically equivalent to single-device training with a larger effective batch size.
  • AllReduce — a collective communication primitive that takes a tensor distributed across \(N\) workers and produces the sum (or mean) of those tensors on every worker simultaneously; the core operation in data-parallel gradient synchronization.
  • Ring-AllReduce — an implementation of AllReduce that arranges workers in a logical ring and pipelines gradient chunks in two phases (reduce-scatter then all-gather), achieving bandwidth utilization that does not degrade as \(N\) increases.
  • Gradient bucketing — the technique of grouping parameters into fixed-size buckets and launching AllReduce on a bucket as soon as all its gradients are ready, enabling communication to overlap with the backward pass for later layers.
  • Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) — an extension of data parallelism where parameters, gradients, and optimizer states are sharded across workers rather than replicated; each worker reconstructs the full layer via AllGather only when needed, reducing per-GPU memory from \(O(M)\) to \(O(M/N)\).
  • ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer) — the memory optimization framework (Rajbhandari et al., 2020) underlying FSDP, partitioned into three stages that progressively shard optimizer states, gradients, and parameters across data-parallel workers.
  • Communication-computation overlap — the scheduling technique of initiating gradient AllReduce for earlier layers while the backward pass is still computing gradients for later layers, hiding network latency behind GPU computation.

docs.title: Mathematical foundations
docs.text:
The fundamental identity that makes data parallelism exact is the linearity of the gradient over a batch. For a loss \(L\) computed over a batch \(\mathcal{B}\) of \(B\) samples split across \(N\) workers each holding \(B/N\) samples:

\[ abla_ heta L(\mathcal{B}) = rac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^{B} abla_ heta \ell(x_i, heta) = rac{1}{N} \sum_{k=1}^{N} \left( rac{1}{B/N} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}_k} abla_ heta \ell(x_i, heta) ight) \]

where \( heta\) is the parameter vector, \(\ell(x_i, heta)\) is the per-sample loss, \(\mathcal{B}_k\) is the shard of the batch assigned to worker \(k\), and \(N\) is the total number of workers. This equation says that the full-batch gradient is exactly the average of the per-shard gradients — no approximation is introduced by distributing the computation.

The Ring-AllReduce algorithm achieves the following communication volume per worker:

\[ ext{Data transferred} = 2 \cdot rac{N-1}{N} \cdot |\mathbf{g}| \]

where \(N\) is the number of workers and \(|\mathbf{g}|\) is the size of the gradient tensor in bytes. This equation says that as \(N o \infty\), each worker sends and receives approximately \(2|\mathbf{g}|\) bytes total — the communication cost per worker is bounded and does not grow with the number of workers, which is why Ring-AllReduce scales.

The convergence guarantee for synchronous SGD under standard assumptions (L-smooth, bounded variance) is:

\[ rac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \mathbb{E}\left[\| abla L( heta_t)\|^2 ight] \leq rac{2(L( heta_0) - L^*)}{\eta T} + \eta L \sigma^2 \]

where \( heta_t\) is the parameter vector at step \(t\), \(T\) is the total number of steps, \(\eta\) is the learning rate, \(L\) is the Lipschitz constant of the gradient, \(\sigma^2\) is the variance of the stochastic gradient, and \(L^*\) is the minimum loss value. This equation says that synchronous SGD converges at rate \(O(1/\sqrt{T})\) — identical to single-device SGD — confirming that distributing the batch does not degrade the optimization trajectory.

The memory savings from FSDP sharding are captured by the per-worker memory footprint:

\[ M_{ ext{FSDP}} = rac{M_ heta + M_g + M_{ ext{opt}}}{N} + M_{ ext{act}} \]

where \(M_ heta\) is the memory for parameters, \(M_g\) for gradients, \(M_{ ext{opt}}\) for optimizer states (e.g., Adam's first and second moments), \(N\) is the number of sharding workers, and \(M_{ ext{act}}\) is the activation memory which is not sharded in standard FSDP. This equation says that the three largest memory consumers scale inversely with the number of workers, while activation memory — which can dominate for long sequences — remains per-worker.

docs.title: Key algorithms / techniques
docs.text:
• Parameter Server (Dean et al., 2012) — the original distributed SGD architecture where workers push gradients to a central server that aggregates and broadcasts updates; simple to implement but creates a bandwidth bottleneck at the server that limits scaling beyond ~100 workers.
  • Ring-AllReduce (Baidu Research, 2017) — a decentralized collective that pipelines gradient chunks around a logical ring in two phases (reduce-scatter, all-gather), achieving \(O(|\mathbf{g}|)\) communication per worker independent of \(N\); the algorithm underlying NCCL and most modern distributed training.
  • Gradient Bucketing / DDP (Li et al., 2020) — PyTorch's DistributedDataParallel groups parameters into buckets and fires AllReduce on each bucket as its gradients complete during the backward pass, overlapping communication with computation for subsequent layers.
  • ZeRO Stage 1/2/3 (Rajbhandari et al., 2020) — progressively shards optimizer states (Stage 1), gradients (Stage 2), and parameters (Stage 3) across data-parallel workers, reducing per-GPU memory from \(16\Psi\) bytes (mixed precision) to \(16\Psi/N\) bytes at Stage 3.
  • Fully Sharded Data Parallel / FSDP (Zhao et al., 2023) — PyTorch's production implementation of ZeRO Stage 3, with support for mixed precision, activation checkpointing, and CPU offloading; used to train Llama 2 and Llama 3 at Meta.
  • Gradient Compression (Lin et al., 2018 — Deep Gradient Compression) — reduces AllReduce communication volume by 99.9× by transmitting only the top-0.1% of gradient values by magnitude and accumulating the rest locally; effective for bandwidth-constrained inter-node communication.
  • SimpleFSDP (2024) — a compiler-native FSDP implementation using torch.compile and DTensor that automatically generates communication-computation overlap schedules, achieving up to 68.67% throughput improvement over eager FSDP without manual bucket tuning.
  • 3D Parallelism (Narayanan et al., 2021) — the composition of data parallelism (across replica groups), tensor parallelism (within a node), and pipeline parallelism (across pipeline stages) used to train Megatron-LM scale models; data parallelism is the outermost dimension.
