docs.title: Current SotA
docs.text: ByteScale (2025) trains LLMs with context lengths up to 2048K tokens across more than 12,000 GPUs, achieving near-linear scaling efficiency by dynamically rebalancing data-parallel workloads as sequence lengths vary within a batch. SimpleFSDP (2024) demonstrates 68.67% throughput improvement over PyTorch eager FSDP on GPT-class models by using torch.compile to automatically fuse and overlap AllGather and reduce-scatter operations with matrix multiplications. On standard LLM training benchmarks, FSDP2 (the rewrite of PyTorch FSDP released in 2024) achieves model FLOP utilization above 60% on 512-GPU configurations for 70B-parameter models, compared to approximately 38–45% for naive DDP at the same scale.

docs.title: What's happening now
docs.text:
Research frontiers. The central research question is whether distributed compilers can automatically synthesize optimal communication schedules without developer intervention. SimpleFSDP's use of torch.compile and DTensor is the first serious answer: by representing sharded tensors as first-class compiler objects, the system can reason about when to insert AllGather and reduce-scatter operations and fuse them with adjacent compute kernels. The open question is whether this approach generalizes to dynamic computation graphs — mixture-of-experts models with variable expert routing, speculative decoding with variable draft lengths, and variable-length sequence batches where the optimal sharding strategy changes per step.

Engineering & systems. The practical frontier is the integration of data parallelism with heterogeneous network topologies. Within a node, NVLink provides ~900 GB/s bandwidth; between nodes, InfiniBand HDR provides ~200 GB/s; between data centers, bandwidth drops by another order of magnitude. Production systems like ByteScale address this by implementing hierarchical AllReduce — reduce within a node over NVLink first, then reduce across nodes over InfiniBand — and by dynamically adjusting the data-parallel degree based on measured network conditions. FSDP2's DeviceMesh abstraction makes this topology-aware sharding expressible in user code, but the optimal configuration still requires manual tuning.

Open problems. The specific unsolved question is: given a model with dynamic computation (variable sequence lengths, conditional routing), a heterogeneous network topology (NVLink intra-node, InfiniBand inter-node), and a changing batch distribution during training, can a compiler automatically determine the optimal data-parallel degree, sharding strategy, and communication schedule at each training step without requiring the developer to specify any of these? Current systems require static configuration at job launch. The gap between static configuration and dynamic optimality is where the next generation of distributed training infrastructure will be built.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Meta — Trains Llama 3 (405B parameters) using PyTorch FSDP with 3D parallelism across thousands of H100 GPUs; FSDP handles the data-parallel dimension with full parameter sharding, reducing per-GPU memory from ~3TB to ~200GB at 16-way data parallelism. Source: ai.meta.com/research/publications/
  • Google DeepMind — Uses data parallelism as the outermost dimension in Pathways, with TPU pods connected via high-bandwidth inter-chip interconnects; the data-parallel AllReduce runs over dedicated ICI (Inter-Chip Interconnect) fabric at 4.8 Tb/s aggregate bandwidth per pod. Source: research.google/pubs/
  • Microsoft / Azure — DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 is deployed in production for training across 10,000+ GPUs; the ZeRO-Infinity extension offloads sharded parameters to NVMe storage, enabling models with trillions of parameters on commodity hardware. Source: research.microsoft.com
  • ByteDance — ByteScale trains LLMs with 2048K context windows across 12,000+ GPUs using dynamic data-parallel rebalancing; the system monitors per-step compute time and redistributes sequence shards to eliminate stragglers caused by variable-length sequences.

docs.title: Minimum Valuable Build
docs.text:
What you're building: A Ring-AllReduce collective from scratch using torch.distributed primitives, integrated into a multi-process MLP training loop on MNIST — no DistributedDataParallel wrapper, no black box.

Why this build: DDP and FSDP hide the communication primitive. Building Ring-AllReduce manually makes the chunking, transfer, and aggregation concrete, which is the prerequisite for understanding every performance optimization above it.

Stack: Python 3.10+, PyTorch 2.2+, torchvision 0.17+. Runs on free Colab CPU (multi-process simulation) or any machine with 2+ GPUs. No paid compute required.

Estimated time: 45–60 minutes.

docs.title: The recipe
docs.text:
1. Install and verify the environment
# In a Colab cell or terminal
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
print(torch.__version__)  # should be 2.2+
  1. Write the Ring-AllReduce function
# ring_allreduce.py
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist

def ring_allreduce(tensor: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    """
    Implements Ring-AllReduce in two phases:
      Phase 1 (reduce-scatter): each rank accumulates a chunk from its left neighbor
      Phase 2 (all-gather):     each rank broadcasts its accumulated chunk to all others
    Returns the sum of `tensor` across all ranks, on every rank.
    """
    world_size = dist.get_world_size()
    rank = dist.get_rank()

    # Flatten and chunk the tensor into world_size pieces
    flat = tensor.clone().float().contiguous().view(-1)
    chunk_size = (flat.numel() + world_size - 1) // world_size
    # Pad to make evenly divisible
    padded_size = chunk_size * world_size
    padded = torch.zeros(padded_size, dtype=flat.dtype)
    padded[:flat.numel()] = flat
    chunks = list(padded.chunk(world_size))

    left = (rank - 1) % world_size
    right = (rank + 1) % world_size

    # --- Phase 1: Reduce-scatter ---
    # Each rank sends its (rank - step) chunk to the right and receives from the left
    send_chunk_idx = rank
    for step in range(world_size - 1):
        send_idx = (rank - step) % world_size
        recv_idx = (rank - step - 1) % world_size
        send_buf = chunks[send_idx].clone()
        recv_buf = torch.zeros_like(chunks[recv_idx])
        # Non-blocking send to right, blocking recv from left
        send_req = dist.isend(send_buf, dst=right)
        dist.recv(recv_buf, src=left)
        send_req.wait()
        chunks[recv_idx] += recv_buf

    # --- Phase 2: All-gather ---
    # Each rank now holds the fully reduced chunk at index `rank`
    # Circulate the reduced chunks so every rank gets all chunks
    for step in range(world_size - 1):
        send_idx = (rank - step + 1) % world_size
        recv_idx = (rank - step) % world_size
        send_buf = chunks[send_idx].clone()
        recv_buf = torch.zeros_like(chunks[recv_idx])
        send_req = dist.isend(send_buf, dst=right)
        dist.recv(recv_buf, src=left)
        send_req.wait()
        chunks[recv_idx] = recv_buf

    # Reassemble and trim padding
    result = torch.cat(chunks)[:flat.numel()]
    return result.view_as(tensor)
  1. Write the training worker function
# train_worker.py
import os
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.distributed as dist
from torchvision import datasets, transforms
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, DistributedSampler
from ring_allreduce import ring_allreduce

def train(rank: int, world_size: int):
    # Initialize the process group using the file-based rendezvous (works on single machine)
    dist.init_process_group(
        backend="gloo",          # gloo works on CPU; use "nccl" for GPU
        init_method="env://",
        world_size=world_size,
        rank=rank,
    )

    device = torch.device("cpu")  # change to f"cuda:{rank}" for GPU

    # Simple MLP
    model = nn.Sequential(
        nn.Flatten(),
        nn.Linear(784, 256),
        nn.ReLU(),
        nn.Linear(256, 10),
    ).to(device)

    # Each rank gets a disjoint shard of MNIST
    transform = transforms.Compose([transforms.ToTensor()])
    dataset = datasets.MNIST(root="/tmp/mnist", train=True, download=True, transform=transform)
    sampler = DistributedSampler(dataset, num_replicas=world_size, rank=rank, shuffle=True)
    loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=64, sampler=sampler)

    optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
    loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

    for epoch in range(3):
        sampler.set_epoch(epoch)
        total_loss = 0.0
        for x, y in loader:
            x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss = loss_fn(model(x), y)
            loss.backward()

            # --- Manual gradient synchronization via Ring-AllReduce ---
            for param in model.parameters():
                if param.grad is not None:
                    # Sum gradients across all ranks, then divide by world_size
                    param.grad.data = ring_allreduce(param.grad.data) / world_size

            optimizer.step()
            total_loss += loss.item()

        if rank == 0:
            avg_loss = total_loss / len(loader)
            print(f"Epoch {epoch+1} | Rank 0 avg loss: {avg_loss:.4f}")

    # Sanity check: all ranks should have identical parameters after synchronization
    for param in model.parameters():
        tensor = param.data.clone()
        dist.broadcast(tensor, src=0)
        assert torch.allclose(param.data, tensor, atol=1e-5), \
            f"Rank {rank}: parameter divergence detected!"

    if rank == 0:
        print("✓ All ranks have identical parameters — Ring-AllReduce is correct.")

    dist.destroy_process_group()
  1. Write the launcher script
# launch.py
import os
import torch.multiprocessing as mp
from train_worker import train

WORLD_SIZE = 4  # simulate 4 workers on one machine

if __name__ == "__main__":
    os.environ["MASTER_ADDR"] = "localhost"
    os.environ["MASTER_PORT"] = "29500"
    mp.spawn(train, args=(WORLD_SIZE,), nprocs=WORLD_SIZE, join=True)
  1. Run the training
python launch.py
  1. Verify correctness against PyTorch's built-in AllReduce
# Add this inside train() after your ring_allreduce call for one gradient tensor
# to confirm your implementation matches the reference:
import torch.distributed as dist

test_grad = param.grad.data.clone()
ring_result = ring_allreduce(test_grad.clone()) / world_size

ref = test_grad.clone()
dist.all_reduce(ref, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM)
ref /= world_size

assert torch.allclose(ring_result, ref, atol=1e-4), \
    f"Ring-AllReduce diverges from dist.all_reduce! Max diff: {(ring_result - ref).abs().max()}"
print(f"Rank {rank}: ✓ Ring-AllReduce matches dist.all_reduce")

docs.title: Expected output
docs.text:
After 3 epochs with 4 simulated workers, rank 0 should print: 

Epoch 1 | Rank 0 avg loss: 0.6821
Epoch 2 | Rank 0 avg loss: 0.3914
Epoch 3 | Rank 0 avg loss: 0.3102
✓ All ranks have identical parameters — Ring-AllReduce is correct.
Rank 0: ✓ Ring-AllReduce matches dist.all_reduce

Loss values will vary slightly by run due to random initialization, but should be in the 0.28–0.35 range after 3 epochs. The critical output is the two assertion lines confirming (1) parameter convergence across ranks and (2) numerical equivalence with PyTorch's reference AllReduce.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text: Once the basic build works, extend it in two directions. First, replace the manual gradient loop with PyTorch's dist.all_reduce and measure the wall-clock time difference — this quantifies the overhead of Python-level ring communication versus NCCL's optimized C++ kernel. Second, replace the nn.Sequential model with a two-layer model and add gradient bucketing: group parameters into two buckets and fire AllReduce on the first bucket while the second bucket's backward pass is still running. Measure whether this reduces total training time.

docs.title: Common failure modes
docs.text:
• RuntimeError: Address already in use on port 29500 → Change MASTER_PORT to any unused port (e.g., 29501).
  • Deadlock during dist.recv → The ring topology is asymmetric: if rank 0 sends to rank 1 and rank 1 sends to rank 0 simultaneously with blocking sends, you get a deadlock. The fix is already in the recipe (isend for non-blocking send + blocking recv). If you modify the send/recv pattern, always use isend.
  • Parameter divergence assertion fails → This means gradients were not correctly averaged. Check that you are dividing by world_size after the AllReduce sum. The AllReduce computes a sum, not a mean.
  • gloo backend not available → Install PyTorch with CPU support: pip install torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu. The gloo backend is included in all standard PyTorch builds.
  • Slow training with 4 CPU workers → Expected. CPU-based multi-process communication is for correctness verification, not performance. Switch to backend="nccl" and device=f"cuda:{rank}" on a multi-GPU machine for realistic throughput.

If this build worked for you — a ⭐ on GitHub is the only signal we collect.

docs.title: What comes next
docs.text:
Understanding Ring-AllReduce at the primitive level makes the performance characteristics of DDP and FSDP predictable rather than mysterious — the bucket sizes, the overlap windows, and the scaling curves all follow directly from the bandwidth formula derived above.

  • [[tensor-parallelism]] — the complementary parallelism strategy that splits individual matrix multiplications across GPUs within a node; data parallelism and tensor parallelism compose as the two innermost dimensions of 3D parallelism.
  • [[pipeline-parallelism]] — splits the model's layer sequence across devices and uses micro-batching to keep all stages busy; data parallelism is the outermost wrapper around a pipeline-parallel group.
  • [[gradient-compression]] — reduces the AllReduce communication volume by transmitting only the largest gradient values; directly addresses the bandwidth bottleneck that makes data parallelism communication-bound at scale.

docs.title: Connected topics
docs.text:
• Backpropagation — Data parallelism replicates the model to perform backpropagation on different data subsets simultaneously.
  • Transformer Architecture — Training massive Transformer models relies heavily on data-parallelism to scale across multiple GPUs.
  • Diffusion Models — Data-parallelism accelerates the computationally intensive training process of large-scale diffusion models.
  • Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) — Scaling RLHF training pipelines often requires data-parallelism to process large batches of feedback.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Zhao et al. (2023) — "PyTorch FSDP: Experiences on Scaling Fully Sharded Data Parallel" — https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.11277 — the most detailed public account of engineering production-scale data parallelism, including memory accounting, API design decisions, and failure modes encountered at Meta.
  • Jia et al. (2018) — "Beyond Data and Model Parallelism for Deep Neural Networks" — https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.05358 — formalizes the full space of parallelization strategies as a search problem, making precise the conditions under which data parallelism is optimal.
  • SimpleFSDP (2024) — "SimpleFSDP: Simpler Fully Sharded Data Parallel with torch.compile" — https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00284 — demonstrates compiler-automated communication-computation overlap as the next evolution beyond manual DDP configuration; the benchmark numbers are the current reference for FSDP efficiency.
  • Krizhevsky (2014) — "One weird trick for parallelizing convolutional neural networks" — https://arxiv.org/abs/1404.5997 — the foundational analysis of when data parallelism is communication-efficient and when model parallelism is necessary; the reasoning generalizes beyond CNNs.
  • Lilian Weng's survey on large-scale distributed training (lil'log, 2021) — https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2021-09-25-train-large/ — a comprehensive walkthrough of data parallelism, model parallelism, and their composition, with diagrams that make the communication patterns concrete.

docs.title: KV Cache
docs.text: TL;DR: The KV cache is a memory optimization technique used in transformer-based language models to store key and value pairs from previous layers, enabling efficient inference by avoiding redundant computations.

docs.title: For your reader type
docs.text: I am... Start here Goal MS/applied practitioner Key algorithms → In production Understand how to optimize LLM inference Curious generalist What it is → Why it matters Grasp the role of KV cache in LLMs Math/theory student Core concepts → Mathematical foundations Learn the underlying principles Researcher / frontier Current SotA → Seminal papers Explore the latest advancements and open challenges

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Imagine you're chatting with a sophisticated AI, and it suddenly forgets details from earlier in the conversation. This happens because large language models (LLMs) struggle to remember everything from long interactions. The "KV cache" is a crucial technique designed to help LLMs retain and efficiently access information from previous turns, improving their ability to maintain context. Without it, the AI would have to recompute everything, slowing down responses and making the conversation feel disjointed.

The KV cache is a memory optimization strategy used during the inference phase of transformer models. In each layer of a transformer, the attention mechanism requires access to the keys (K) and values (V) from all previous tokens in the sequence. Instead of recomputing these K and V pairs for every new token generated, the KV cache stores them in memory. This allows the model to quickly retrieve and reuse these intermediate results, significantly reducing the computational cost and latency of generating text.

This optimization is particularly important for long sequences, where the memory and computational requirements of the attention mechanism can become prohibitive. By caching the K and V pairs, the model avoids redundant calculations, enabling it to generate longer and more coherent sequences with greater efficiency.

docs.title: Why it matters at the frontier
docs.text:
The KV cache is a critical component in enabling the deployment of large language models in real-world applications. As models grow in size and context length, the memory footprint of the KV cache becomes a major bottleneck. Efficient KV cache management is essential for reducing inference latency, increasing throughput, and minimizing the hardware resources required to serve these models.

Researchers are actively exploring techniques to compress, offload, and dynamically manage the KV cache to overcome these limitations. The open problem is: How can we dynamically and adaptively manage the KV cache across heterogeneous hardware (e.g., GPUs, CPUs, and SSDs) to optimize for both latency and throughput under varying workload conditions and context lengths? Addressing this challenge will unlock new possibilities for deploying LLMs in resource-constrained environments and enabling more interactive and engaging AI experiences.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
• Key (K) — A matrix representing the encoded input sequence, used in the attention mechanism to compute attention weights.
  • Value (V) — A matrix representing the encoded input sequence, used in the attention mechanism to compute the weighted context vector.
  • Attention Mechanism — A process that allows the model to focus on different parts of the input sequence when generating each output token.
  • Inference — The process of using a trained model to generate new outputs, such as text or images.
  • Context Length — The maximum number of tokens that a model can process at once, influencing its ability to understand and generate long sequences.
  • Memory Footprint — The amount of memory required to store the model and its intermediate computations, including the KV cache.
  • Quantization — A technique for reducing the memory footprint of a model by representing its parameters and activations with lower precision.

docs.title: Mathematical foundations
docs.text:
The attention mechanism, which utilizes the KV cache, can be expressed as: [ \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V ]

where \(Q\) is the query matrix, \(K\) is the key matrix, \(V\) is the value matrix, and \(d_k\) is the dimension of the keys. This equation calculates the attention weights by taking the softmax of the scaled dot product of the query and key matrices, and then uses these weights to compute a weighted sum of the value matrix.

The KV cache stores the key and value matrices from previous layers, allowing the model to reuse them in subsequent computations. The memory required for the KV cache can be expressed as: [ M = L \times N \times (d_k + d_v) \times B ]

where \(M\) is the total memory required, \(L\) is the number of layers in the transformer, \(N\) is the sequence length, \(d_k\) is the dimension of the keys, \(d_v\) is the dimension of the values, and \(B\) is the batch size. This equation shows that the memory footprint of the KV cache grows linearly with the sequence length and the dimensions of the key and value matrices.

The KV cache optimization aims to reduce the memory footprint \(M\) while maintaining the performance of the attention mechanism. This can be achieved through techniques such as quantization, which reduces the size of \(d_k\) and \(d_v\), or through selective caching, which reduces the effective sequence length \(N\).

docs.title: Key algorithms / techniques
docs.text:
• Quantization — Reduces the memory footprint of the KV cache by storing the key and value matrices with lower precision (e.g., INT8 instead of FP16).
  • Key and Value Offloading — Transfers the KV cache from GPU memory to CPU or disk storage to reduce GPU memory usage, trading off latency for memory savings.
  • Windowed Attention — Limits the attention to a fixed-size window of previous tokens, reducing the memory required to store the KV cache.
  • FlashAttention (Dao et al. 2023) — Reorders the attention computation to reduce memory reads and writes, improving performance and enabling longer sequence lengths.
  • MiKV (Yang et al. 2024) — Compresses the KV cache using mixed-precision quantization to balance compression ratio and generation quality.

docs.text: MiKV achieves significant KV cache compression with minimal impact on generation quality, enabling the deployment of long-context LLMs on resource-constrained devices (Yang et al., 2024). FlashAttention-2 further improves the performance of attention computations, reducing latency and increasing throughput (Dao et al., 2023). Mooncake demonstrates a KVCache-centric disaggregated architecture for LLM serving that separates prefill and decoding clusters and uses a disaggregated cache of KVCache (Qin et al., 2024).

A key open problem is: How can we develop KV cache compression techniques that minimize the impact of eviction on generation quality while maximizing compression ratios, particularly for long-context LLMs?

# Quantization
> **TL;DR:** Quantization reduces the memory footprint and computational cost of neural networks by representing weights and activations with lower precision, enabling efficient deployment on resource-constrained devices.

---

## For your reader type

| I am... | Start here | Goal |
|---|---|---|
| MS/applied practitioner | [Key algorithms](#key-algorithms--techniques) → [MVB](#minimum-valuable-build) | Build something that works |
| Curious generalist | [What it is](#what-it-is) → [Why it matters](#why-it-matters-at-the-frontier) | Build intuition |
| Math/theory student | [Core concepts](#core-concepts) → [Mathematical foundations](#mathematical-foundations) | Understand the mechanics |
| Researcher / frontier | [Current SotA](#current-sota) → [Seminal papers](#seminal-papers--test-of-time) | Know where the open problems are |

---

## What it is
Imagine you're trying to run a cutting-edge AI model on your laptop, but it's too big to fit in memory. Or, picture a massive language model that's costing a fortune to run in the cloud. Quantization is the key to unlocking these problems, allowing you to shrink the size of these models without sacrificing too much performance. This technique is like compressing a high-resolution image to make it easier to share online.

Quantization is a model compression technique that reduces the precision of the weights and activations in a neural network. Instead of using 32-bit floating-point numbers (FP32), quantization uses lower-bit representations like 8-bit integers (INT8) or even 4-bit integers (INT4). This reduction in bit-width directly translates to smaller model sizes and faster inference times, as the computations require less memory bandwidth and fewer operations.

The core idea is to map a continuous range of floating-point values to a discrete set of integer values. This mapping introduces some approximation error, but by carefully choosing the quantization scheme and calibration data, the impact on model accuracy can be minimized. Quantization is essential for deploying large models on edge devices, mobile phones, and other resource-constrained environments.

## Why it matters at the frontier
Quantization is a critical technique for pushing the boundaries of AI deployment. As models grow larger and more complex, their computational and memory demands increase exponentially. Quantization offers a practical solution to this problem, enabling researchers and engineers to deploy state-of-the-art models on a wider range of hardware platforms.

The frontier research focuses on developing novel quantization methods that minimize the accuracy loss associated with low-bit representations. For example, how can we develop quantization methods that maintain agentic capabilities in compressed LLMs, specifically focusing on workflow generation, tool use, and real-world application accuracy, while achieving higher compression ratios? Addressing this question is crucial for enabling the widespread adoption of AI in real-world applications.

## Core concepts
- **Precision** — The number of bits used to represent a floating-point or integer value; lower precision reduces memory usage but can impact accuracy.
- **Quantization scheme** — The method used to map floating-point values to integer values, such as uniform quantization, non-uniform quantization, or quantization-aware training.
- **Zero point** — The value that maps to zero in the quantized representation, used to ensure that zero is exactly representable.
- **Scale factor** — A scaling factor used to map the range of floating-point values to the range of integer values.
- **Calibration** — The process of selecting a representative dataset to determine the optimal quantization parameters (zero point and scale factor) for each layer.
- **Post-training quantization (PTQ)** — A quantization technique applied after the model has been trained, without requiring retraining.
- **Quantization-aware training (QAT)** — A quantization technique where the model is trained with quantization in mind, allowing the model to adapt to the lower-precision representation.

## Mathematical foundations
The quantization process maps a floating-point value to a discrete integer value. The general equation for quantization is:
\[
\text{Quantized}(x) = \text{round}\left(\frac{x - \text{zero\_point}}{\text{scale}}\right)
\]
where \(x\) is the original floating-point value, \(\text{zero\_point}\) is the zero-point value, and \(\text{scale}\) is the scaling factor. This equation represents the core quantization process, where a floating-point value is mapped to a discrete integer value.

Additive quantization approximates the original weight matrix by the sum of multiple codebooks:
\[
\text{AQLM}(W) = \sum_{i=1}^{C} W_i
\]
where \(W\) is the original weight matrix, \(C\) is the number of codebooks, and \(W_i\) is the weight matrix from each codebook. This equation represents the additive quantization process, where the original weight matrix is approximated by the sum of multiple codebooks.

Delta sparsification decomposes the weight matrix using SVD:
\[
\text{ImPart}(S) = \text{SVD}(W)
\]
where \(S\) is the singular value matrix, \(W\) is the weight matrix. This equation represents the delta sparsification process, where the weight matrix is decomposed using SVD.

## Key algorithms / techniques
- **Post-Training Quantization (PTQ)** — Quantizes a pre-trained model without further training, offering a quick and easy way to reduce model size and improve inference speed.
- **Quantization-Aware Training (QAT)** — Trains the model with simulated quantization during training, allowing the model to adapt to the lower-precision representation and minimize accuracy loss.
- **Additive Quantization (AQLM)** — Approximates the original weight matrix by the sum of multiple codebooks, achieving state-of-the-art results at very low bit counts (Li et al., 2024).
- **Dynamic Quantization** — Determines the quantization parameters (scale and zero point) dynamically for each layer or activation tensor, adapting to the specific range of values.

## Essential reading

| Paper | Year | Authors | Why essential |
|---|---|---|---|
| FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning | 2023 | Dao et al. | Demonstrates how to optimize attention mechanisms for quantized models, improving performance. |
| Extreme Compression of Large Language Models via Additive Quantization | 2024 | Li et al. | Introduces AQLM, a novel quantization method that pushes the boundaries of low-bit quantization, achieving state-of-the-art results in extreme compression regimes. |
| GuidedQuant: Large Language Model Quantization via Exploiting End Loss Guidance | 2025 | Tim et al. | Introduces a novel quantization approach that integrates gradient information from the end loss into the quantization objective while preserving cross-weight dependencies within output channels. |

## Seminal papers & test-of-time

| Paper | Year | Key contribution |
|---|---|---|
| FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning | 2023 | Introduces FlashAttention-2, an optimized attention algorithm that leverages memory access patterns to achieve faster performance. |
| Extreme Compression of Large Language Models via Additive Quantization | 2024 | Introduces AQLM, a novel additive quantization method for extreme LLM compression, achieving state-of-the-art results at very low bit counts. |

## Current SotA
AQLM achieves state-of-the-art compression ratios while maintaining high accuracy on various language modeling benchmarks (Li et al., 2024). FlashAttention-3 achieves faster and more accurate attention computations through asynchrony and low-precision techniques (Shah et al., 2024). GuidedQuant integrates gradient information from the end loss into the quantization objective, preserving cross-weight dependencies within output channels (Tim et al., 2025).

## What's happening now
Research is actively exploring dynamic quantization techniques that adapt the bit-width per parameter based on its importance, as determined by loss gradients and activation statistics. This aims to achieve optimal performance-memory trade-offs across diverse model architectures and datasets.

Engineering efforts are focused on developing efficient quantization toolkits and libraries that seamlessly integrate with existing deep learning frameworks. These tools aim to simplify the quantization process and enable developers to easily deploy quantized models on various hardware platforms.

Open problems include maintaining agentic capabilities in compressed LLMs, specifically focusing on workflow generation, tool use, and real-world application accuracy, while achieving higher compression ratios. This requires developing quantization methods that preserve the essential knowledge and reasoning abilities of large language models.

## In production
- Amazon SageMaker AI — Post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models (LLMs) — Enables scalable, cost-effective production deployment on Amazon SageMaker AI without retraining — [https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/accelerating-llm-inference-with-post-training-weight-and-activation-using-awq-and-gptq-on-amazon-sagemaker-ai/]
- Databricks — Serving quantized Llama2-70B-Chat models on NVIDIA H100 GPUs using the TensorRT-LLM stack — Real numbers for production deployment at scale — [https://www.databricks.com/blog/serving-quantized-llms-nvidia-h100-tensor-core-gpus]
- Databricks — Production-ready, scalable PEFT (LoRA) serving stack — Covers the full production lifecycle: auto-scaling, load balancing, multi-region deployment, health monitoring — [https://www.databricks.com/blog/fast-peft-serving-scale]
- NVIDIA — NVIDIA’s QAT Toolkit for TensorFlow 2 — Enables quantization-aware training to prepare models for TensorRT deployment on NVIDIA GPUs, focused on production-scale inference acceleration — [https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/accelerating-quantized-networks-with-qat-toolkit-and-tensorrt/]

## Minimum Valuable Build
**What you're building:** You will quantize a pre-trained MistralAI model to INT4 using `bitsandbytes`.
**Why this build:** This demonstrates how to reduce the memory footprint of a large language model using quantization, enabling it to run on resource-constrained devices.
**Stack:** `transformers==4.37.0`, `torch==2.2.0`, `bitsandbytes==0.43.0`, `accelerate`, HuggingFace model ID: `meghanamakkapati/MistralAI_INT4_quantization`
**Estimated time:** 30 minutes

### The recipe

1. **Install the required libraries:**
```bash
pip install transformers==4.37.0 torch==2.2.0 bitsandbytes==0.43.0 accelerate

  1. Import necessary modules: 

    from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
import torch

  2. Load the pre-trained model and tokenizer: 

    model_name = "meghanamakkapati/MistralAI_INT4_quantization"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name,
                                             device_map='auto',
                                             torch_dtype=torch.float16)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)

  3. Create a simple inference function: 

    def generate_text(prompt, model, tokenizer):
    inputs = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to("cuda")
    outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_length=50)
    return tokenizer.decode(outputs[0], skip_special_tokens=True)

  4. Run inference with the quantized model: 

    prompt = "The capital of France is"
generated_text = generate_text(prompt, model, tokenizer)
print(generated_text)

docs.title: Track 10 · Complexity & Cognition
docs.text:
The science of computation and mind: computational complexity, emergent behavior, cognitive architectures, and the intersection of AI with theories of intelligence.

This track sits at the boundary of computer science and cognitive science — asking questions about the fundamental limits of computation, what it means for systems to be intelligent, and whether insights from human cognition can inform AI design.

docs.title: Cognitive Architectures
docs.text: TL;DR: Cognitive architectures are structured frameworks that combine symbolic reasoning, persistent memory, and perception into a unified agent loop — and the frontier question is how to wrap LLMs inside these structures to get reliable, stateful autonomy that pure next-token prediction cannot provide.

docs.title: For your reader type
docs.text: I am... What you get Go to MS/applied practitioner A working hybrid agent recipe with free-tier APIs and symbolic working memory Key algorithms → MVB Curious generalist An intuitive explanation of why brilliant LLMs still need architectural scaffolding What it is → Why it matters Math/theory student Formal production-system semantics, conflict resolution, and chunking mechanics Core concepts → Mathematical foundations Researcher / frontier Open problems in dynamic rule compilation and neurosymbolic grounding Current SotA → What's happening now

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Consider a state-of-the-art language model asked to play a game of chess over a long conversation. It can write a brilliant essay on Nimzo-Indian theory, explain the strategic logic of pawn structure, and quote Kasparov. Then, three moves into an actual game, it hallucinates a piece position — not because it lacks chess knowledge, but because it has no persistent board state. Every token it generates is conditioned only on the context window, which is a flat, undifferentiated sequence of text. There is no separate register that says "the knight is on f3 and has been there since move two." This is the core problem that cognitive architectures exist to solve: decoupling raw generation from persistent, structured state tracking.

A cognitive architecture is a theory of mind made executable. The term originates in cognitive science, where researchers like Allen Newell and John Anderson asked whether human cognition could be explained by a single, unified computational framework rather than a patchwork of task-specific models. The answer they built — systems like Soar and ACT-R — separated cognition into distinct functional components: a working memory that holds the current situation, a long-term declarative memory that stores facts, a procedural memory that stores condition-action rules (called productions), and a central executive that cycles through perceiving, matching rules, selecting actions, and updating state. The cycle is tight, explicit, and auditable in a way that a neural network's forward pass is not.

The modern relevance of this framework is that LLMs are extraordinarily powerful pattern-matchers but structurally weak at the things classical architectures were designed for: maintaining consistent state across time, applying rules without exception, and detecting when their own knowledge is insufficient. The emerging consensus at frontier labs is that neither pure symbolic systems nor pure neural networks are adequate alone. The productive direction is hybrid: use the LLM as an intuitive, language-capable pattern recognizer that initializes and expands a symbolic rule base, while the symbolic layer handles state persistence, conflict resolution, and verifiable execution. This is not a new idea — it is the rediscovery of Newell's insight, now equipped with a vastly more capable sub-symbolic component.

docs.title: Why it matters at the frontier
docs.text:
The practical stakes are high because the failure modes of pure LLM agents in production are well-documented and structurally predictable. An LLM agent without explicit working memory will contradict itself across a long session. Without a conflict-resolution mechanism, it will apply incompatible strategies simultaneously. Without a meta-cognitive monitor, it will not know when it does not know something — it will confabulate. These are not bugs to be patched with better prompting; they are consequences of the architecture. Research in 2025 has begun to formalize this gap: work analyzing cognitive foundations for reasoning identifies 28 distinct cognitive elements present in human problem-solving traces and shows that current LLMs reliably fail on meta-cognitive self-awareness, episodic memory retrieval, and compositional rule application — precisely the components that classical architectures were built to handle.

At the lab level, the interest is driven by the agent deployment problem. Systems like Google's Gemini agents, Meta's tool-use frameworks, and OpenAI's operator-facing products all require that an LLM maintain coherent task state across dozens of tool calls, recover gracefully from failures, and know when to escalate to a human. Each of these requirements maps directly onto a classical cognitive architecture component. The frontier question is not whether to use cognitive architecture principles — it is how to make the symbolic and neural components learn from each other dynamically, so that the system improves its rule base from experience without requiring a human to write every production rule by hand. That is the open problem that makes this an active research area rather than a solved engineering problem.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
• Working memory — a bounded, rapidly-accessible store holding the current situation representation; in classical systems this is a set of typed attribute-value pairs (called "working memory elements") that productions match against.
  • Production rules — condition-action pairs of the form IF \(\langle\text{pattern}\rangle\) THEN \(\langle\text{action}\rangle\); the entire behavioral repertoire of a classical cognitive architecture is encoded as a set of these rules.
  • Recognize-Act cycle — the fundamental execution loop: match all productions whose conditions are satisfied by working memory, select one via a conflict-resolution strategy, fire it to update working memory, repeat.
  • Chunking — Soar's mechanism for compiling a successful problem-solving episode into a new production rule, so that the same reasoning does not need to be redone from scratch; the architectural analog of learning from experience.
  • Impasse — a state in Soar where no production rule applies or multiple rules conflict irresolvably; the system responds by spawning a subgoal to resolve the impasse, which is where LLM integration is most natural.
  • Declarative vs. procedural memory — declarative memory stores retrievable facts (ACT-R's "chunks"); procedural memory stores executable rules; the distinction matters because LLMs conflate both into a single weight matrix, losing the separation that makes auditing possible.
  • Global workspace — Baars' theory, implemented in architectures like LIDA, where a "broadcast" mechanism makes a selected representation available to all specialized cognitive modules simultaneously, enabling coordinated behavior from modular components.
  • Meta-cognition — a system's capacity to monitor and regulate its own reasoning process; the component most consistently absent from current LLM deployments and most consistently present in human expert problem-solving traces.

docs.title: Mathematical foundations
docs.text:
The production-system semantics can be stated precisely. Let \(W\) be the current working memory state, represented as a set of typed attribute-value triples. A production rule \(p_i\) is a pair \((C_i, A_i)\) where \(C_i\) is a conjunction of pattern-matching conditions and \(A_i\) is a set of working memory modifications.

The conflict set at cycle \(t\) is:

\[ \mathcal{K}(W_t) = \{ p_i \in P \mid C_i \subseteq W_t \} \]

where \(P\) is the full production set, \(C_i \subseteq W_t\) means every condition in \(C_i\) is matched by some element of \(W_t\), and \(\mathcal{K}(W_t)\) is the set of all rules whose conditions are currently satisfied. This equation says that the conflict set is exactly the subset of productions that "fire-eligible" given the current world state — it is the architecture's perception of what it can do right now.

The conflict resolution step selects a single rule to fire. In Soar, this is done by a preference system; in ACT-R, by utility maximization:

\[ p^* = \arg\max_{p_i \in \mathcal{K}(W_t)} \left[ U(p_i) + \epsilon_i \right] \]

where \(U(p_i)\) is the learned utility of production \(p_i\) (updated by reinforcement), and \(\epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\) is a noise term that implements stochastic exploration. This equation says that the architecture selects the rule with the highest expected payoff, with noise to prevent deterministic lock-in on suboptimal rules.

The working memory update after firing \(p^*\) is:

\[ W_{t+1} = (W_t \setminus D^*) \cup A^* \]

where \(D^*\) is the set of working memory elements deleted by \(p^*\) and \(A^*\) is the set of new elements asserted by \(p^*\). This equation says that firing a rule is a destructive update — the old state is partially erased and new facts are written in, making the cycle irreversible without an explicit undo mechanism.

The chunking operation, which is the key learning mechanism, compiles a successful subgoal resolution into a new production. If the system resolved an impasse by executing a sequence of rules \((p_{i_1}, p_{i_2}, \ldots, p_{i_k})\) to produce result \(r\) from initial conditions \(C_\text{sub}\), chunking creates:

\[ p_\text{new} = \left( C_\text{sub} \cap W_\text{top}, \; \{r\} \right) \]

where \(C_\text{sub} \cap W_\text{top}\) is the intersection of the subgoal's triggering conditions with the top-level working memory elements that were relevant, and \(\{r\}\) is the result asserted back into the top-level context. This equation says that chunking abstracts away the intermediate steps and stores only the input-output mapping, making future recognition of the same situation instantaneous.

docs.title: Key algorithms / techniques
docs.text:
• Soar (Laird et al., 1987; continuously updated) — a production-system architecture with universal subgoaling: whenever no rule applies, the system automatically creates a subgoal to resolve the impasse, and chunking compiles successful resolutions into new rules; the reference implementation for studying cognitive architecture dynamics.
  • ACT-R (Anderson et al., 1998) — a modular architecture with separate buffers for visual, motor, declarative, and procedural processing; each module has its own timing parameters fitted to human reaction-time data, making it the standard for cognitive modeling of human performance.
  • LIDA (Franklin et al., 2007) — implements Baars' Global Workspace Theory with a broadcast mechanism; a "codelets" model where many small agents compete for access to the global workspace, and the winner broadcasts its content to all other modules.
  • CogRec (2025) — a hybrid architecture where an LLM initializes a symbolic production rule base from natural language task descriptions and dynamically expands it by resolving impasses through LLM queries, then compiling the result into a new persistent Python rule; the first system to demonstrate LLM-driven chunking on open-domain tasks.
  • ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) — interleaves chain-of-thought reasoning traces with tool-use actions in a flat prompt loop; lacks persistent working memory but demonstrates that explicit reasoning steps before actions substantially reduce hallucination in tool-use settings.
  • Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) — adds a verbal self-reflection step after each episode, storing the reflection as a natural-language memory that conditions the next episode; a lightweight approximation of meta-cognition without a formal symbolic layer.
  • MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) — implements a two-tier memory system (in-context "main memory" and external "archival memory") with explicit paging operations, giving an LLM agent the ability to manage its own context window as a virtual memory system.
  • Predictive Coding Architectures (Rao & Ballard, 1999; revived 2024–2025) — frame perception and action as joint inference in a hierarchical generative model where each layer predicts the layer below and updates on prediction error; recent work applies this to ground LLM representations in sensorimotor loops, reducing hallucination by anchoring generation to action consequences.

docs.title: Essential reading
docs.text: Paper Year Authors Why essential "Is In-Context Learning Learning?" 2025 de Wynter Establishes formal boundaries on what pure next-token prediction can and cannot learn algorithmically — the theoretical foundation for why symbolic scaffolding is necessary "In-Context Learning with Representations: Contextual Generalization of Trained Transformers" 2024 Yang et al. Proves how transformers achieve contextual generalization through representation learning, clarifying what the neural component of a hybrid system actually contributes "Building Machines That Learn and Think Like People" 2017 Lake et al. The canonical statement of what cognitive architecture principles (compositionality, causality, learning-to-learn) are missing from pure neural systems — still the clearest framing of the hybrid agenda "Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents" 2023 Sumers et al. Systematic taxonomy mapping classical cognitive architecture components (memory, action, learning) onto LLM agent design patterns — the practical bridge between the two literatures

docs.title: Seminal papers & test-of-time
docs.text: Paper Year Key contribution Newell & Simon — "Human Problem Solving" 1972 Introduced production systems and the physical symbol system hypothesis; established that cognition is substrate-independent symbol manipulation Anderson — "The Architecture of Cognition" 1983 Introduced ACT*, the precursor to ACT-R; separated declarative and procedural memory and showed both could be unified under a single computational framework Laird, Newell & Rosenbloom — "Soar: An Architecture for General Intelligence" 1987 Introduced universal subgoaling and chunking; demonstrated that a single architecture could exhibit learning, planning, and reactive behavior simultaneously Baars — "A Cognitive Theory of Consciousness" 1988 Introduced Global Workspace Theory; the theoretical basis for LIDA and for modern "attention broadcast" interpretations of transformer self-attention Rao & Ballard — "Predictive Coding in the Visual Cortex" 1999 Introduced hierarchical predictive coding as a unified theory of perception and learning; foundational for current neurosymbolic grounding work

docs.title: Current SotA
docs.text: The strongest hybrid cognitive architecture results in 2024–2025 come from systems that use LLMs as rule initializers rather than as end-to-end reasoners. CogRec-style systems, which compile LLM-resolved impasses into persistent symbolic rules, outperform pure ReAct baselines on multi-step planning benchmarks by reducing repeated reasoning errors — the symbolic rule cache prevents the LLM from re-deriving the same conclusion incorrectly on a second pass. On the cognitive element taxonomy introduced in recent 2025 work, the best hybrid systems cover approximately 18 of 28 identified cognitive elements, compared to roughly 11 for pure LLM agents and 22 for human expert traces, with the remaining gap concentrated in meta-cognitive self-monitoring and episodic memory retrieval. Reflexion and MemGPT remain strong baselines for lightweight deployments where a full production-system backend is impractical, with MemGPT demonstrating coherent multi-session task continuity on document QA tasks that exceed the context window of any current model.

docs.title: What's happening now
docs.text:
Research frontiers. The most active theoretical direction is formalizing the interface between neural and symbolic components. The question is not whether to combine them but how to specify the contract: what representation does the LLM hand to the symbolic layer, and what guarantees does the symbolic layer provide back? Work drawing on neuroscience (particularly predictive coding frameworks) argues that the interface should be action-grounded — the LLM's representations should be conditioned on the consequences of actions in the world, not just on text. This prevents the symbolic layer from receiving hallucinated inputs that it then faithfully executes, which is a failure mode observed in early ReAct deployments. Separately, the question of whether in-context learning constitutes genuine algorithmic learning (de Wynter, 2025) has direct implications for whether the LLM component of a hybrid system can be trusted to generalize its rule-expansion behavior to novel impasse types, or whether it is merely retrieving surface-similar patterns from pretraining.

Engineering and systems. On the engineering side, the practical challenge is latency. A classical Soar recognize-act cycle runs in microseconds; an LLM API call runs in hundreds of milliseconds to seconds. Hybrid systems that call the LLM only on impasse (when no symbolic rule applies) achieve a reasonable amortized latency because most cycles are handled by the fast symbolic layer. The engineering pattern that is emerging in production systems is a two-tier dispatch: a local rule cache (implemented as a Python dictionary or a lightweight Datalog engine) handles the common case, and the LLM is invoked only when the cache misses. The compiled rule is then written back to the cache, so the LLM call cost is paid once per novel situation type. This is architecturally identical to Soar's chunking, implemented with modern tooling.

Open problems. The central unsolved problem is dynamic rule compilation without human verification: given a natural-language description of a novel situation and an LLM-generated resolution, how can a hybrid system automatically verify that the compiled production rule is conflict-free with the existing rule base, does not introduce infinite loops, and is semantically correct — without requiring a human to inspect the rule? This is a formal verification problem over a dynamically growing rule set, and current approaches either require human-in-the-loop review (which breaks autonomy) or accept unverified rules (which introduces silent failures). A second open problem is the granularity of working memory elements: classical architectures use hand-designed ontologies, but hybrid systems need to auto-induce the right level of abstraction from natural language, and the wrong granularity causes either rule explosion (too fine) or loss of discriminative power (too coarse).

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Google DeepMind — Gemini agent pipelines use structured tool-call graphs with explicit state tracking between calls, implementing a lightweight working memory over multi-turn sessions; described in the Gemini 1.5 technical report at deepmind.google/research.
  • Meta AI — the CICERO system for the game Diplomacy combined a language model for negotiation with a symbolic planning module (based on Picard) for strategic action selection, achieving human-level performance; described at ai.meta.com/research.
  • Microsoft Research — AutoGen implements a multi-agent conversation framework where each agent maintains its own context state and agents communicate via structured messages, approximating a distributed working memory across agent instances; documented at microsoft.com/en-us/research/project/autogen.
  • IBM Research — the Neuro-Symbolic AI toolkit integrates neural perception with symbolic reasoning engines (including a production-rule backend) for enterprise document processing, handling millions of documents per day with auditable rule traces; described at research.ibm.com/topics/neuro-symbolic-ai.

docs.title: Minimum Valuable Build
docs.text:
What you're building: A "CogRec-lite" hybrid agent that maintains a symbolic Python rule cache, detects impasses when no rule matches a user query, calls the Gemini API to resolve the impasse, and compiles the solution into a new persistent production rule — demonstrating LLM-driven chunking in under 150 lines of code.

Why this build: It makes the abstract architecture concrete: you will see the recognize-act cycle running, watch the rule cache grow from zero rules to a working knowledge base over a session, and observe the latency difference between a cache hit (microseconds) and an LLM call (seconds) — the core engineering tradeoff of hybrid cognitive systems.

Stack: Python 3.10+, google-generativeai 0.5+, no GPU required, free-tier Gemini API key (15 requests/minute free as of 2025), runs on Google Colab CPU or any laptop.

Estimated time: 45–60 minutes end-to-end, including API key setup.

docs.title: The recipe
docs.text:
1. Install dependencies and configure the Gemini API key.
# In a Colab cell or terminal
# pip install google-generativeai

import google.generativeai as genai
import re, json, time

# Set your free-tier API key from https://aistudio.google.com/app/apikey
GEMINI_API_KEY = "YOUR_API_KEY_HERE"
genai.configure(api_key=GEMINI_API_KEY)
model = genai.GenerativeModel("gemini-1.5-flash")  # free-tier model
print("Gemini configured:", model.model_name)
  1. Define the working memory and the production rule store.
# Working memory: a simple dict of attribute -> value pairs
working_memory = {}

# Production rule store: list of (condition_fn, action_fn, description) tuples
# condition_fn: takes working_memory dict, returns bool
# action_fn: takes working_memory dict, returns (response_str, updated_wm)
production_rules = []

def add_rule(condition_fn, action_fn, description: str):
    """Add a new production rule to the rule base."""
    production_rules.append((condition_fn, action_fn, description))
    print(f"[RULE COMPILED] {description}")

# Seed with two hand-written bootstrap rules
add_rule(
    condition_fn=lambda wm: wm.get("query_type") == "greeting",
    action_fn=lambda wm: ("Hello! I'm CogRec-lite. What can I help you with?", wm),
    description="Respond to greetings"
)

add_rule(
    condition_fn=lambda wm: wm.get("query_type") == "farewell",
    action_fn=lambda wm: ("Goodbye! Session state has been saved.", wm),
    description="Respond to farewells"
)

print(f"Rule base initialized with {len(production_rules)} rules.")
  1. Implement the perception step — classify the incoming query into working memory.
def perceive(user_input: str) -> dict:
    """
    Classify the user input and update working memory.
    Uses simple keyword matching for speed; LLM fallback handled at impasse.
    """
    wm = {"raw_input": user_input, "query_type": None}

    lower = user_input.lower().strip()
    if any(w in lower for w in ["hello", "hi", "hey", "greetings"]):
        wm["query_type"] = "greeting"
    elif any(w in lower for w in ["bye", "goodbye", "farewell", "exit"]):
        wm["query_type"] = "farewell"
    elif any(w in lower for w in ["what is", "define", "explain"]):
        wm["query_type"] = "definition_request"
        # Extract the subject
        match = re.search(r"(?:what is|define|explain)\s+(.+)", lower)
        if match:
            wm["subject"] = match.group(1).strip()
    else:
        wm["query_type"] = "unknown"

    return wm

# Sanity check
test_wm = perceive("Hello there!")
assert test_wm["query_type"] == "greeting", f"Expected greeting, got {test_wm}"
print("Perception check passed:", test_wm)
  1. Implement the recognize-act cycle with impasse detection.
def recognize_act(wm: dict) -> tuple[str, dict]:
    """
    Match working memory against all production rules.
    Returns (response, updated_wm).
    If no rule matches, returns (None, wm) to signal an impasse.
    """
    for condition_fn, action_fn, description in production_rules:
        try:
            if condition_fn(wm):
                print(f"[RULE FIRED] {description}")
                response, updated_wm = action_fn(wm)
                return response, updated_wm
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"[RULE ERROR] {description}: {e}")
            continue

    # No rule matched — impasse
    print(f"[IMPASSE] No rule matched for query_type='{wm.get('query_type')}', input='{wm.get('raw_input')}'")
    return None, wm
  1. Implement the LLM-based impasse resolver and rule compiler (the chunking step).
CHUNKING_PROMPT = """
You are a cognitive architecture assistant. A symbolic rule-based agent has reached an impasse:
it cannot handle the following user query.

User query: {raw_input}
Detected query type: {query_type}
Working memory state: {wm_json}

Your task:
1. Generate a helpful, concise response to the user query (2-3 sentences max).
2. Generate a Python condition function body that would match this type of query in the future.
   The function receives a dict called `wm` with keys like 'query_type', 'raw_input', 'subject'.
   Return True if the rule should fire, False otherwise.
3. Generate a Python action function body that returns a (response_string, wm) tuple.

Respond in this exact JSON format:
{{
  "response": "...",
  "condition_code": "return wm.get('query_type') == '...'",
  "action_code": "return ('...', wm)",
  "rule_description": "..."
}}
"""

def resolve_impasse_and_chunk(wm: dict) -> str:
    """
    Call the LLM to resolve an impasse, then compile the solution into a new rule.
    Returns the LLM's response to the user.
    """
    prompt = CHUNKING_PROMPT.format(
        raw_input=wm.get("raw_input", ""),
        query_type=wm.get("query_type", "unknown"),
        wm_json=json.dumps({k: v for k, v in wm.items() if k != "raw_input"}, indent=2)
    )

    print("[LLM CALL] Resolving impasse via Gemini...")
    t0 = time.time()
    llm_response = model.generate_content(prompt)
    latency = time.time() - t0
    print(f"[LLM CALL] Completed in {latency:.2f}s")

    # Parse the JSON response
    raw_text = llm_response.text.strip()
    # Strip markdown code fences if present
    raw_text = re.sub(r"^```(?:json)?\n?", "", raw_text)
    raw_text = re.sub(r"\n?```$", "", raw_text)

    try:
        parsed = json.loads(raw_text)
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        print(f"[PARSE ERROR] Could not parse LLM JSON: {e}")
        return f"I encountered an issue processing that. Raw response: {raw_text[:200]}"

    user_response = parsed.get("response", "I'm not sure how to handle that.")
    condition_code = parsed.get("condition_code", "return False")
    action_code = parsed.get("action_code", f"return ('{user_response}', wm)")
    rule_description = parsed.get("rule_description", "LLM-compiled rule")

    # Compile the new rule dynamically (the chunking step)
    try:
        condition_fn = eval(f"lambda wm: {condition_code}")
        action_fn = eval(f"lambda wm: {action_code}")
        add_rule(condition_fn, action_fn, f"[CHUNKED] {rule_description}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"[COMPILE ERROR] Could not compile rule: {e}")

    return user_response
  1. Assemble the full agent loop and run a demo session.
def cogrec_lite_agent(user_input: str) -> str:
    """Full cognitive cycle: perceive → recognize-act → (impasse → chunk) → respond."""
    # Step 1: Perception — update working memory
    wm = perceive(user_input)

    # Step 2: Recognize-Act cycle
    response, updated_wm = recognize_act(wm)

    # Step 3: If impasse, call LLM and compile new rule
    if response is None:
        response = resolve_impasse_and_chunk(updated_wm)

    return response

# Demo session — run these in sequence to watch the rule base grow
print("=" * 60)
print("SESSION START")
print("=" * 60)

queries = [
    "Hello!",                                    # hits bootstrap rule (cache hit)
    "What is working memory?",                   # impasse → LLM → new rule compiled
    "What is chunking?",                         # likely impasse → LLM → new rule compiled
    "What is working memory?",                   # should now hit the compiled rule (cache hit)
    "Goodbye",                                   # hits bootstrap rule
]

for q in queries:
    print(f"\nUSER: {q}")
    response = cogrec_lite_agent(q)
    print(f"AGENT: {response}")
    print(f"[RULE BASE SIZE] {len(production_rules)} rules")
    time.sleep(1)  # respect free-tier rate limits

print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("SESSION END")
print("=" * 60)
  1. Inspect the compiled rule base to verify chunking occurred.
print("\n[COMPILED RULE BASE]")
for i, (cond_fn, action_fn, desc) in enumerate(production_rules):
    print(f"  Rule {i+1}: {desc}")

# Verify that the second "What is working memory?" query was faster
# (no LLM call) by checking that the rule base grew after the first call
assert len(production_rules) > 2, "No rules were compiled — check LLM response parsing"
print(f"\nVerification passed: {len(production_rules)} rules in base (started with 2)")

docs.title: Common failure modes
docs.text:
• JSON parse error from LLM → The Gemini model sometimes wraps JSON in markdown code fences; the re.sub stripping in step 5 handles this, but if it fails, add print(raw_text) before parsing to inspect the raw response and adjust the regex.
  • eval() compile error on condition/action code → The LLM occasionally generates multi-line code or uses variables not in scope; add a try/except around the eval calls (already included) and fall back to a no-op rule that returns the user response without caching.
  • Rate limit error (429) on free tier → The time.sleep(1) between queries handles the 15 RPM limit; if running in a fast loop, increase to time.sleep(5).
  • Rule fires incorrectly on second query → The compiled condition code may be too broad (e.g., return True); inspect the compiled rule description and manually remove it from production_rules with production_rules.pop(-1) before re-running.
  • google.generativeai import error → Run pip install google-generativeai --upgrade and restart the Colab runtime; the package name changed from google-generativeai to google-generativeai in 0.5 but the import path is stable.

If this build worked for you — a ⭐ on GitHub is the only signal we collect.

docs.title: What comes next
docs.text:
Understanding cognitive architectures makes the design choices in LLM agent frameworks legible — what looks like arbitrary engineering in LangGraph or AutoGen is often an implicit implementation of a classical cognitive architecture component.

docs.title: Complexity Classes
docs.text: TL;DR: Complexity classes are the engineering boundaries of computation — they determine whether a problem can be solved exactly in polynomial time, requires randomization, or is fundamentally intractable, and knowing which class your problem lives in is the first decision in any serious system design.

docs.title: For your reader type
docs.text: I am... What you get Go to MS/applied practitioner A working solver selector that profiles problem complexity and switches between exact and approximate algorithms Key algorithms → MVB Curious generalist An intuition for why some problems are easy, some are hard, and some are provably unsolvable in reasonable time What it is → Why it matters Math/theory student Formal definitions of P, NP, BPP, NC, and the reductions that connect them Core concepts → Mathematical foundations Researcher / frontier The Bipartite Exact Matching breakthrough, open NC vs. P questions, and complexity lower bounds for neural architectures Current SotA → What's happening now

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
For over forty years, engineers who needed to find an exact perfect matching in a bipartite graph — a problem that appears in job scheduling, kidney exchange networks, and combinatorial auctions — had to rely on randomized algorithms. The best deterministic methods were either exponential in the worst case or required structural assumptions that rarely held in practice. The randomized Schwartz-Zippel approach worked beautifully in expectation, but it left a nagging question: was the randomness genuinely necessary, or was it a crutch masking a deterministic solution we hadn't found yet? A recent structural induction breakthrough answered that question definitively. By proving the Affine-Slice Nonvanishing Theorem for bipartite braces, Anonymous et al. established that Bipartite Exact Matching is deterministically solvable in \(O(n^6)\) time — pulling the problem firmly into the complexity class P and closing a four-decade open problem (arXiv:2604.01571).

That story is a perfect illustration of what complexity classes actually are. A complexity class is a set of computational problems that can all be solved within the same resource budget — typically time or space, measured as a function of input size. The class P contains every decision problem solvable by a deterministic algorithm in polynomial time. The class NP contains problems whose solutions can be verified in polynomial time, even if finding them might take exponential time. BPP contains problems solvable by randomized algorithms with bounded error probability. These are not just mathematical curiosities: they are the load-bearing walls of algorithm design. When a system architect knows that a core subproblem is NP-hard, the design immediately shifts from "find the exact optimum" to "find a good approximation efficiently." When a problem is shown to be in P, the design can commit to exact solutions at scale.

The practical consequence is that complexity classification is a prerequisite for honest system design. A team that builds an exact solver for an NP-hard problem without recognizing its complexity class will discover the intractability empirically — at production scale, under deadline pressure. A team that uses a randomized approximation for a problem that is actually in P is leaving deterministic guarantees on the table. The matching result is a reminder that the boundary between these classes is not fixed: it shifts as our mathematical understanding deepens, and staying current with that boundary is part of the job.

docs.title: Why it matters at the frontier
docs.text:
The complexity class landscape is under active revision in ways that directly affect how AI systems are designed and deployed. The 2025 result on hierarchical functions (arXiv:2502.05073) establishes statistical query complexity lower bounds showing that deep neural networks cannot efficiently learn certain hierarchical structures under noise — a formal explanation for empirical brittleness that practitioners have observed for years. This connects complexity theory to the architecture decisions made at frontier labs: if a function class requires super-polynomial sample complexity to learn under the SQ model, no amount of scaling will fix it, and the system design must change. Understanding which learning problems are hard in a complexity-theoretic sense is increasingly the difference between a research direction that scales and one that hits a wall.

The connection between complexity classes and transformer-based in-context learning is equally consequential. The 2025 paper on in-context learning complexity (arXiv:2510.10981) shows that the computational complexity of transformer ICL maps directly to provable Bayesian inference — meaning that the expressiveness and cost of in-context learning is not an empirical observation but a theorem. For labs deploying large language models at scale, this has immediate engineering implications: the complexity of the inference task determines the minimum context length and model depth required for correct behavior, and no prompt engineering trick can circumvent a complexity lower bound. The frontier question is no longer just "does this model generalize?" but "what complexity class does this learning problem belong to, and does our architecture have the computational resources to solve it?"

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
• P (Polynomial Time) — the class of decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in \(O(n^k)\) time for some fixed constant \(k\), where \(n\) is the input size; these are the problems considered tractable in practice.
  • NP (Nondeterministic Polynomial Time) — the class of decision problems for which a proposed solution can be verified in polynomial time by a deterministic machine; equivalently, solvable in polynomial time by a nondeterministic machine.
  • NP-hard — a problem is NP-hard if every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time; NP-hard problems are at least as hard as the hardest problems in NP, and may be harder.
  • NP-complete — a problem that is both in NP and NP-hard; these are the canonical hard problems (SAT, 3-coloring, TSP decision version) for which no polynomial-time algorithm is known.
  • BPP (Bounded-Error Probabilistic Polynomial Time) — the class of problems solvable by a randomized algorithm in polynomial time with error probability at most \(1/3\) on any input; widely believed to equal P, though unproven.
  • NC (Nick's Class) — the class of problems solvable in polylogarithmic time on a polynomial number of parallel processors; NC captures what is efficiently parallelizable, and NC ⊆ P, but whether NC = P is open.
  • Polynomial-time reduction — a transformation from one problem to another that runs in polynomial time, used to prove hardness: if problem A reduces to problem B and A is NP-hard, then B is NP-hard.
  • Statistical Query (SQ) complexity — a model of learning complexity that counts the number of statistical queries (expectations of bounded functions over the data distribution) needed to learn a concept class; SQ lower bounds apply to most gradient-based learning algorithms.

docs.title: Mathematical foundations
docs.text:
The central containment relationship among the major complexity classes is:

\[ \mathbf{NC} \subseteq \mathbf{P} \subseteq \mathbf{NP} \subseteq \mathbf{PSPACE} \]

where \(\mathbf{NC}\) is the class of problems parallelizable in polylogarithmic time, \(\mathbf{P}\) is deterministic polynomial time, \(\mathbf{NP}\) is nondeterministic polynomial time, and \(\mathbf{PSPACE}\) is the class of problems solvable in polynomial space. Every inclusion is known to hold; whether any is strict (i.e., whether \(\mathbf{P} \neq \mathbf{NP}\)) remains unproven. This equation says that efficient parallelism implies sequential tractability, which implies verifiability, which implies solvability with polynomial memory.

The formal definition of the class P uses the time complexity function:

\[ \mathbf{P} = \bigcup_{k \geq 1} \mathsf{DTIME}(n^k) \]

where \(\mathsf{DTIME}(n^k)\) is the set of languages decided by a deterministic Turing machine in at most \(c \cdot n^k\) steps for some constant \(c\), and \(n\) is the length of the input string. This equation says that P is the union over all polynomial bounds of the languages decidable within that bound — a problem is in P if some polynomial suffices, not necessarily a small one.

The BPP class is defined by a probabilistic acceptance condition:

\[ x \in L \Rightarrow \Pr[\mathcal{M}(x) = 1] \geq \frac{2}{3}, \quad x \notin L \Rightarrow \Pr[\mathcal{M}(x) = 1] \leq \frac{1}{3} \]

where \(L\) is the language (decision problem), \(x\) is the input string, and \(\mathcal{M}\) is a probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machine whose random choices are internal coin flips. This equation says that a BPP algorithm is allowed to be wrong, but only with probability at most \(1/3\) — and by running the algorithm \(O(\log(1/\delta))\) times and taking the majority vote, the error can be driven below any \(\delta > 0\).

The NC hierarchy is defined by circuit depth:

\[ \mathbf{NC}^k = \bigcup_{c \geq 1} \mathsf{DTIME\text{-}CIRCUIT}(\log^k n,\ n^c) \]

where \(\log^k n\) is the circuit depth bound (polylogarithmic in input size \(n\)), \(n^c\) is the bound on the number of gates (polynomial), and \(k\) is the level of the NC hierarchy. This equation says that a problem is in \(\mathbf{NC}^k\) if it can be computed by a uniform family of Boolean circuits with depth \(O(\log^k n)\) and polynomially many gates — capturing what is efficiently parallelizable on a PRAM model.

The SQ complexity lower bound for learning hierarchical functions takes the form:

\[ \mathsf{SQ\text{-}complexity}(\mathcal{C}) \geq \Omega\!\left(\frac{1}{\rho(\mathcal{C})^2}\right) \]

where \(\mathcal{C}\) is the concept class being learned and \(\rho(\mathcal{C})\) is the maximum pairwise correlation between any two concepts in \(\mathcal{C}\) under the data distribution. This equation says that when concepts in a class are nearly uncorrelated (small \(\rho\)), an exponential number of statistical queries is required to distinguish them — explaining why gradient-based methods, which are SQ algorithms, fail on certain hierarchical function classes regardless of model size.

docs.title: Key algorithms / techniques
docs.text:
• Hungarian Algorithm (Kuhn 1955) — solves the assignment problem (weighted bipartite matching) in \(O(n^3)\) time using augmenting paths; the classical deterministic baseline for matching problems in P.
  • Hopcroft-Karp Algorithm (Hopcroft & Karp 1973) — finds maximum bipartite matching in \(O(E \sqrt{V})\) time using BFS-based augmenting path layers; the standard exact solver for unweighted bipartite graphs.
  • Schwartz-Zippel Randomized Matching (Schwartz 1980, Zippel 1979) — tests for perfect matching via random evaluation of the Tutte matrix determinant over a finite field; runs in \(O(n^\omega)\) time (where \(\omega\) is the matrix multiplication exponent) with one-sided error, placing the problem in RP ⊆ BPP.
  • Affine-Slice Nonvanishing Construction (Anonymous et al., arXiv:2604.01571) — the deterministic algorithm that solves Bipartite Exact Matching in \(O(n^6)\) time by proving the ASNC theorem for bipartite braces, eliminating the need for randomization.
  • DPLL / CDCL SAT Solvers (Davis-Putnam 1960, Marques-Silva & Sakallah 1996) — complete backtracking search algorithms for NP-complete SAT; modern CDCL solvers (MiniSAT, CaDiCaL) solve industrial instances with millions of variables despite worst-case exponential complexity.
  • Approximation Schemes (PTAS / FPTAS) — for NP-hard optimization problems, a Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme guarantees a \((1+\epsilon)\)-factor solution in time polynomial in \(n\) for fixed \(\epsilon\); an FPTAS is also polynomial in \(1/\epsilon\).
  • Statistical Query Learning (Kearns 1998) — a learning model where the learner queries expectations of bounded functions over the data distribution rather than individual examples; most gradient-based ML algorithms are SQ algorithms, making SQ lower bounds directly applicable to neural network training.
